$\frac{5 x \left(x - 7\right) + 25 \left(x + 5\right) - 300}{\left(x + 5\right) \left(x - 7\right)}$

> *Expand the brackets in the numerator.*

$\frac{5 x^{2} - 35 x + 25 x + 125 - 300}{\left(x + 5\right) \left(x - 7\right)}$

**[1]**

> *Collect "like" terms in the numerator.*

$\frac{5 x^{2} - 10 x - 175}{\left(x + 5\right) \left(x - 7\right)}$

**[1]**

> *The numerator factorises.  Taking a factor of 5 out first will make the (remaining) quadratic easier to deal with.*

$\frac{5 \left(x^{2} - 2 x - 35\right)}{\left(x + 5\right) \left(x - 7\right)} = \frac{5 \left(x - 7\right) \left(x + 5\right)}{\left(x + 5\right) \left(x - 7\right)}$

**[1]**

> *There are now factors of (**x** - 7) and (**x** + 5) on both the numerator and the denominator, so these cancel.*

$\frac{5 \cancel{\left(x - 7\right)} \bcancel{\left(x + 5\right)}}{\bcancel{\left(x + 5\right)} \cancel{\left(x - 7\right)}} = 5$

$\therefore\frac{5x}{x+5}+\frac{25}{x-7}-\frac{300}{(x+5)(x-7)}=5$* ***[1***]*

parts.problemMd:

parts.solutionMd:

*lowest common denominator is *$\left(x - 3\right) \left(x + 3\right)$

**[1]**

$\frac{2 \left(x - 3\right) \left(x + 3\right)}{\left(x - 3\right) \left(x + 3\right)} - \frac{\left(x + 2\right) \left(x + 3\right)}{\left(x - 3\right) \left(x + 3\right)} - \frac{\left(x - 3\right) \left(x - 6\right)}{\left(x - 3\right) \left(x + 3\right)}$ * *

$\frac{2 \left(x - 3\right) \left(x + 3\right) - \left(x + 2\right) \left(x + 3\right) - \left(x - 3\right) \left(x - 6\right)}{\left(x - 3\right) \left(x + 3\right)}$

*Expand the brackets in the numerator (keeping their results in brackets)* * *

$\frac{2 \left(x^{2} - 9\right) - \left(x^{2} + 5 x + 6\right) - \left(x^{2} - 9 x + 18\right)}{\left(x - 3\right) \left(x + 3\right)}$

parts.problemMd: Show that $\frac{1}{6x^{2}+7x-5}\div\frac{1}{4x^{2}-1}$ simplifies to $\frac{ax+b}{cx+d}$ where $a,b,c$ and $d$ are integers.
parts.solutionMd:
*Dividing by *$\frac{a}{b}$* is the same as multiplying by *$\frac{b}{a}$

*Flip the second fraction and change ÷ into ×* * *

$\frac{1}{6x^{2}+7x-5}\times\frac{4x^{2}-1}{1}$ * *

*"Simplify" for algebraic fractions means factorise and cancel* *Factorise the numerator of the second fraction using the "difference of two squares" **a*<sup>*2*</sup>* - **b*<sup>*2*</sup>* = (**a **+ **b**)(**a **- **b**)   *

$\begin{aligned}4 x^{2} - 1 & = & \left(2 x\right)^{2} - 1^{2} \\ & = & \left(2 x + 1\right) \left(2 x - 1\right)\end{aligned}$

**[1]*** *

*The calculation is now*

$\frac{1}{6 x^{2} + 7 x - 5} \times \frac{\left(2 x + 1\right) \left(2 x - 1\right)}{1}$

> *The harder quadratic on the denominator is likely to have (2**x** + 1) or (2**x** - 1) as a factor*

*Try factorising with (2**x** + 1)* * *

$6 x^{2} + 7 x - 5 = \left(3 x \pm . . .\right) \left(2 x + 1\right) ?$ * *

> *The whole number -5 in the first bracket would multiply by +1 in the second bracket to give -5 on the left *

*But expanding this attempt gives an incorrect middle term* * *

> $\left(3 x - 5\right) \left(2 x + 1\right) = 6 x^{2} \underline{- 7 x} - 5$*  *

*Try factorising with (2**x** - 1)* * *

$6 x^{2} + 7 x - 5 = \left(3 x \pm . . .\right) \left(2 x - 1\right) ?$ * *

> *The whole number +5 in the first bracket would multiply by -1 in the second bracket to give -5 on the left *

*Expanding this attempt shows it is correct* * *

$\left(3 x + 5\right) \left(2 x - 1\right) = 6 x^{2} + 7 x - 5$

**[1]**

*Cancel common brackets from top-and-bottom (this is possible across the × sign)* * *

> $\frac{1}{\left(3 x + 5\right) \cancel{\left(2 x - 1\right)}} \times \frac{\left(2 x + 1\right) \cancel{\left(2 x - 1\right)}}{1}$*  *

> *Combine into one single fraction by multiplying the numerators together and multiplying the denominators together *

> *This is now in the form *$\frac{ax+b}{cx+d}$* where **a**, **b**, **c** and **d** are integers (whole numbers)*

$\frac{2x+1}{3x+5}$* ***[1]**

parts.problemMd: Simplify fully       $\frac{3-x}{3x^{2}-5x-12}$
parts.solutionMd:
> *Simplify for algebraic fractions means factorise and cancel *

*To factorise the denominator, first multiply 3 by -12*

*3 × -12 = -36*

*Find two numbers that multiply to give -36 and add to give -5 (the middle number)*

*-9 and 4*

*Split the middle term into -9**x** and 4**x*

$3x^{2}-9x+4x-12$

*Factorise fully the first pair of terms and the second pair of terms *

$3 x \left(x - 3\right) + 4 \left(x - 3\right)$

*Factorise out the whole (**x** - 3) bracket as if it were one term, leaving 3**x** and +4 in their own bracket*

$\left(x - 3\right) \left(3 x + 4\right)$

**[1]**

> *Write the fraction with the denominator factorised  *

> $\frac{3 - x}{\left(x - 3\right) \left(3 x + 4\right)}$*  *

> *The 3 - **x** almost cancels with the **x** - 3 but the signs are wrong*

> * A good trick here is to factorise out -1 from 3 - **x**  *

> $3 - x = - 1 \left(- 3 + x\right)$*  *

> *Reorder the two terms inside the bracket (write the **x** first)  *

> $3 - x = - 1 \left(x - 3\right)$*  *

> *Write the algebraic fraction with this new form of the numerator  *

> $\frac{- 1 \left(x - 3\right)}{\left(x - 3\right) \left(3 x + 4\right)}$*  *

> *The brackets can now be more clearly cancelled on top-and-bottom  *

$\frac{- 1 \cancel{\left(x - 3\right)}}{\cancel{\left(x - 3\right)} \left(3 x + 4\right)}$

$\frac{-1}{3x+4}$ **[1]**

parts.problemMd:
Write $\frac{25 x^{2} - 64}{5 x^{2} - 13 x - 6} \times \frac{x^{2} - 8 x + 15}{5 x + 8} - \left(x - 7\right)$

as a single fraction in its simplest form.

Show clear algebraic working.
parts.solutionMd:
> *The two fractions are being multiplied and involve three quadratic expressions.*

> * Factorise these expressions as this will make them easier to multiply.*

$\begin{aligned}25 x^{2} - 64 & = & \left(5 x - 8\right) \left(5 x + 8\right) \\ 5 x^{2} - 13 x - 6 & = & \left(5 x + 2\right) \left(x - 3\right) \\ x^{2} - 8 x + 15 & = & \left(x - 5\right) \left(x - 3\right)\end{aligned}$

**One quadratic correctly factorise****d [1]**
**Two quadratics correctly factorised**** [1]**

> *Rewrite the product of the fractions.*

$\frac{25 x^{2} - 64}{5 x^{2} - 13 x - 6} \times \frac{x^{2} - 8 x + 15}{5 x + 8} = \frac{\left(5 x - 8\right) \left(5 x + 8\right)}{\left(5 x + 2\right) \left(x - 3\right)} \times \frac{\left(x - 5\right) \left(x - 3\right)}{\left(5 x + 8\right)}$

> *Look to cancel any factors before multiplying.*

$\frac{\left(5 x - 8\right) \cancel{\left(5 x + 8\right)}}{\left(5 x + 2\right) \bcancel{\left(x - 3\right)}} \times \frac{\left(x - 5\right) \bcancel{\left(x - 3\right)}}{\cancel{\left(5 x + 8\right)}} = \frac{\left(5 x - 8\right) \left(x - 5\right)}{\left(5 x + 2\right)}$

> *Now we need to include the third term, *$- \left(x - 7\right)$*, and make a common denominator.*

$\frac{\left(5 x - 8\right) \left(x - 5\right)}{\left(5 x + 2\right)} - \left(x - 7\right) = \frac{\left(5 x - 8\right) \left(x - 5\right) - \left(x - 7\right) \left(5 x + 2\right)}{\left(5 x + 2\right)}$

**[1]**

> *Expand and simplify the numerator.*

$\begin{aligned}\frac{\left(5 x - 8\right) \left(x - 5\right) - \left(x - 7\right) \left(5 x + 2\right)}{\left(5 x + 2\right)} & = & \frac{5 x^{2} - 33 x + 40 - \left(5 x^{2} - 33 x - 14\right)}{\left(5 x + 2\right)} \\ & = & \frac{5 x^{2} - 33 x + 40 - 5 x^{2} + 33 x + 14}{\left(5 x + 2\right)} \\ & = & \frac{54}{\left(5 x + 2\right)}\end{aligned}$

> *Nothing else can be simplified or cancelled.*

$\frac{25x^{2}-64}{5x^{2}-13x-6}\times\frac{x^{2}-8x+15}{5x+8}=\frac{54}{5x+2}$* ***[1]**

parts.problemMd:
Given that  $x=\frac{5}{9y+5}$ and that $y=\frac{5}{5a-2}$

find an expression for $x$ in terms of $a$.

Give your expression as a single fraction in its simplest form.
parts.solutionMd:
> *Substitute the second equation into the the first.*

$x = \frac{5}{9 \left(\frac{5}{5 a - 2}\right) + 5}$

**[1]**

> *Work carefully as you will be dealing with fractions within fractions - to deal with this you can write the 'main' fraction as a division statement, as below.*

$x = 5 \div \left[9 \left(\frac{5}{5 a - 2}\right) + 5\right]$

> *Multiply out the (round) brackets.*

$x = 5 \div \left[\frac{45}{5 a - 2} + 5\right]$

> *Make a common denominator within the square brackets.*

$x = 5 \div \left[\frac{45 + 5 \left(5 a - 2\right)}{5 a - 2}\right]$

**[1]**

> *Simplify the numerator.*

$\begin{aligned}x & = & 5 \div \left[\frac{45 + 25 a - 10}{5 a - 2}\right] \\ x & = & 5 \div \left[\frac{35 + 25 a}{5 a - 2}\right] \\ x & = & 5 \div \left[\frac{5 \left(7 + 5 a\right)}{5 a - 2}\right]\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *This is 'dividing by a fraction' so use the shortcut of switching ÷ to × and flipping the (second) fraction.*

$x = \cancel{5} \\times \frac{5 a - 2}{ \cancel{5} ( 7 + 5 a )}$
$x = \frac{5 a - 2}{7 + 5 a}$

> *There isn't anything else that can be simplified or cancelled.*

$x=\frac{5a-2}{7+5a}$* ***[1]**

parts.problemMd: Express  $\frac{1}{9x^{2}-25}-\frac{1}{6x+10}$ as a single fraction in its simplest form.
parts.solutionMd:
> *Start by factorsing the (numerators and) denominators. *

> *Spot that the denominator on the left-hand side is the difference of two squares.*

$\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{9 x^{2} - 25} & = & \frac{1}{\left(3 x - 5\right) \left(3 x + 5\right)} \\ \frac{1}{6 x + 10} & = & \frac{1}{2 \left(3 x + 5\right)}\end{aligned}$

> *Now look for the lowest common denominator (lcd) of (3**x** - 5)(3**x** + 5) and 2(3**x** + 5).*

*lcd of (3***x*** - 5)(3***x*** + 5) and 2(3***x*** + 5) is 2(3***x*** + 5)(3***x*** - 5)*

> *Write the difference over a single denominator.*

$\frac{1}{9 x^{2} - 25} - \frac{1}{6 x + 10} = \frac{1 \times 2 - 1 \times \left(3 x - 5\right)}{2 \left(3 x + 5\right) \left(3 x - 5\right)}$

> *Simplify the numerator.*

$\frac{1}{9x^{2}-25}-\frac{1}{6'+10}=\frac{7-3x}{2(3x+5)(3x-5)}$

> *Check to see if anything cancels or simplifies further.*

*In this case nothing else does.*

$\frac{1}{9x^{2}-25}-\frac{1}{6x+10}=\frac{7-3x}{2(3x+5)(3x-5)}$ **[1]**

parts.problemMd: Simplify  $\frac{2^{n}-1}{4^{n}-1}$
parts.solutionMd:
*To simpfy we are usually looking for factors.*

*There is nothing we can do with the numerator; 2 is a prime number.*

> *However we can manipulate 4*<sup>*n*</sup>* using the laws of indices.*

> *Rewrite 4 as 2*<sup>*2*</sup>* and use the law of indices "*$\left(a^{m}\right)^{n} = a^{m n}$*".*

$\frac{2^{n} - 1}{\left(2^{2}\right)^{n} - 1} = \frac{2^{n} - 1}{\left(2^{n}\right)^{2} - 1}$

> *The denominator is of the form "*$a^{2}-b^{2}$*" and so is the difference of two squares.*

$\frac{2^{n} - 1}{\left(2^{n} - 1\right) \left(2^{n} + 1\right)}$

**[1]**

> *There is now a factor of *$2^{n}-1$*on the numerator and denominator.*

$\frac{\cancel{\left(2^{n} - 1\right)}}{\cancel{\left(2^{n} - 1\right)} \left(2^{n} + 1\right)}$

$\therefore\frac{2^{n}-1}{4^{n}-1}=\frac{1}{2^{n}+1}$* ***[1]**

parts.problemMd:
The flight of a plane was in two stages.

The table shows information about the flight.

|   | **Distance (miles)** | **Speed (mph)** | **Time (hours)** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1st stage** | 731 | $x$ | $\frac{731}{x}$ |
| **2nd stage** | 287 | $x-24$ | $\frac{287}{x-24}$ |

In total, the flight lasted 2 hours. 
Work out the value of $x$.
parts.solutionMd:
*At first, this looks like it could be very complicated and involved the relationship between distance, speed and time.*

> *However, we are given the total time of the flight, so we only need be concerned with the time entries from the table.*

*The sum of the two times for each stage of the flight will be 2.* *Use this to set up an equation involving algebraic fractions.*

$\frac{731}{x}+\frac{287}{x-24}=2$

**[1]**

*To begin solving this equation, we first need to make a common denominator for the fractions on the left-hand side.*

> *The lowest common denominator (lcd) will be found by multiply **x** by (**x** - 24).*

*lcd of ***x*** and (***x*** - 24) is ***x***(***x*** - 24)*

> *Now write the left-hand side of the equation such that both fractions have the same denominator; the first will need both numerator and denominator multiplying by (**x** - 24); the second will need both multiplying by **x**.*

$\frac{731}{x} + \frac{287}{x - 24} = \frac{731 \left(x - 24\right)}{x \left(x - 24\right)} + \frac{287 x}{x \left(x - 24\right)}$

**[1]**

> *Now the left-hand side can be written as a single fraction. Expand the bracket and simplify the numerator.*

$\begin{aligned}\frac{731 \left(x - 24\right)}{x \left(x - 24\right)} + \frac{287 x}{x \left(x - 24\right)} & = & \frac{731 x - 17 544 + 287 x}{x \left(x - 24\right)} \\ & = & \frac{1018 x - 17 544}{x \left(x - 24\right)}\end{aligned}$

> *Now bring in the right-hand side of the equation. *

> *To remove the fraction, multiply both sides of the equation by its denominator (**x**(**x** - 24)).*

$\begin{aligned}\frac{1018 x - 17 544}{x \left(x - 24\right)} & = & 2 \\ 1018 x - 17 544 & = & 2 x \left(x - 24\right)\end{aligned}$

> *Expand the brackets and rearrange to form a quadratic equation.*

$\begin{aligned}1018 x - 17 544 & = & 2 x^{2} - 48 x \\ 2 x^{2} - 1066 x + 17 544 & = & 0\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *If you spot it, divide through by 2 to make the values smaller and easier to work with.*

$x^{2}-533x+8772=0$

> *This does factorise!  But as the values are awkward you may find it easier to use the quadratic formula.*

$\begin{aligned}x & = & \frac{533 \pm \sqrt{\left(- 533\right)^{2} - 4 \left(1\right) \left(8772\right)}}{2} \\ x & = & \frac{533 \pm 499}{2} \\ x & = & 516 or x = 17\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Looking at the speed column, x = 17 would give a negative speed for the 2nd stage of the flight. *

> *This is nonsense, so reject the answer x = 17.*

$\thereforex=516$* ***[1]**

**[1]**

$x = \frac{ - 2 \pm 2 \sqrt{46}}{6}$
x equals 1.927 space 443 space... space space or space space x equals negative 2.594 space 109 space...

> *Round your final answers to 3 significant figures.*

$x=1.93,x=-2.59$**  (3 s.f.)*** ***[1]**

parts.problemMd:
Solve $\frac{x}{4}-\frac{2x}{x+2}=1$

Give your solutions to 2 decimal places. 
You **must** show your working.
parts.solutionMd:
*Start by making a common denominator on the left-hand side.* *To do this we need the lowest common denominator (lcd) of 4 and (**x** + 2).*

> *This can be found by multiplying them together.*

*lcd of 4 and (***x*** + 2) is 4(***x*** + 2)*

*Rewrite both fractions with the common denominator.*

> *The first fraction will need its numerator multiplying by (**x** + 2) and the second fraction by 4.*

$\frac{x}{4} - \frac{2 x}{x + 2} = \frac{x \left(x + 2\right)}{4 \left(x + 2\right)} - \frac{2 x \times 4}{4 \left(x + 2\right)}$

**[1]**

> *Write as a single fraction over the common denominator;  expand and simplify the numerator.*

$\begin{aligned}\frac{x \left(x + 2\right)}{4 \left(x + 2\right)} - \frac{2 x \times 4}{4 \left(x + 2\right)} & = & \frac{x^{2} + 2 x - 8 x}{4 \left(x + 2\right)} \\ & = & \frac{x^{2} - 6 x}{4 \left(x + 2\right)}\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Factorise the numerator and cancel any common factors.*

$\frac{x^{2} - 6 x}{4 \left(x + 2\right)} = \frac{x \left(x - 6\right)}{4 \left(x + 2\right)}$

*There are no common factors to cancel.*

> *Bring in the right-hand side of the equation and remove the fraction by multiplying both sides of the equation by the denominator.*

$\begin{aligned}\frac{x \left(x - 6\right)}{4 \left(x + 2\right)} & = & 1 \\ x \left(x - 6\right) & = & 4 \left(x + 2\right)\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Expand and rearrange to get a quadratic equation.*

$\begin{aligned}x^{2} - 6 x & = & 4 x + 8 \\ x^{2} - 10 x - 8 & = & 0\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *The question suggests this quadratic will not factorise. (easily) as it is asking for answers to 2 decimal places so use the quadratic formula.*

$\begin{aligned}x & = & \frac{10 \pm \sqrt{\left(- 10\right)^{2} - 4 \left(1\right) \left(- 8\right)}}{2 \times 1} \\ x & = & 5 \pm \sqrt{33} \\ x & = & 10 . 744 562 . . . or x = - 0 . 744 562 . . .\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Round final answers to 2 decimal places.*

$x=10.74,x=-0.74$  **(2 d.p.)** **[1]**

parts.problemMd:
Solve this equation, giving your answers correct to 1 decimal place.

$\frac{5}{x+2}+\frac{3}{x-3}=2$

$x$ = ........... or $x$ = ...........
parts.solutionMd:
> *First we need the lowest common denominator of (**x** + 2) and (**x** - 3) on the left-hand side of the equation*

*lowest common denominator is** *$\left(x + 2\right) \left(x - 3\right)$

**[1]**

> *Multiply the numerators and denominators of the fractions on the left-hand side by the factor required to create a coommon denominator.*

$\frac{5 \left(x - 3\right)}{\left(x + 2\right) \left(x - 3\right)} + \frac{3 \left(x + 2\right)}{\left(x + 2\right) \left(x - 3\right)} = 2$

> *Write the left-hand side as one single fraction over the common denominator. *

> *Expand and simplify the numerators*

$\begin{aligned}\frac{5 \left(x - 3\right) + 3 \left(x + 2\right)}{\left(x + 2\right) \left(x - 3\right)} & = & 2 \\ \frac{5 x - 15 + 3 x + 6}{\left(x + 2\right) \left(x - 3\right)} & = & 2 \\ \frac{8 x - 9}{\left(x + 2\right) \left(x - 3\right)} & = & 2\end{aligned}$

** Numerator**** [1]**

> *Multiply both sides of the equation by the denominator to remove the fraction.*

$8 x - 9 = 2 \left(x + 2\right) \left(x - 3\right)$

> *Expand the brackets, collect 'like' terms and rearrange so the equation" equals zero ".*

$\begin{aligned}8 x - 9 & = & 2 \left(x^{2} - x - 6\right) \\ 0 & = & 2 x^{2} - 2 x - 12 - 8 x + 9 \\ 2 x^{2} - 10 x - 3 & = & 0\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Solve this quadratic equation.  As the question asks for answer to be given to 1 decimal place, it is unlikely to factorise.*

$\begin{aligned}x & = & \frac{- \left(- 10\right) \pm \sqrt{\left(- 10\right)^{2} - 4 \left(2\right) \left(- 3\right)}}{2 \left(2\right)} \\ x & = & \frac{10 \pm \sqrt{100 + 24}}{4} \\ x & = & \frac{10}{4} \pm \frac{2 \sqrt{31}}{4} \\ x & = & \frac{5}{2} \pm \frac{\sqrt{31}}{2}\end{aligned}$

**Method of solving quadratic**** [1]**

> *Decimals are required for the final answers.*

$\begin{aligned}x & = & \frac{5}{2} + \frac{\sqrt{31}}{2} = 5 . 283 882 . . . \\ x & = & \frac{5}{2} - \frac{\sqrt{31}}{2} = - 0 . 283 882 . . .\end{aligned}$

$\thereforex=5.3\mathrm{or}x=-0.3(1d.p.)$
**One mark for each**** [2]**

parts.problemMd:
Write $\frac{5}{4 x^{2} - 25} - \left(2 x + 3\right) \div \left(\frac{4 x^{2} + 16 x + 15}{7}\right)$  as a single fraction in its simplest form.

Show clear algebraic working
parts.solutionMd:
> **[exam-tip]**
> Simplifying algebraic fraction questions are commonly written with quadratic expressions that are able to be factorised.
> 
> Recognising this early on in the question will often result in opportunities to simplify earlier on meaning fewer instances to expand double or triple brackets unnecessarily.

> *The two quadratic expressions forming part of the question can be factorised*

> $4x^{2}-25$* is a difference of two squares*

$4 x^{2} - 25 = \left(2 x + 5\right) \left(2 x - 5\right)$

> $4x^{2}+16x+15$* can be factorised into double brackets*

- *First multiply the coefficient of the *$x^{2}$* term and constant term together*

$4\times15=60$

- *List the factor pairs of this product and identify the factor pair that add up to the value of the coefficient of the *$x$* term*

$\begin{aligned}60 & = & 1 \times 60 \\ & = & 2 \times 30 \\ & = & 3 \times 20 \\ & = & 4 \times 15 \\ & = & 5 \times 12 \\ & = & 6 \times 10\end{aligned}$

*In this case *$6+10=16$* so this is the pair of values to use*

> *Split the *$x$*term of the quadratic expression into two separate terms using the selected factor pair values as coefficients of the terms*

$4x^{2}+16x+15=4x^{2}+6x+10x+15$

> *Factorise the first two terms and the last two terms of the expression separately into single brackets*

$4 x^{2} + 6 x + 10 x + 15 = 2 x \left(2 x + 3\right) + 5 \left(2 x + 3\right)$

> *The bracketed expression is the same in both parts*

> *Factor out this term*

$4 x^{2} + 16 x + 15 = \left(2 x + 3\right) \left(2 x + 5\right)$

> *Rewrite the original question with the quadratic expressions replaced with the factorised form*

$\frac{5}{\left(2 x + 5\right) \left(2 x - 5\right)} - \left(2 x + 3\right) \div \frac{\left(2 x + 3\right) \left(2 x + 5\right)}{7}$

> *Applying the order of operations means that the division must be calculated first*

$\left(2 x + 3\right) \div \frac{\left(2 x + 3\right) \left(2 x + 5\right)}{7}$

> *Multiplying by the reciprocal of the divisor is equivalent to dividing*

$\left(2 x + 3\right) \times \frac{7}{\left(2 x + 3\right) \left(2 x + 5\right)}$

**[M1]**

> *Multiply the numerators and multiply the denominators to give:*

$\frac{7 \left(2 x + 3\right)}{\left(2 x + 3\right) \left(2 x + 5\right)}$

> *Simplify the fraction by dividing through by the common factor *$2x+3$

$\frac{7}{\left(2 x + 5\right)}$

> *Put this back into the question to solve the subtraction part*

$\frac{5}{\left(2 x + 5\right) \left(2 x - 5\right)} - \frac{7}{\left(2 x + 5\right)}$

**[M1]**

> *To subtract fractions there must be a common denominator*

> $2x+5$* is already common to both denominators but *$2x-5$* is not*

> *Multiplying the second fraction by 1 in the form *$\frac{2x-5}{2x-5}$* will result in a common denominator*

$\frac{5}{\left(2 x + 5\right) \left(2 x - 5\right)} - \frac{7}{\left(2 x + 5\right)} \times \frac{\left(2 x - 5\right)}{\left(2 x - 5\right)}$

$= \frac{5}{\left(2 x + 5\right) \left(2 x - 5\right)} - \frac{7 \left(2 x - 5\right)}{\left(2 x + 5\right) \left(2 x - 5\right)}$

> *Subtract the numerators now that the denominators are the same*

$\frac{5 - 7 \left(2 x - 5\right)}{\left(2 x + 5\right) \left(2 x - 5\right)}$

**[M1]**

> *Expand and simplify the numerator*

$\frac{5 - 14 x + 35}{\left(2 x + 5\right) \left(2 x - 5\right)} = \frac{40 - 14 x}{\left(2 x + 5\right) \left(2 x - 5\right)}$

**[A1]**

> *Factorise the numerator to check if any further simplifying can take place*

$\frac{2 \left(20 - 7 x\right)}{\left(2 x + 5\right) \left(2 x - 5\right)}$

> *There are no common factors of the numerator and denominator so it cannot be simplified any further*

$\frac{2 \left(20 - 7 x\right)}{\left(2 x + 5\right) \left(2 x - 5\right)}$

> **[mark-scheme]**
> Any equivalent expression will get the final mark (e.g. $\frac{40-14x}{4x^{2}-25}$)

parts.problemMd:
Solve $\frac{45 x^{3} - 80 x}{3 x^{2} + x - 4} \times \left(\frac{1}{3 x - 4} + \frac{1}{x}\right) = \frac{4 \left(x + 2\right)}{5 x - 8}$

Show clear algebraic working.
parts.solutionMd:
> *First add together the fractions in the bracket using a common denominator*

$\frac{1}{3 x - 4} + \frac{1}{x} = \frac{x + 3 x - 4}{x \left(3 x - 4\right)} \\$


> *Factorise the numerator*

$\frac{4 x - 4}{x \left(3 x - 4\right)} = \frac{4 \left(x - 1\right)}{x \left(3 x - 4\right)}$

**[M1]**

> *Factorise the expressions in the first fraction as much as possible*

$\frac{5 x \left(9 x^{2} - 16\right)}{\left(3 x + 4\right) \left(x - 1\right)}$

$\frac{5 x \left(3 x + 4\right) \left(3 x - 4\right)}{\left(3 x + 4\right) \left(x - 1\right)}$

**[M1]**

> *Divide top and bottom by *$3x+4$

$\frac{5 x \left(3 x - 4\right)}{x - 1}$

> *Rewrite the original equation with the simplified terms*

$\frac{5 x \left(3 x - 4\right)}{x - 1} \times \frac{4 \left(x - 1\right)}{x \left(3 x - 4\right)} = \frac{4 \left(x + 2\right)}{5 x - 8}$

**[M1]**

> *Cross cancel *

$\frac{5 \cancel{x} \cancel{\left(3 x - 4\right)}}{\cancel{x - 1}} \times \frac{4 \cancel{\left(x - 1\right)}}{\cancel{x} \cancel{\left(3 x - 4\right)}} = \frac{4 \left(x + 2\right)}{5 x - 8}$

$20 = \frac{4 \left(x + 2\right)}{5 x - 8}$

**[M1]**

> *Multiply both sides by *$5x-8$

$20 \left(5 x - 8\right) = 4 \left(x + 2\right)$

> *Expand and simplify*

$100x-160=4x+8$

> *Rearrange to get *$x$* on its own*

$96x=168$

> *Divide both sides by 96*

$x=\frac{168}{96}=\frac{7}{4}$

$\frac{7}{4}$

**[A1]**

parts.problemMd:
Prove algebraically that

$(2n+1)^{2}-(2n+1)$ is an even number

for all positive integer values of $n$.
parts.solutionMd:
*Method 1*

*Expand (2**n** + 1)*<sup>*2*</sup>* (by writing it as the product of two brackets)* * *

$( 2 n + 1 ) ^{2} = ( 2 n + 1 ) ( 2 n + 1 )$
equals 4 n squared plus 2 n plus 2 n plus 1 * *

*Collect "like" **n** terms* * *

$\left(2 n + 1\right)^{2} = 4 n^{2} + 4 n + 1$

**[1]**

*Substitute this result into the original expression* * *

$4 n^{2} + 4 n + 1 - \left(2 n + 1\right)$ * *

*Remove the brackets (by multiplying each term inside by -1)* * *

$4n^{2}+4n+1-2n-1$ * *

*Collect "like" terms* * *

$4n^{2}+2n$

**[1]**

*Show that this expression is an even number (by writing it as 2 × ... )* * *

$2 \times \left(2 n^{2} + n\right)$ * *

*If **n** is a positive integer then this expression is always even (as it is 2 x "an integer")* * *

$2\times(2n^{2}+n)$** is an even number for all positive integer values of ****n*** ***[1]**

*Method 2*

*Factorise the whole bracket (2**n** + 1) out of the expression* * *

$\left(2 n + 1\right) \left[\left(2 n + 1\right) - 1\right]$

**[1]**

*Collect the terms inside the square brackets* * *

$( 2 n + 1 ) [ 2 n ]$
$=2 n\left(2 n + 1\right)$

**[1]**

> *Show that this is an even number (by writing it as 2 x "an integer")  *

> $2 \times n \left(2 n + 1\right)$*  *

*If **n** is a positive integer then **n**(2**n** + 1) will also be a positive integer, so the result above has the form 2 × "an integer"* * *

$2\timesn(2n+1)$* *** is an even number for all positive integer values of ****n ****[1]**

parts.problemMd: Show that $\left(n + 3\right)^{2}  -  \left(n - 3\right)^{2}$  is an even number for all positive integer values of $n$.
parts.solutionMd:
*Expand (**n** + 3)*<sup>*2*</sup>* (by writing it as the product of two brackets) and collect "like" terms* * *

$\begin{aligned}\left(n + 3\right)^{2} & = & \left(n + 3\right) \left(n + 3\right) \\ & = & n^{2} + 3 n + 3 n + 9 \\ & = & n^{2} + 6 n + 9\end{aligned}$ * *

*Expand (**n** - 3)*<sup>*2*</sup>* (by writing it as the product of two brackets) and collect "like" terms* * *

$\begin{aligned}\left(n - 3\right)^{2} & = & \left(n - 3\right) \left(n - 3\right) \\ & = & n^{2} - 3 n - 3 n + 9 \\ & = & n^{2} - 6 n + 9\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

*Put these results in brackets and subtract the second from the first* * *

$\left(n + 3\right)^{2} - \left(n - 3\right)^{2} = \left(n^{2} + 6 n + 9\right) - \left(n^{2} - 6 n + 9\right)$ * *

*Expand the brackets on the right-hand side (multiplying each term in the last bracket by -1)* *Collect "like" terms* * *

$n^{2}+6n+9-n^{2}+6n-9\,=12n$

**[1]**

*Show that this expression is an even number (by writing it as 2 × "an integer" )* * *

$2\times6n$ * *

*If **n** is a positive integer then 6**n** will also be a positive integer, so the result above has the form 2 × "an integer"* * *

$2\times6n$** is an even number for all positive integer values of ****n**** ****[1]**

parts.problemMd:
$n$ is an integer greater than $1$

Prove algebraically that  $n^{2}  -  2  -  \left( n - 2\right)^{2}$ is always an even number.
parts.solutionMd:
*Expand (**n** - 2)*<sup>*2*</sup>* (by writing it as the product of two brackets) and collect "like" terms* * *

$\begin{aligned}\left(n - 2\right)^{2} & = & \left(n - 2\right) \left(n - 2\right) \\ & = & n^{2} - 2 n - 2 n + 4 \\ & = & n^{2} - 4 n + 4\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

*Replace (**n** - 2)*<sup>*2*</sup>* in the original expression with the result above in brackets* * *

$n^{2} - 2 - \left(n^{2} - 4 n + 4\right)$

**[1]**

*Expand the brackets (by multiplying each term in the bracket by -1)* *Collect "like" terms* * *

$n^{2}-2-n^{2}+4n-4\,=4n-6$

**[1]**

*Show that this expression is an even number (by writing it as 2 × ... )* * *

> $2 \times \left(2 n - 3\right)$*  *

*If **n** is an integer greater than 1 then (2**n **- 3) will also be an integer greater than 1, so the result above has the form 2 × "an integer"* * *

$2\times(2n-3)$** is an even number for all integer values of ****n**** greater than 1*** ***[1]**

parts.problemMd:
Prove that the difference between two consecutive square numbers is always an odd number. 
Show clear algebraic working.
parts.solutionMd:
> *Two consecutive numbers would be *$n$* and *$n+1$* so ...*

*Let the two consecutive square numbers be *$n^{2}$* and *$\left(n + 1\right)^{2}$

> *We now need the difference between these (clearly *$\left(n + 1\right)^{2}$* will be the larger of the two).*

$\left(n + 1\right)^{2} - n^{2}$

**[1]**

> *Expand and simplify, bearing in mind to show an odd number we require a result in the form "*$2k\pm1$*".*

$\begin{aligned}\left(n + 1\right)^{2} - n^{2} & = & n^{2} + 2 n + 1 - n^{2} \\ & = & 2 n + 1\end{aligned}$

**Expanding brackets**** [1]**

> *Which is in the required from so we can write a statement for the proof.*

**Since **$(n+1)^{2}-n^{2}=2n+1$**, the difference between any two consecutive square numbers is always an odd number ****[1]**

parts.problemMd:
$N$ is a multiple of 5

$\begin{aligned}A  & = &  N  +  1 \\ B  & = &  N  –  1\end{aligned}$

Prove, using algebra, that $A^{2}--B^{2}$ is always a multiple of 20
parts.solutionMd:
> *As *$N$* is a multiple of 5,*

*Let *$N=5k$*, were *$k$* is an integer*

> *Rewrite *$A$* and *$B$* in terms of *$k$*.*

$\begin{aligned}A & = & 5 k + 1 \\ B & = & 5 k - 1\end{aligned}$

> *Now consider *$A^{2}-B^{2}$* - this is the difference of two squares.*

$A^{2} - B^{2} = \left(A + B\right) \left(A - B\right)$

**[1]**

> *Substitute *$A$* and *$B$* in terms of *$k$*.*

$\left(A + B\right) \left(A - B\right) = \left[\left(5 k + 1\right) + \left(5 k - 1\right)\right] \left[\left(5 k + 1\right) - \left(5 k - 1\right)\right]$

> *Simplify, bearing in mind to show a multiple of 20 we require a result in the form "*$8k$*".*

$\begin{aligned}\left[\left(5 k + 1\right) + \left(5 k - 1\right)\right] \left[\left(5 k + 1\right) - \left(5 k - 1\right)\right] & = & \left(10 k\right) \left(2\right) \\ & = & 20 k\end{aligned}$

**For "**$20k$**" [1]**

> *Which is in the required from so we can write a statement for the proof.*

**Since **$A^{2}-B^{2}=20k$**, for some integer **$k$**, **$A^{2}-B^{2}$** is always a multiple of 20 ****[1]**

**If you don't spot the difference of two squares, this question can still be completed but it will involve a lot of expanding brackets and simplifying - try it!**

$n=2E=2^{2}+2+5=11Prime\,n=3E=3^{2}+3+5=17Prime\,n=4E=4^{2}+4+5=25Notprime$

**Correctly evaluating E for any value of n ****[1]**

parts.problemMd:
Prove that

$\left(2 n  +  3\right)^{2}  -  \left(2 n  -  3\right)^{2}$  is a multiple of $8$

for all positive integer values of $n$.
parts.solutionMd:
*Method 1*

*Expand (2**n** + 3)*<sup>*2*</sup>* * * *

$\begin{aligned}\left(2 n + 3\right)^{2} & = & \left(2 n + 3\right) \left(2 n + 3\right) \\ & = & 4 n^{2} + 6 n + 6 n + 9 \\ & = & 4 n^{2} + 12 n + 9\end{aligned}$ * *

*Expand (2**n** - 3)*<sup>*2*</sup>* * * *

$\begin{aligned}\left(2 n - 3\right)^{2} & = & \left(2 n - 3\right) \left(2 n - 3\right) \\ & = & 4 n^{2} - 6 n - 6 n + 9 \\ & = & 4 n^{2} - 12 n + 9\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

*Put these results in brackets and subtract the second from the first* * *

$\left(2 n + 3\right)^{2} - \left(2 n - 3\right)^{2} = \left(4 n^{2} + 12 n + 9\right) - \left(4 n^{2} - 12 n + 9\right)$ * *

*Expand the brackets on the right-hand side* *Collect "like" terms* * *

$4n^{2}+12n+9-4n^{2}+12n-9\,=24n$

**[1]**

*Show that this expression is a multiple of 8 (by writing it as 8 × "an integer" )* * *

$8\times3n$ * *

*If **n** is a positive integer then 3**n** will also be a positive integer, so the result above has the form 8 × "an integer"* * *

$8\times3n$** is a multiple of 8 for all positive integer values of ****n**** ****[1]**

*Method 2*

*The "difference of two squares" says **a*<sup>*2*</sup>* - **b*<sup>*2 *</sup>*= (**a **+ **b**)(**a** - **b**) Factorise (2**n** + 3)*<sup>*2*</sup>* - (2**n** - 3)*<sup>*2 *</sup>*using the "difference of two squares" where** a** = 2**n** + 3 and **b** = 2**n** - 3* * *

$\begin{aligned}\left(2 n + 3\right)^{2} - \left(2 n - 3\right)^{2} & = & \left(\left(2 n + 3\right) + \left(2 n - 3\right)\right) \times \left(\left(2 n + 3\right) - \left(2 n - 3\right)\right)\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

*Simplify the brackets on the right-hand side* * *

$\begin{aligned} & & \left(2 n + 3 + 2 n - 3\right) \left(2 n + 3 - 2 n + 3\right) \\ & = & \left(4 n\right) \left(6\right) \\ & = & 24 n\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

*Show that this expression is a multiple of 8 (by writing it as 8 × "an integer" )* * *

$8\times3n$ * *

*If **n** is a positive integer then 3**n** will also be a positive integer, so the result above has the form 8 × "an integer"* * *

$8\times3n$** is a multiple of 8 for all positive integer values of ****n**** ****[1]**

$\begin{aligned}\left(n + 1\right)^{2} & = & \left(n + 1\right) \left(n + 1\right) \\ & = & n^{2} + n + n + 1 \\ & = & n^{2} + 2 n + 1 \\ & & \end{aligned}$

**[1]**

*Put these results in brackets and subtract the second from the first* * *

$\left(n + 2\right)^{2} - \left(n + 1\right)^{2} = \left(n^{2} + 4 n + 4\right) - \left(n^{2} + 2 n + 1\right)$ * *

*Expand the brackets on the right-hand side * *Collect "like" terms* * *

> $\frac{\cancel{2 n + 3}}{n \cancel{\left(2 n + 3\right)}} = \frac{1}{n}$*  *

$\begin{aligned}\left(n + 2\right)^{2} - \left(n + 1\right)^{2} & = & \left(\left(n + 2\right) + \left(n + 1\right)\right) \times \left(\left(n + 2\right) + \left(n + 1\right)\right)\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

*Simplify the brackets on the right-hand side * * *

$\begin{aligned} & & \left(n + 2 + n + 1\right) \left(n + 2 - n - 1\right) \\ & = & \left(2 n + 3\right) \left(1\right) \\ & = & 2 n + 3\end{aligned}$

*Write the algebraic fraction with the numerator as 2**n** + 3* * *

$\frac{2n+3}{2n^{2}+3n}$* *

> *Factorise the denominator   *

> *Cancel the (2**n** + 3) bracket from top-and-bottom  *

> $\frac{\cancel{2 n + 3}}{n \cancel{\left(2 n + 3\right)}} = \frac{1}{n}$*  *

$\frac{1}{n}$** ****[1]**

parts.problemMd:

$\frac{n \left(n + 1\right)}{2} + \frac{\left(n + 1\right) \left(n + 2\right)}{2} = \frac{n \left(n + 1\right) + \left(n + 1\right) \left(n + 2\right)}{2}$

*Expand and simplify the numerator.* *If you spot it, the numerator has a factor of (**n** + 1) which can make simplifying easier.*

$\begin{aligned}\frac{n \left(n + 1\right) + \left(n + 1\right) \left(n + 2\right)}{2} & = & \frac{\left(n + 1\right) \left(n + \left(n + 2\right)\right)}{2}\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

$\begin{aligned}\frac{\left(n + 1\right) \left(n + \left(n + 2\right)\right)}{2} & = & \frac{\left(n + 1\right) \left(2 n + 2\right)}{2}\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *There is a factor of 2 in the second bracket on the numerator that will then cancel with the denominator.*

$\frac{\left(n + 1\right) \left(2 n + 2\right)}{2} = \frac{\cancel{2} \left(n + 1\right) \left(n + 1\right)}{\cancel{2}}$

> *We are left with the product of two equal brackets.*

$\left(n + 1\right) \left(n + 1\right) = \left(n + 1\right)^{2}$

**[1]**

> *This is the form **k*<sup>*2*</sup>*, for an integer **k** (assuming **n** is an integer) and so is a square number.*

**Since the sum of two consecutive triangular numbers can be written in the form (****n**** + 1)**<sup>**2**</sup>**, for integer ****n****, it is always a square number** **[1]**

parts.problemMd: The lengths of the sides of a right-angled triangle are all integers. Prove that if the lengths of the two shortest sides are even, then the length of the third side must also be even.
parts.solutionMd:
*Pythagoras' theorem links the three sides, **a**, **b** and **c** of a right angled triangle.* *If **a** is the longest side, the hypotenuse, then *$a^{2}=b^{2}+c^{2}$*.*

> *Start by introducing the two shorter sides as even values.*

*Let the two shorter sides be 2***m*** and 2***n***, where ***m*** and ***n*** are integers*

> *Apply Pythagoras' theorem, where these two sides/values would be **b** and **c*

$a^{2} = \left(2 m\right)^{2} + \left(2 n\right)^{2}$

> *Expand the right-hand side.*

$\begin{aligned}a^{2} & = & 4 m^{2} + 4 n^{2} \\ a^{2} & = & 4 \left(m^{2} + n^{2}\right)\end{aligned}$

> *Since we are given all three sides are integers, we can assume that *$4 \left(m^{2} + n^{2}\right)$* is a square number.*

**a***<sup>2</sup>** has a factor of 4, which is even and so ***a***<sup>2</sup>** is even*

*if a square number is even, its (positive) square root is even ***a***<sup>2</sup>** is even, therefore ***a*** is even*

**Therefore if the two shorter sides of a right-angled triangle with integer sides are even, the third side is even too ****[1]**

parts.problemMd:
Express as a single fraction.

$\frac{m+1}{n+1}-\frac{m}{n}$

Simplify your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
> *Find the lowest common denominator (lcd) by multiplying (**n** + 1) by **n**.*

*lcd is (***n*** + 1) × ***n*** = ***n***(***n*** + 1)*

> *Multiply numerator-and-denominator of each fraction by the factor needed to form this denominator.*

$\frac{\left(m + 1\right) n}{n \left(n + 1\right)} - \frac{m \left(n + 1\right)}{n \left(n + 1\right)}$

> *Write as one single fraction over the common denominator. Subtract the numerators.*

$\frac{n \left(m + 1\right) - m \left(n + 1\right)}{n \left(n + 1\right)}$

**[1]**

> *Expand the brackets in the numerator.*

$\frac{m n + n - m n - m}{n \left(n + 1\right)}$

> *Collect "like" terms in the numerator.*

$\frac{n - m}{n \left(n + 1\right)}$

> *Nothing else factorises or cancels.*

$\therefore\frac{m+1}{n+1}-\frac{m}{n}=\frac{n-m}{n(n+1)}$* ***[1]**

parts.problemMd: Prove algebraically that the difference between the squares of any two consecutive odd numbers is always a multiple of 8
parts.solutionMd:
> *Define expressions for consecutive odd numbers*

*Let *$n$* equal any integer*

*Therefore *$2n+1$* equals any odd number*

*And *$2n+3$* equals the next consecutive odd number*

**[M1]**

> *Use your expressions to set up an expression to show the difference between the squares of consecutive odd numbers*

$\left(2 n + 3\right)^{2} - \left(2 n + 1\right)^{2}$

> *Expand the brackets, using FOIL method for example*

$\begin{aligned}\left(2 n + 3\right)^{2} - \left(2 n + 1\right)^{2} & = & \left(4 n^{2} + 6 n + 6 n + 9\right) - \left(4 n^{2} + 2 n + 2 n + 1\right)\end{aligned}$

**[M1]**

> *Simplify the expression by collecting terms*

$\begin{aligned} & = & \left(4 n^{2} + 12 n + 9\right) - \left(4 n^{2} + 4 n + 1\right) \\ & = & 4 n^{2} + 12 n + 9 - 4 n^{2} - 4 n - 1 \\ & = & 8 n + 8\end{aligned}$

**[M1]**

> *Factorise the simplified expression by dividing the expression by the highest common factor of the terms*

**Final answer:** $8 n + 8 = 8 \left(n + 1\right)$** therefore it is a multiple of 8**

**[A1]**

[2]

The expression $2t^{2}+5t+2$ can never have a value that is a prime number.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:

parts.problemMd:
$n$ is an integer.

Prove algebraically that the sum of  $\frac{1}{2}n(n+1)$ and $\frac{1}{2}(n+1)(n+2)$ is always a square number.
parts.solutionMd:
> *Find the sum of the two expressions*

$\frac{1}{2} n \left(n + 1\right) + \frac{1}{2} \left(n + 1\right) \left(n + 2\right)$ * *

> *Method 1** *

> *Expand the brackets*

$1 half ( n ^{2} + n ) + 1 half ( n ^{2} + n + 2 n + 2 )$
$= 1 half n ^{2} + 1 half n + 1 half ( n ^{2} + 3 n + 2 )$
equals 1 half n squared plus 1 half n plus 1 half n squared plus 3 over 2 n plus 1

**[1]**

> *Collect "like" terms*

$n^{2}+2n+1$

*This is meant to be a square number* *Factorise the quadratic expression*

$\left(n + 1\right) \left(n + 1\right)$

> *Write this as the "square" of a bracket*

$\left(n + 1\right)^{2}$

> *If **n** is an integer then (**n** + 1) is an integer so (**n** + 1)*<sup>*2*</sup>* is a square number*

$(n+1)^{2}$** ****is a square number**** [1]**

> *Method 2 *

> *Factorise out the whole of *$\frac{1}{2} \left(n + 1\right)$* from both terms*

$\frac{1}{2} \left(n + 1\right) \left[n + \left(n + 2\right)\right]$

**[1]**

> *Collect "like" terms*

$\frac{1}{2} \left(n + 1\right) \left(2 n + 2\right)$

> *Factorise the 2 out of the second bracket (and multiply it by the half)*

> * *$\frac{1}{2} \left(n + 1\right)\times 2\left(n + 1\right)$
$=\frac{1}{2}\times 2\times\left(n + 1\right) \left(n + 1\right)$
$=\left(n + 1\right)^{2}$

> * If **n** is an integer then (**n** + 1) is an integer so (**n** + 1)*<sup>*2*</sup>* is a square number*

$(n+1)^{2}$** ****is a square number**** [1]**

parts.problemMd:
Here are the first five terms of an arithmetic sequence.

7      13      19      25      31

Prove that the difference between the squares of any two terms of the sequence is always a multiple of 24.
parts.solutionMd:
*The **n**th term of a linear (arithmetic) sequence is **dn** + **b*

> *Find the common difference, **d** (the amount by which the sequence goes up each time)*

**d*** = 6*

> *Find **b** (either by finding the term before the first term shown, or by solving 6**n** + **b** = 7 when **n** = 1)*

**b*** = 7 - 6 = 1* * *

> *Write down the formula for the **n**th term of the sequence *

**n***th term = 6***n*** + 1*

**d or b correct**** [1]** 
**[1]**

*For any two terms in the sequence, we can write the "**n**th term" as one of them and the "**p**th term" as the other*

> *Write down the formula for the **p**th term of the sequence*

**p***th term = 6***p*** + 1* * *

> *Find an expression for the difference between the squares of the **n**th and the **p**th term*

$\left(6 n + 1\right)^{2} - \left(6 p + 1\right)^{2}$

**[1]**

> *Expand (6**n** + 1)*<sup>*2*</sup>

> $\begin{aligned}\left(6 n + 1\right) \left(6 n + 1\right) & = & 36 n^{2} + 6 n + 6 n + 1 \\ & = & 36 n^{2} + 12 n + 1\end{aligned}$* *

> *Use this result to expand (6**n** + 1)*<sup>*2*</sup>*- (6**p** + 1)*<sup>*2*</sup>

> $\left(6 n + 1\right)^{2} - \left(6 p + 1\right)^{2} = \left(36 n^{2} + 12 n + 1\right) - \left(36 p^{2} + 12 p + 1\right)$* *

*Expand the brackets on the right-hand side*

> *Collect "like" terms*

$36n^{2}+12n+1-36p^{2}-12p-1\,=36n^{2}-36p^{2}+12n-12p$

**[1]**

> *This does not yet look like a multiple of 24 (further algebra is needed) *

> *Factorise the first two terms and the last two terms*

> $36 \left(n^{2} - p^{2}\right) + 12 \left(n - p\right)$* *

> *Use the difference of two squares to factorise **n*<sup>*2*</sup>* - **p*<sup>*2*</sup>* further*

$36 \left(n + p\right) \left(n - p\right) + 12 \left(n - p\right)$

> *Factorise out the 12 and (**n** - **p**) *

$12 \left(n - p\right) \left[3 \left(n + p\right) + 1\right]$

> *As **n** and **p** are integers, this result is a multiple of 12 (as it is "12 × an integer")  *

> *Think how this result can be a multiple of 24 (for example 12 × 2, or "12 × even number" )*

*to be a multiple of 24, either (***n*** - ***p***) must be even or 3(***n*** + ***p***) + 1 must be even*

**[1]**

> *Remember "odd - odd = even", "even - even = even", "odd + even = odd", "even + odd = odd" *

> *By considering **n** and **p** being odd and even, prove the statement above*

*if ***n*** is odd and ***p*** is odd, then ***n*** - ***p*** is even*
* **if ***n*** is even and ***p*** is even, then ***n*** - ***p*** is even** *
*if ***n*** is odd and ***p*** is even, then ***n*** +*** p*** is odd, so 3(***n*** + ***p***) is odd, so 3(***n*** + ***p***) + 1 is even** *
*if ***n*** is even and ***p*** is odd, then*** n*** + ***p*** is odd, so 3(***n*** + ***p***) is odd, so 3(***n*** + ***p***) + 1 is even**  *

**In all cases of ****n**** and ****p**** being odd and even, either (****n**** - ****p****) is even or 3(****n**** + ****p****) + 1 is even so **`equation`** is a multiple of 24 ****[1]**

parts.problemMd:
The table gives information about the first six terms of a sequence of numbers.

| **  Term number** | 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **  Term of sequence** | $\frac{1\times2}{2}$ | $\frac{2\times3}{2}$ | $\frac{3\times4}{2}$ | $\frac{4\times5}{2}$ | $\frac{5\times6}{2}$ | $\frac{6\times7}{2}$ |

Prove algebraically that the sum of any two consecutive terms of this sequence is always a square number.
parts.solutionMd:
> *First write down the **n*<sup>*th*</sup>* term of the sequence*

$n^{th} term is \frac{n \left(n + 1\right)}{2}$

**[1]**

> *So the (**n** + 1)*<sup>*th*</sup>* term will be*

$\left(n + 1\right)^{th} term is \frac{\left(n + 1\right) \left(n + 2\right)}{2}$

> *Adding these two together*

$\frac{n \left(n + 1\right)}{2} + \frac{\left(n + 1\right) \left(n + 2\right)}{2} = \frac{n \left(n + 1\right) + \left(n + 1\right) \left(n + 2\right)}{2}$

**[1]**

> *Expand and simplify the numerator (it's easier if you spot that (**n** + 1) if a factor of the numerator)*

$\begin{aligned}\frac{n \left(n + 1\right) + \left(n + 1\right) \left(n + 2\right)}{2} & = & \frac{\left(n + 1\right) \left(n + \left(n + 2\right)\right)}{2} \\ & = & \frac{\left(n + 1\right) \left(2 n + 2\right)}{2} \\ & = & \frac{2 n^{2} + 4 n + 2}{2} \\ & = & \frac{2 \left(n^{2} + 2 n + 1\right)}{2} \\ & = & n^{2} + 2 n + 1 \\ & = & \left(n + 1\right)^{2}\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *(**n** + 1)*<sup>*2*</sup>* is a square number (since **n** is an integer)*

**Final answer:** **Therefore the sum of two consecutive terms in the sequence is a square number**** [1]**

> *For the expression " *$x^{2}+bx+c$* " this will be " *$\left(x + \frac{b}{2}\right)^{2} - \frac{b^{2}}{4} + c$* ".*

$\begin{aligned}x^{2} + x + 1 & = & \left(x + \frac{1}{2}\right)^{2} - \frac{1^{2}}{4} + 1 \\ & = & \left(x + \frac{1}{2}\right)^{2} + \frac{3}{4}\end{aligned}$

**One mark for **$\left(x + \frac{1}{2}\right)^{2}$** [1] **
**Fully correct completed square form**** [1]**

> *Thinking about the values of the squared part and what is then added we can conclude the proof.*

$(x+\frac{1}{2})^{2}\geq0$** for all values of ****x****, **$\therefore(x+\frac{1}{2})^{2}+\frac{3}{4}>0$** for all values of ****x**** and so **$x^{2}+x+1$** is always positive** **[1]**

parts.problemMd:
The diagram shows a cross placed on a number grid.

![A grid of numbers 1 to 60 in sequential order. Numbers 25, 34, 35, and 36 are shaded to highlight them distinctively.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-18-higher/2-equations-formulae-and-identities/algebraic-proof/assets/002-a-grid-of-numbers-1-to-60-in-sequential-order-nu.png)

$L$ is the product of the left and right numbers of the cross.
 $T$ is the product of the top and bottom numbers of the cross.
 $M$ is the middle number of the cross.

Show that when $M=35,L--T=99.$
parts.solutionMd:
> *When **M** = 35, the left and right numbers of the cross are 34 and 36.*

**L*** = 34 × 36 = 1224*

> *When **M** = 35, the top and bottom numbers of the cross are 25 and 45.*

**T*** = 25 × 45 = 1125*

**[1]**

> *Now find **L** - **T**.*

**L*** - ***T*** = 1224 - 1125 = 99*

**L**** - ****T**** = 99*** ***[1]**

parts.problemMd: Prove that, for any position of the cross on the number grid above, $L--T=99.$
parts.solutionMd:
> *(We may assume that **M** only takes values that means the cross can be drawn on the grid.  So **M** ≠ 30 for example.)*

> *For middle value **M*

*the left and right numbers of the cross will be (***M*** - 1) and (***M*** + 1)* *∴ ***L*** = (***M*** - 1)(***M*** + 1)*

**[1]**

*the top and bottom numbers of the cross will be (M - 10) and (M + 10)* *∴ ***T*** = (***M*** - 10)(***M*** + 10)*

**[1]**

> *So*

$L - T = \left(M - 1\right) \left(M + 1\right) - \left(M - 10\right) \left(M + 10\right)$

> *Expand each pair of brackets, being careful with the subtraction sign between them. Both brackets are in the difference of two squares form.*

$L - T = \left(M^{2} - 1\right) - \left(M^{2} - 100\right)$

**For (M**<sup>**2**</sup>** -1)**** [1] **
**For (M**<sup>**2**</sup>** -100)**** [1]**

> *Remove the brackets and simplify.*

$\begin{aligned}L - T & = & M^{2} - 1 - M^{2} + 100 \\ & = & 100 - 1 \\ & = & 99\end{aligned}$

$\thereforeL-T=99$* ***for any position of the cross on the number grid*** ***[1]**

parts.problemMd: Express $3x^{2}--6x+5$  in the form $a(x--b)^{2}+c$
parts.solutionMd:
**Method 1**

> *To complete the square, start by taking a factor of 3 out of the first two terms*

$3 x^{2} - 6 x + 5 = 3 \left(x^{2} - 2 x\right) + 5$

**[M1]**

> *Then complete the square on the function in the brackets*

- *Halve the coefficient of  *$x$* for the constant inside the curved brackets*
- *and subtract that value squared*

$3 \left[\left(x - 1\right)^{2} - 1^{2}\right] + 5$

**[M1]**

> *Expand the square brackets and simplify*

$= 3 ( x - 1 ) ^{2} - 3 + 5$
$=3 \left(x - 1\right)^{2} + 2$

> *That's in the form required, with *$a=3$*, *$b=1$* and *$c=2$

$3 \left(x - 1\right)^{2} + 2$

**[A1]**

**Method 2**

> *You could expand the *$a(x--b)^{2}+c$* and compare coefficients*

$\begin{aligned}a \left(x – b\right)^{2} + c & = & a \left(x^{2} - 2 b x + b^{2}\right) + c \\ & = & a x^{2} - 2 a b x + a b^{2} + c\end{aligned}$

**[M1]**

> *Set that equal to the original quadratic*

$3x^{2}-6x+5=ax^{2}-2abx+ab^{2}+c$

> *Comparing coefficients*

$a=3$

$\begin{aligned}- 2 a b & = & - 6 \\ - 2 \times 3 \times b & = & - 6 \\ b & = & 1\end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned}a b^{2} + c & = & 5 \\ 3 \times 1^{2} + c & = & 5 \\ c + 3 & = & 5 \\ c & = & 2\end{aligned}$

**[M1]**

$3 \left(x - 1\right)^{2} + 2$

**[A1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> For Method 2:
> 
> **M1**: For expanding the expression correctly.
> 
> **M1**: For equating the coefficients of at least two of these.
> 
> **A1**: For writing the correct answer with *a*, *b* and *c* in the right places.

parts.problemMd: Write $2x^{2}+16x+35$ in the form $a \left(x + b\right)^{2}  +  c$ where $a,b,$ and $c$ are integers.
parts.solutionMd:
> *The result required is in completed square form. As the coefficient of **x*<sup>*2 *</sup>*is not 1, begin by factorising the number 2 from the first two terms of the expression. *

$\begin{aligned}2 x^{2} + 16 x + 35 & = & 2 \left(x^{2 } + 8 x\right) + 35\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Complete the square on the expression in the brackets. *

> *Set up a squared bracket with two terms; *$x$* and half of the coefficient of the *$x$* term - in this case 4. *

> *Considering that (**x **+ 4)*<sup>*2 *</sup>*= **x*<sup>*2 *</sup>*+ 8**x** + 16, we need to subtract 16.*

$\begin{aligned}2 \left(x^{2 } + 8 x\right) + 35 & = & 2 \left[\left(x + 4\right)^{2} - 16\right] + 25\end{aligned}$

> *Multiply out the 2.*

$\begin{aligned}2 x^{2} + 16 x + 35 & = & 2 \left[\left(x + 4\right)^{2} - 16\right] + 35 \\ & = & 2 \left(x + 4\right)^{2} - 32 + 35\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

$\begin{aligned} & = & 2 \left(x + 4\right)^{2} + 3\end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned}\mathbf{\mathit{a}} & = & 2 , \mathbf{\mathit{b}} = 4 , \mathbf{\mathit{c}} = 3\end{aligned}$ **[1]**

parts.problemMd: Express $7+12x--3x^{2}$ in the form $a+b(x+c)^{2}$ where $a,b$ and$c$are integers.
parts.solutionMd:
*Completing the square is easiest when dealing with a single, positive **x*<sup>*2*</sup>* term, so take a factor of -3.*

> *To avoid fractions, take this factor out of the **x*<sup>*2*</sup>* and **x** terms only.*

$7 + 12 x - 3 x^{2} = 7 - 3 \left(x^{2} - 4 x\right)$

**[1]**

> *Complete the square for the part in brackets.*

$7 - 3 \left(x^{2} - 4 x\right) = 7 - 3 \left[\left(x - 2\right)^{2} - 4\right]$

**[1]**

> *Expand and rearrange into the required form.*

$\begin{aligned}7 - 3 \left[\left(x - 2\right)^{2} - 4\right] & = & 7 - 3 \left(x - 2\right)^{2} + 12 \\ & = & 19 - 3 \left(x - 2\right)^{2}\end{aligned}$

$\therefore7+12x-3x^{2}=19-3(x-2)^{2}$ **[1]**

**i.e. **$a=19,b=-3,c=-2$**.**

parts.problemMd: Simplify fully $\left(\sqrt{a} + \sqrt{4 b} \right) \left(\sqrt{a} - 2 \sqrt{b}\right)$
parts.solutionMd:
*Method 1*

*Expand the brackets (by multiplying all terms in the first bracket by all terms in the second)* * *

$\sqrt{a \\times \sqrt{a} + \sqrt{a} \\times ( - 2 \sqrt{b} ) + \sqrt{4} b} \\times \sqrt{a + \sqrt{4} b} \\times ( - 2 \sqrt{b} )$
$= \sqrt{a \sqrt{a} - 2 \sqrt{a} \sqrt{b} + \sqrt{4} b} \sqrt{a - 2 \sqrt{4} b} \sqrt{b}$ * *

*Simplify *$\sqrt{4b}$* using the surd rule that *$\sqrt{xy}=\sqrt{x}\sqrt{y}$ * *

$\sqrt{4b}=\sqrt{4}\sqrt{b}=2\sqrt{b}$

**[1]**

*Replace *$\sqrt{4b}$*with *$2\sqrt{b}$*in the expansion above and cancel the middle terms* * *

$\sqrt{a} \sqrt{a} - \cancel{2 \sqrt{a} \sqrt{b} } + \cancel{2 \sqrt{b} \sqrt{a} } - 4 \sqrt{b} \sqrt{b}$
$=\sqrt{a} \sqrt{a}-4\sqrt{b} \sqrt{b}$ * *

*Simplify *$\sqrt{a}\sqrt{a}$* using the surd rule that *$\sqrt{x} \sqrt{x} = \left(\sqrt{x}\right)^{2} = x$ * *

$\sqrt{a}\sqrt{a}=a$

**[1]**

> *Replace *$\sqrt{a}\sqrt{a}$* with *$a$* and *$\sqrt{b}\sqrt{b}$* with *$b$* in the expansion*

$a-4b$* ***[1]**

> *Method 2*

*Simplify *$\sqrt{4b}$* using the surd rule that *$\sqrt{xy}=\sqrt{x}\sqrt{y}$ * *

$\sqrt{4b}=\sqrt{4}\sqrt{b}=2\sqrt{b}$

**[1]**

*Replace *$\sqrt{4b}$*with *$2\sqrt{b}$*in the question* * *

$\left(\sqrt{a} + 2 \sqrt{b}\right) \left(\sqrt{a} - 2 \sqrt{b}\right)$ * *

*This is the "difference of two squares", (**p** + **q**)(**p** - **q**) = **p*<sup>*2*</sup>* - **q*<sup>*2*</sup> *Use the "difference of two squares" to expand the brackets* * *

$\left(\sqrt{a}\right)^{2} - \left(2 \sqrt{b}\right)^{2}$ * *

*Square the terms* * *

$a-2^{2}b$

**[1]**

$a-4b$**[1]**

parts.problemMd: Solve           $\left(1 - x\right)^{2} < \frac{9}{25}$
parts.solutionMd:
*This is a quadratic inequality question*

*Method 1*

*Expand the brackets on the left, by writing it as (1 - **x**)(1 - **x**)* * *

$1-2x+x^{2}<\frac{9}{25}$ * *

*Multiply both sides by 25* * *

$25-50x+25x^{2}<9$ * *

*Subtract 9 from both sides* * *

$16-50x+25x^{2}<0$

**[1]*** *

*Reorder the terms* * *

$25x^{2}-50x+16<0$ * *

*Either "see" the factorisation or use solutions from a calculator that solves quadratic equations to skip to the next line* * *

$\left(5 x - 8\right) \left(5 x - 2\right) < 0$

*Find the critical points (the values of **x** that make each bracket zero)* * *

$\frac{8}{5}$* **and** *$\frac{2}{5}$

**[1]*** *

*These are the **x**-intercepts of the positive quadratic graph *$y = \left(5 x - 8\right) \left(5 x - 2\right)$

> *Find where the graph is below the **x**-axis, "< 0"*

*between the ***x***-intercepts*

$\frac{2}{5}<x<\frac{8}{5}$** [1]**

*Method 2*

*See that if *$a^{2}<\frac{9}{25}$* then *$a$* must be any number between *$-\frac{3}{5}<a<\frac{3}{5}$* (as "squaring" this part of the number line gives values that are <*$\frac{9}{25}$*)* * *

$-\frac{3}{5}<1-x<\frac{3}{5}$

**[1]*** *

*Multiply both sides by -1 (this will flip the inequality signs too)* * *

$\frac{3}{5}>-1+x>-\frac{3}{5}$ * *

*Add 1 to both sides* * *

$1+\frac{3}{5}>x>-\frac{3}{5}+1\,\frac{8}{5}>x>\frac{2}{5}$

**adding 1 to both sides ****[1]*** *

> *Write with the inequality signs the standard way round*

$\frac{2}{5}<x<\frac{8}{5}$* ***[1]**

parts.problemMd:
![q5-hard-2-3-expanding-brackets-edexcel-gcse-maths](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-18-higher/2-equations-formulae-and-identities/expanding-brackets/assets/001-q5-hard-2-3-expanding-brackets-edexcel-gcse-math.png)

The area of square $ABCD$ is $10$ cm<sup>2</sup>.

Show that $x^{2}+6x=1$
parts.solutionMd:
> *Method 1*

> *Add the two parts together to write down an expression for the side of the square.*

$AB=AD=3+x$

> *The total area of the square will be this expression squared. Form an expression for the total area of the square.*

$Total area = \left(3 + x\right)^{2}$

** ****[1]**

> *Expand the brackets, remember to multiply each term in the first by each term in the second.*

$\begin{aligned}\left(3 + x\right) \left(3 + x\right) & = & 9 + 3 x + 3 x + x^{2}\end{aligned}$

> *Simplify.*

$\begin{aligned}Total area & = & x^{2} + 6 x + 9 \end{aligned}$

> *Form an equation by setting this equal to 10.*

$\begin{aligned}x^{2} + 6 x + 9 & = & 10\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Reach the equation given in the question by subtracting 9 from each side.*

$\begin{aligned}x^{2} + 6 x + 9 & = & 10 \\ - 9 & = & - 9 \\ x^{2} + 6 x & = & 1\end{aligned}$

$x^{2}+6x=1$** [1]**

> *Method 2*

> *Write down an expression for the area of each part of the square individually.*

![lI_QDSbV_2-10-forming-and-solving-equations-easy-q5](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-18-higher/2-equations-formulae-and-identities/expanding-brackets/assets/002-li-qdsbv-2-10-forming-and-solving-equations-easy.png)

**At least two correct ****[1]**

> *The total area of the square will be the total of these four areas added together. *

> *Form an expression for the total area of the square.*

$\mathrm{Total} \mathrm{area}=9+3x+3x+x^{2}$

> *Form an equation by setting the total area equal to 10.*

$\begin{aligned}9 + 3 x + 3 x + x^{2} & = & 10\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Simplify.*

$\begin{aligned}x^{2} + 6 x + 9 & = & 10\end{aligned}$

> *Reach the equation given in the question by subtracting 9 from each side.*

$\begin{aligned}x^{2} + 6 x + 9 & = & 10 \\ - 9 & = & - 9 \\ x^{2} + 6 x & = & 1\end{aligned}$

$x^{2}+6x=1$** [1]**

parts.problemMd: Expand and simplify            $5 x \left(x + 2\right) \left(3 x - 4\right)$
parts.solutionMd:
*This can be considered as expanding three brackets, with the factor "5**x**" being the first bracket.*

> *The order of expanding brackets does not matter but it is easier here to start with the last two brackets.*

$\begin{aligned}5 x \left(x + 2\right) \left(3 x - 4\right) & = & 5 x \left(3 x^{2} - 4 x + 6 x - 8\right) \\ & = & 5 x \left(3 x^{2} + 2 x - 8\right)\end{aligned}$

**Expanding two brackets/factors**** [1]**

> *Now expand the "third" bracket, which in this case would be like expanding one bracket.*

parts.problemMd:
Given that $\left(8 - \sqrt{x}\right) \left(5 + \sqrt{x}\right) = y \sqrt{x} + 21$  where $x$ is a prime number and $y$ is an integer,

find the value of $x$ and the value of $y$.

Show each stage of your working clearly.

x = .............................................................

y = ............................................................
parts.solutionMd:
> *Expand the two brackets/factors on the left hand side.*

$\left(8 - \sqrt{x}\right) \left(5 + \sqrt{x}\right) = 40 + 8 \sqrt{x} - 5 \sqrt{x} - \left(\sqrt{x}\right)^{2}$

> *Simplify as far as possible.*

$40 + 8 \sqrt{x} - 5 \sqrt{x} - \left(\sqrt{x}\right)^{2} = 40 + 3 \sqrt{x} - x$

**[1]**

> *Now compare the left hand side and right hand side of the equation.*

$40+3\sqrt{x}-x=y\sqrt{x}+21$

> *The constant parts should be equal.*

$\begin{aligned}40 - x & = & 21 \\ x & = & 19\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

*(This meets the requirement that **x** is a prime number.)* *The "*$\sqrt{x}$*" terms should also be equal.*

$\begin{aligned}3 \sqrt{x} & = & y \sqrt{x} \\ y & = & 3\end{aligned}$

$x=19,y=3$** [1]**

> *Although this may at first appear to be a quadratic equations question, it's actually a linear equations question "in disguise"!*

> *Expand the brackets, noting that *$\left(2 x + 5\right)^{2} = \left(2 x + 5\right) \left(2 x + 5\right)$*.*

$4x^{2}+10x+10x+25=4x^{2}-2x+6x-3$

**[1]**

> *Collect like terms on both sides.*

$4x^{2}+20x+25=4x^{2}+4x-3$

> *Now subtract *$4x^{2}$* from both sides, to reveal the linear equation!*

$\begin{aligned}4 x^{2} + 20 x + 25 & = & 4 x^{2} + 4 x - 3 \\ - 4 x^{2 } & = & - 4 x^{2} \\ 20 x + 25 & = & 4 x - 3\end{aligned}$

> *Solve the linear equation. Subtract *$4x$* from both sides.*

$\begin{aligned}16 x + 25 & = & - 3\end{aligned}$

> *Subtract 25 from both sides.*

$\begin{aligned}16 x & = & - 28\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Divide both sides by 16.*

$\begin{aligned}x & = & \frac{- 28}{16} = - \frac{7}{4}\end{aligned}$

$x=-\frac{7}{4}$ ** [1]**

**−1.75 is accepted**

$\begin{aligned}- 20 x & = & - 100\end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned}x & = & \frac{- 100}{- 20} = 5\end{aligned}$

$x=5$ ** [1]**

parts.problemMd:
Here is an identity.

$a(3x--10)\equiv21x+2b$

Work out the values of $a$ and $b$.
parts.solutionMd:
> *Expand the brackets on the left hand side.*

$\begin{aligned}a \times 3 x + a \times \left(- 10\right) & \equiv & 21 x + 2 b \\ 3 a x - 10 a & \equiv & 21 x + 2 b\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Compare the *$x$* terms on both sides.*

$3ax=21x$

> *Solve the equation to find the value of *$a$*.*

$\begin{aligned}3 a & = & 21 \\ a & = & \frac{21}{3}\end{aligned}$

$a=7$* ***[1]**

> *Compare the constant terms in the original expanded identity.*

$-10a=2b$

> *Substitute *$a=7$* into the equation.*

$-10\times7=2b$

> *Solve to find the value of *$b$*.*

$\begin{aligned}- 70 & = & 2 b \\ - 35 & = & b\end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned}\mathbf{\mathit{b}} & = & - 35\end{aligned}$* ***[1]**

> *Expand the first two brackets by multiplying everything in the first bracket by everything in the second bracket.*

$\left(x \times x + 5 \times x + x \times 2 + 5 \times 2\right) \left(x + a\right)$

> *Simplify by completing the multiplications.*

$\left(x^{2} + 5 x + 2 x + 10\right) \left(x + a\right)$

> *Simplify the terms inside the first bracket by collecting "like" terms.*

$\left(x^{2} + 7 x + 10\right) \left(x + a\right)$

> *Expand the two remaining brackets by multiplying all three terms inside the first bracket by each of the terms inside the second bracket.*

$x^{2}\timesx+x^{2}\timesa+7x\timesx+7x\timesa+10\timesx+10\timesa$

> *Simplify by completing the multiplications.*

$x^{3}+ax^{2}+7x^{2}+7ax+10x+10a$

> *Simplify by collecting "like terms".*

$x^{3} + \left(a + 7\right) x^{2} + \left(7 a + 10\right) x + 10 a$

> *Equate the expanded expression to the given result.*

$x^{3} + \left(a + 7\right) x^{2} + \left(7 a + 10\right) x + 10 a \equiv x^{3} + b x^{2} + c x - 30$

> *Compare the constant term on both sides.*

$10a=-30$

> *Solve to find the values of *$a$*.*

$a=\frac{-30}{10}$

$a=-3$* ***[1]**

> *Compare the *$x^{2}$* term on both sides.*

$\begin{aligned}\left(a + 7\right) x^{2} & = & b x^{2} \\ a + 7 & = & b\end{aligned}$

> *Substitute *$a=-3$* into the equation and solve to find the value of *$b$*.*

$\left(- 3\right) + 7 = b$

$b=4$* ***[1]**

> *Compare the *$x$* term on both sides.*

$\begin{aligned}\left(7 a + 10\right) x & = & c x \\ 7 a + 10 & = & c\end{aligned}$

> *Substitute *$a=-3$* into the equation and solve to find the value of *$c$*.*

$\begin{aligned}7 \times \left(- 3\right) + 10 & = & c \\ - 21 + 10 & = & c\end{aligned}$

$c=-11$** [1]**

$a^{2}-b^{2}$

**[1]**

$\left(a + b\right) \left(a - b\right)$ * *

*Replace *$a$* with *$x^{2}+4$* in brackets and *$b$* with *$x^{2}-2$* in brackets* * *

$\left(\left(x^{2} + 4\right) + \left(x^{2} - 2\right)\right) \left(\left(x^{2} + 4\right) - \left(x^{2} - 2\right)\right)$ * *

*Expand inside the brackets* * *

$\left(x^{2} + 4 + x^{2} - 2\right) \left(x^{2} + 4 - x^{2} + 2\right)$

**[1]**

*Collect "like" terms* * *

$\left(2 x^{2} + 2\right) \left(6\right)$ * *

> *Multiply out the brackets (it may help to write the 6 at the front)*

$12x^{2}+12$* ***[1]**

*Method 2*

*Following the "or otherwise", write out the squared brackets as the product of two brackets* * *

$\left(x^{2} + 4\right) \left(x^{2} + 4\right) - \left(x^{2} - 2\right) \left(x^{2} - 2\right)$ * *

*Multiply out the two sets of brackets and collect like terms (keeping the results in their own separate brackets)* * *

$( x^{4} + 4 x ^{2} + 4 x ^{2} + 16 ) - ( x^{4} - 2 x ^{2} - 2 x ^{2} + 4 )$
$= ( x^{4} + 8 x ^{2} + 16 ) - ( x^{4} - 4 x ^{2} + 4 )$

**[1]**

*Remove the brackets (by multiplying all terms by -1 in the second bracket)* * *

$x^{4}+8x^{2}+16-x^{4}+4x^{2}-4$

**[1]**

> *Collect like terms*

$12x^{2}+12$* ***[1]**

parts.problemMd: Factorise fully  $15b^{5}c-35b^{3}c^{9}$
parts.solutionMd:
> *There is a lot going on in this question so deal with numbers first, then letters (in order they appear, usually alphabetically).*

*15 and 35 have a common factor of 5 so 5 will be "outside the bracket"*

> *There are *$b$*'s in both terms - the lowest power of which is *$b^{3}$*.*

$b^{3}$* will be outside the bracket*

> *The lowest power of *$c$*'s is *$c$*.*

$c$* will be outside the bracket*

> *Now construct the factorised answer by consider what is left by dividing each term by each factor listed above.*

$\begin{aligned}15 \div 5 & = & 3 and 35 \div 5 = 7 \\ b^{5} \div b^{3 } & = & b^{2} and b^{3} \div b^{3} = 1 \\ c \div c & = & 1 and c^{9} \div c = c^{8}\end{aligned}$

> *and so*

**Final answer:** `equation`** **

**Partially factorised ****[1] **
**Fully factorised ****[1]**

parts.problemMd: Factorise fully $2e^{2}--18$
parts.solutionMd:
> *We can see straight away there is a factor of 2 in both terms.*

$2 e^{2} - 18 = 2 \left(e^{2} - 9\right)$

**[1]**

> *Spot that *$e^{2}-9$* is the difference of two squares.*

$2 \left(e^{2} - 9\right) = 2 \left(e + 3\right) \left(e - 3\right)$

> *There is nothing else that can be factorised.*

$\therefore2e^{2}-18=2(e+3)(e-3)$ **[1]**

parts.problemMd: Factorise  $4c^{2}--9d^{2}$
parts.solutionMd:
> *Spotting that 4 and 9 are square numbers leads us to this being the difference of two squares.*

$4 c^{2} - 9 d^{2} = \left(2 c\right)^{2} - \left(3 d\right)^{2}$

> *So*

$\left(2 c\right)^{2} - \left(3 d\right)^{2} = \left(2 c + 3 d\right) \left(2 c - 3 d\right)$

$4c^{2}-9d^{2}=(2c+3d)(2c-3d)$ **[1]**

parts.problemMd: Factorise  $6y^{2}--y--5$
parts.solutionMd:
> *Recognise this is a quadratic expression and is non-monic (**a** ≠ 1), so use factorising "by grouping". *

> *Find the product "**ac**".*

$a c = 6 \times \left(- 5\right) = - 30$

> *Consider "**b**".*

$b=-1$

> *We need two numbers whose product is -30 and sum is -1.*

$-6\mathrm{and}5$

> *Rewrite the middle term using these values.*

$6y^{2}-y-5=6y^{2}-6y+5y-5$

> *Factorise the first pair of terms and the second pair of terms.*

$6 y^{2} - 6 y + 5 y - 5 = 6 y \left(y - 1\right) + 5 \left(y - 1\right)$

**[1]**

> *Now factorise *$\left(y - 1\right)$* from each of these terms.*

$6 y \left(y - 1\right) + 5 \left(y - 1\right) = \left(y - 1\right) \left(6 y + 5\right)$

$6y^{2}-y-5=(y-1)(6y+5)$ **[1]**

parts.problemMd: Factorise  $3x^{2}+11x--20$
parts.solutionMd:
*Multiply 3 by -20 (the first and last numbers)*

*3 × -20 = -60*

*Find two numbers that multiply to give -60 and add to give 11 (the middle number)*

*15 and -4*

*Split the middle term into 15**x** and -4**x*

$3x^{2}+15x-4x-20$

*Factorise fully the first pair of terms and the second pair of terms *

$3 x \left(x + 5\right) - 4 \left(x + 5\right)$

**or x(3x - 4) + 5(3x - 4) if terms written other way round**** [1] **

*Factorise out the whole (x + 5) bracket as if it were one term, leaving 3**x** and -4 in their own bracket*

$\left(x + 5\right) \left(3 x - 4\right)$

$(x+5)(3x-4)$ **[1]**

parts.problemMd: Factorise   $3x^{2}+14x+8$
parts.solutionMd:
> *The coefficient of the *$x^{2}$* term is not 1 so you can factorise the expression by grouping and factorising.*

> *Find the product of the coefficient of the *$x^{2}$* term and the constant term.*

$3\times8=24$

> *Find the factor pairs of this product.*

$1,24\mathrm{or}-1,-24\,2,12\mathrm{or}-2,-12\,3,8\mathrm{or}-3,-8\,4,6\mathrm{or}-4,-6$

> *Find the factor pair that adds together to give you the same value as the coefficient of the *$x$* term.*

$2,12:2+12=14$

> *Rewrite the original expression splitting up the *$x$* term using the values determined above.*

$3x^{2}+2x+12x+8$

> *Group the terms into two pairs, the first two terms as one pair and the last two terms as the second pair. *

> *Factorise both pairs of terms.*

$x \left(3 x + 2\right) + 4 \left(3 x + 2\right)$

> *Both terms in the expression have a factor of *$\left(3 x + 2\right)$*, so can now be factorised with this as the common factor.*

$(3x+2)(x+4)$

**Factorisation to **$\left(3 x + a\right) \left(x + b\right)$** where **$ab=8$** or  **$a+3b=14$** ****[1] ****Fully correct factorisation**** [1]**

parts.problemMd:
The diagram shows a rectangle.

![q1-easy-2-13-forming-and-solving-equations-edexcel-gcse-maths](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-18-higher/2-equations-formulae-and-identities/forming-and-solving-equations/assets/048-q1-easy-2-13-forming-and-solving-equations-edexc.png)

All measurements are given in centimetres.

The perimeter of the rectangle is 45 cm.

Work out the value of $x.$
parts.solutionMd:
> *The perimeter of a shape is the sum of the lengths of its sides. For a rectangle this is length + width + length + width, or 2(length + width).*

> *Use this to form an expression for the perimeter of the rectangle.*

$\begin{aligned}P & = & l + w + l + w \\ P & = & 2 l + 2 w \\ & = & 2 \left(x\right) + 2 \left(x + 4\right) \end{aligned}$

** **** [1]**

> *Form an equation for the perimeter of the rectangle, setting it equal to 45 cm.*

$\begin{aligned}Perimeter & = & 45 \\ 2 \left(x\right) + 2 \left(x + 4\right) & = & 45\end{aligned}$

** **** [1]**

> *Simplify by first expanding the brackets and collecting the like terms.*

$\begin{aligned}2 x + 2 x + 8 & = & 45 \\ 4 x + 8 & = & 45\end{aligned}$

> *Solve the equation to find *$x$*.*

$\begin{aligned}4 x + 8 & = & 45 \\ - 8 & = & - 8 \\ 4 x & = & 37 \\ \div 4 & = & \div 4 \\ x & = & \frac{37}{4} \end{aligned}$

$x=9.25\mathrm{cm}$**  ****[1]**

parts.problemMd:
Kalinda buys $x$ packs of currant buns and $y$ boxes of iced buns.

There are 6 currant buns in a pack of currant buns.
 There are 8 iced buns in a box of iced buns.

Kalinda buys a total of $T$ buns.
 Write down a formula for $T$ in terms of $x$ and $y$.
parts.solutionMd:
> *Write down an expression, in terms of *$x$* for 6 currant buns.*

$\begin{aligned}1 currant bun & = & x \\ 6 currant buns & = & 6 \times x = 6 x\end{aligned}$

> *Write down an expression, in terms of *$y$* for 8 iced buns.*

$\begin{aligned}1 iced bun & = & y \\ 8 iced buns & = & 8 \times y = 8 y\end{aligned}$

** Either correct ****[1]**

> *T **is the total of 6 currant buns and 8 iced buns.*

> *Use this to write a formula for **T** in terms of **x** and **y**.*

$\begin{aligned}T & = & 6 currant buns + 8 iced buns = 6 x + 8 y\end{aligned}$

**Adding both terms ****[1]**

$T=6x+8y$**  ****[1]**

$\begin{aligned}T & = & 5 x + 20 y\end{aligned}$

parts.problemMd:
3 kg of potatoes and 4 kg of carrots have a total cost of 440p. 
4 kg of potatoes and 3 kg of carrots have a total cost of 470p.

Work out the total cost of 1 kg of potatoes and 1 kg of carrots.
parts.solutionMd:
> *Method 1*

> *Let potatoes be **p** and carrots be **c. *

> *Use the information in the question to write two equations:*

> *3 kg of potatoes = 3**p, **4 kg of carrots = 4**c *

$3p+4c=440$

> *4 kg of potatoes = 4**p, **3 kg of carrots = 3**c *

$4p+3c=470$

> *Number the equations.*

> $\begin{aligned}3 p + 4 c & = & 440 \left(1\right) \\ 4 p + 3 c & = & 470 \left(2\right)\end{aligned}$* *

**[1]**

> *This is a non calculator paper so the easiest method is to spot that adding the two equations will give and equal number of potatoes and carrots.*

> *The questions asks for the price of 1 kg of potatoes and 1 kg of carrots, so there is no need to find their individual prices.*

> *Add equation (1) to equation (2).*

$\begin{matrix} 3 p + 4 c = 440 \\ \underline{+ \left(4 p + 3 c = 470 \right)} \\ 7 p + 7 c = 910 \end{matrix}$

**[1]**

> *This gives the cost of 7 kg of potatoes and 7 kg of carrots. *

> *Find the cost of 1 kg of each by dividing by 7.*

space space 7 p space plus space 7 c space equals space 910 space
$7 ( p + c ) = 910$
$p + c = \frac{ 910}{7}$

**[1]**

> *This finds the total cost of 1 kg of carrots and 1 kg of potatoes.*

$p+c=130p$* ***[1]**

> *Method 2*

> *Let potatoes be **p** and carrots be **c. *

> *Use the information in the question to write two equations:*

> *3 kg of potatoes = 3**p, **4 kg of carrots = 4**c *

$3p+4c=440$

> *4 kg of potatoes = 4**p, **3 kg of carrots = 3**c *

$4p+3c=470$

> *Number the equations.*

> $\begin{aligned}3 p + 4 c & = & 440 \left(1\right) \\ 4 p + 3 c & = & 470 \left(2\right)\end{aligned}$* *

**[1]**

> *Make the **p** terms equal by multiplying all parts of equation (1) by 4 and all parts of equation (2) by 3.*

> $\begin{aligned} & & 4 \left(1\right) 4 \left(3 p + 4 c = 440\right) \\ & & 3 \left(2\right) 3 \left(4 p + 3 c = 470\right) \end{aligned}$*  *

> *This gives the two new equations:*

$\begin{aligned}12 p + 16 c & = & 1760 \left(3\right) \\ 12 p + 9 c & = & 1410 \left(4\right)\end{aligned}$

> *Eliminate the **p** terms by subtracting equation (4) from equation (3).*

$\begin{array}{r} 12 p + 16 c = 1760 \\ \underline{ - \left(12 p + 9 c = 1410\right) } \\ 7 c = 350 \end{array}$

**[1]**

> *Solve the equation to find** c  **by dividing both sides by 7.*

$\begin{aligned}c & = & \frac{350}{7} = 50\end{aligned}$

> *Substitute *$c=50$* into either of the two original equations**.*

$\begin{aligned}\left(2\right) 3 p + 4 c & = & 440 \\ 3 p + 4 \left(50\right) & = & 440 \\ 3 p + 200 & = & 440\end{aligned}$

> *Solve this equation to find** p.*

$\begin{aligned}3 p + 200 & = & 440 \\ 3 p & = & 240 \\ p & = & \frac{240}{3} = 80 \end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *This means that 1 kg of carrots is 50p and 1 kg of potatoes is 80p.*

> *Add them together to get the total.*

$p+c=130p$* ***[1]**

parts.solutionMd:
> *Method 1*

> *Angles in a quadrilateral add up to 360*<sup>*o*</sup>*.*

*Write down an equation adding together all four angles.*

$2x+2x+(3x-15)+(2x+24)=360$

> *You can rewrite the equation without brackets.*

$2x+2x+3x-15+2x+24=360$

**[1]**

> *Rearrange the equation so that like terms are next to each other, remember to keep the sign in front of each term the same as it was when you re-arrange. *

$2x+2x+3x+2x-15+24=360$

> *Add/subtract the like terms, being careful with negatives!*

$9x+9=360$

**[1]**

> *Solve the equation. *

> *It may be easiest to factorise the 9 out first.*

$\begin{aligned}9 x + 9 & = & 360 \\ 9 \left(x + 1\right) & = & 360 \\ x + 1 & = & \frac{ 360}{9} \\ x + 1 & = & 40 \\ x & = & 39\end{aligned}$

$x=39^{\circ}$ **[1]**

> *Method 2*

> *Opposite angles in a parallelogram are equal.*

> *Write down an equation for the two opposite angles that have **different **expressions.*

$3x-15=2x+24$

**[1]**

> *Solve the equation by first bringing the **x** terms to one side. *

> * The easiest method is to subtract the **x** term with the smallest coefficient.*

$\begin{aligned}3 x - 15 & = & 2 x + 24 \\ - 2 x & = & - 2 x \\ x - 15 & = & 24\end{aligned}$

> *Add 15 to both sides.*

$\begin{aligned}x - 15 & = & 24 \\ + 15 & = & + 15 \\ x & = & 39 \end{aligned}$

**[1]**

$x=39^{\circ}$ **[1]**

$\begin{aligned}2 \left(4 + 3 x\right) + 2 \left(x + 6\right) & = & 32 \\ 8 + 6 x + 2 x + 12 & = & 32 \\ 8 x + 20 & = & 32\end{aligned}$

> *Solve the equation to find *$x$*.*

**[1]**

parts.problemMd:
Becky has some marbles. 
Chris has two times as many marbles as Becky. 
Dan has seven more marbles than Chris.

They have a total of 57 marbles.

Dan says, 
"If I give some marbles to Becky, each of us will have the same number of marbles."

Is Dan correct? 
You must show how you get your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
> *Let Becky (**B** ) have *$x$* marbles.*

> *Write down an expression, in terms of *$x$*, for the number of marbles that  Chris (**C **) and Dan (**D **) have.  *

$\begin{aligned}B & = & x \\ C & = & 2 B = 2 x \\ D & = & C + 7 = 2 x + 7\end{aligned}$

**At least**** ****C**** ****or D correct**** [1]**

> *Use this to form an expression for the total number of marbles.*

$\begin{aligned}T & = & B + C + D \\ & = & x + 2 x + \left(2 x + 7\right) \end{aligned}$

> *The total number of marbles is 57. *

> *Form an equation for the total number of marbles, setting it equal to 57.*

$\begin{aligned}T & = & 57 \\ x + 2 x + 2 x + 7 & = & 57 \\ 5 x + 7 & = & 57\end{aligned}$

** **** [1]**

> *Solve the equation to find *$x$*.*

$\begin{aligned}5 x + 7 & = & 57 \\ - 7 & = & - 7 \\ 5 x & = & 50 \\ \div 5 & = & \div 5 \\ x & = & \frac{50}{5} = 10\end{aligned}$

> *Dan can only be correct is his and Becky's marbles add up to double the number of Chris' marbles. *

> $x=10$* so Becky has 10 marbles, Chris has 2(10) = 20 marbles and Dan has 20 + 7 = 27 marbles.*

$\begin{aligned}B + D & = & 10 + 27 \neq 2 C\end{aligned}$

**Dan is not correct, as he and Becky would need to have 40 marbles in total.****  [1]**
