parts.problemMd:
$ABCED$ is a five-sided shape.

![q19-4ma1-1h-qp-nov21-paper1-igcse-maths](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-18-higher/3-sequences-functions-and-graphs/differentiation/assets/004-q19-4ma1-1h-qp-nov21-paper1-igcse-maths.png)

$ABCD$ is a rectangle.
 $CED$ is an equilateral triangle.

$AB=x\mathrm{cm}BC=y\mathrm{cm}$

The perimeter of $ABCED$is 100 cm.
 The area of $ABCED$is $R$ cm<sup>2</sup>

Show that $R = \frac{x}{4} \left(200 - \left[6 - \sqrt{3}\right] x\right)$
parts.solutionMd:
> *The length of **DE **and **CE** are both *$x$* so;*

$\mathrm{perimeter} \mathrm{of}ABCED=3x+2y$

> *Equate this to 100 and write *$y$* in terms of *$x$*.*

$\begin{aligned}3 x + 2 y & = & 100 \\ 2 y & = & 100 - 3 x \\ y & = & \frac{100 - 3 x}{2}\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *We can now write an expression for the area of rectangle **ABCD** in terms of *$x$* *

$\begin{aligned}area A B C D & = & x y \\ & = & x \left(\frac{100 - 3 x}{2}\right)\end{aligned}$

> *Triangle **CED **is equilateral so all its internal angles are 60°. So its area is;*

$\mathrm{area}CED=\frac{1}{2}x\timesx\times\mathrm{sin}60^{\circ}$

> *It's useful to know that *$\mathrm{sin}60^{\circ}=\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}$* (and *$\mathrm{sin}30^{\circ}=\frac{1}{2}$*) but you can also obtain the exact value of *$\mathrm{sin}60^{\circ}$* from your calculator. *

$\begin{aligned}area C E D & = & \frac{1}{2} x^{2} \times \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\ & = & \frac{\sqrt{3}}{4} x^{2}\end{aligned}$

> *Thus *$R$*, the total area of **ABCED **in terms of *$x$*, **is;*

$\begin{aligned}R & = & Area A B C D + Area C E D \\ & = & x \left(\frac{100 - 3 x}{2}\right) + \frac{\sqrt{3}}{4} x^{2}\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Rewrite by factorising *$\frac{x}{4}$* out of both parts of the equation.*

> $\begin{aligned}A & = & \frac{x}{4} \left(2 \left(100 - 3 x\right)\right) + \frac{x}{4} \left(\sqrt{3} x\right) \\ & = & \frac{x}{4} \left(200 - 6 x\right) + \frac{x}{4} \left(\sqrt{3} x\right)\end{aligned}$* *

> *(note that the *$x$* lies outside the *$\sqrt{3}$*)*

> $\frac{x}{4}$* is outside both brackets so this can be simplified into one bracket using the distributive law.*

$\begin{aligned}A & = & \frac{x}{4} \left(200 - 6 x + \sqrt{3} x\right)\end{aligned}$

`equation`** ****[1]**

**Final line with at least one correct step in between this and penultimate method mark.**

parts.problemMd:
(i) Find the value of $x$ for which $R$ has its maximum value.

Give your answer in the form $\frac{p}{q-\sqrt{3}}$ where $p$ and $q$ are integers.

$x=$ ....................................................... [2]

(ii) Explain why the maximum value of $R$ is given by this value of $x$.

[1]
parts.solutionMd:
*i)** **We need to differentiate *$R$*. Start by expanding the outer bracket.*

$\begin{aligned}R & = & \frac{x}{4} \times 200 - \frac{x}{4} \left[6 - \sqrt{3}\right] x \\ & = & 50 x - \left(\frac{6 - \sqrt{3}}{4}\right) x^{2}\end{aligned}$

> *Now differentiate.*

$\begin{aligned}\frac{d R }{d x} & = & 50 - 2 \left(\frac{6 - \sqrt{3}}{4}\right) x\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Simplify and equate to zero to find stationary points.*

$\begin{aligned}50 - \left(\frac{6 - \sqrt{3}}{2}\right) x & = & 0\end{aligned}$

> *Solve for **x. **(This is a linear equation so there is only one stationary point, so it must be the maximum asked for in the question.)*

$\begin{aligned}50 & = & \left(\frac{6 - \sqrt{3}}{2}\right) x \\ 100 & = & \left(6 - \sqrt{3}\right) x\end{aligned}$

$\mathbf{\mathit{x}} = \begin{aligned} & & \frac{100}{6 - \sqrt{3}}\end{aligned}$ **[1]**

> *ii) The intention of this question could be made clearer by asking "Explain how you know this is the maximum value of *$R$* rather than a minimum or point of inflection".*

> *The equation *$\begin{aligned}R & = & 50 x - \left(\frac{6 - \sqrt{3}}{4}\right) x^{2}\end{aligned}$* is a **quadratic equation** with a negative coefficient of *$x^{2}$*. Therefore it is an** n-shaped parabola** and has only one stationary point, which is a maximum.*

$R$** is a quadratic with a negative coefficient of **$x^{2}$** so it is an n-shaped parabola ****[1]**

**Any suitable statement that makes reference to the shape of the quadratic curve of **$R$**.**

**(It is also valid to answer this question using **$\frac{d^{2}R}{dx^{2}}<0$** if you have been taught about second derivatives- though this knowledge is not required for IGCSE exams.)**

parts.problemMd:
A particle moves along a straight line. 
The fixed point $O$ lies on this line. 
The displacement of the particle from $O$ at time $t$ seconds , `t space greater-than or slanted equal to space 0` , is $s$ metres where

$s=t^{3}+4t^{2}-5t+7$

At time $T$ seconds the velocity of $P$ is $Vm/s$ where `V space greater-than or slanted equal to space minus 5`

Find an expression for $T$ in terms of $V$.

Give your expression in the form $\frac{-4+\sqrt{k+mV}}{3}$ where $k$$m$ and  are integers to be found.

$T=...............$
parts.solutionMd:
> *Differentiate *$s$* with respect to *$t$* to get an equation for the velocity.*

$\frac{ds}{dt}=v=3t^{2}+8t-5$

**[1]**

> *Substitute *$\left(V , T\right)$* into the equation for velocity.*

$V=3T^{2}+8T-5$

**[1]**

> *Rearrange to equal zero.*

$\begin{aligned}3 T^{2} + 8 T - 5 - V & = & 0\end{aligned}$

> *Now solve for *$T$*, treating "*$-5-V$*" as the  *$c$* in *$ax^{2}+bx+c=0$* ! This can be done by completing the square or using the quadratic formula- but the quadratic formula is recommended as the easier method in this instance.*

$T = \frac{- 8 \pm \sqrt{8^{2} - 4 \times 3 \times \left(- 5 - V\right)}}{2 \times 3}$

**correct substitution into quadratic formula, or at least one correct step of completing the square ****[1]**

> *Evaluate.*

$\begin{aligned}T & = & \frac{- 8 \pm \sqrt{64 - 12 \times \left(- 5 - V\right)}}{6} \\ & = & \frac{- 8 \pm \sqrt{64 + 60 + 12 V}}{6} \\ & = & \frac{- 8 \pm \sqrt{124 + 12 V}}{6}\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Factorise the 4 from *$124+12V$* so that the surd can be simplified.*

$\begin{aligned} & = & \frac{- 8 \pm \sqrt{4 \left(31 + 3 V\right)}}{6} \\ & = & \frac{- 8 \pm \sqrt{4} \sqrt{31 + 3 V}}{6} \\ & = & \frac{- 8 \pm 2 \sqrt{31 + 3 V}}{6}\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Finally, cancel down the fraction.*

$\begin{aligned} & = & \frac{- \cancel{8} \pm \cancel{2} \sqrt{31 + 3 \mathbf{V}}}{\cancel{6}} = \frac{- 4 \pm \sqrt{31 + 3 \mathbf{V}}}{3}\end{aligned}$* ***[1]**

$g \left(2 x - 5\right) = \left(2 x - 5\right)^{2} - 10$

**[1]**

> *Form an equation for **x** by setting this expression equal to -1  *

> * *$\left(2 x - 5\right)^{2} - 10 = - 1$*  *

**[1]**

> *Method 1** *

> *Make **x** the subject *

> *Start by adding 10 to both sides  *

> $\left(2 x - 5\right)^{2} = 9$*  *

> *Take square roots of both sides and include a ± sign  *

$2x-5=\pm\sqrt{9}\,2x-5=\pm3$

**[1]**

> *Solve 2**x** - 5 = 3 and 2**x** - 5 = -3 separately (by adding 5 to both sides and dividing both sides by 2)  *

$2x-5=3\,2x=8\,x=4$* **and**   *$2x-5=-3\,2x=2\,x=1$

**x**** = 1 or ****x**** = 4*** ***[1]**

> *Method 2** *

> *Form a quadratic equation in **x** *

> *Start by expanding (2**x** - 5)2  *

> $\begin{aligned}\left(2 x - 5\right)^{2} & = & \left(2 x - 5\right) \left(2 x - 5\right) \\ & = & 4 x^{2} - 10 x - 10 x + 25 \\ & = & 4 x^{2} - 20 x + 25\end{aligned}$*  *

> *Write the result back in the equation  *

$\begin{aligned}4 x^{2} - 20 x + 25 - 10 & = & - 1 \\ 4 x^{2} - 20 x + 15 & = & - 1\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Make the right-hand side zero (by adding 1 to both sides)  *

> $4x^{2}-20x+16=0$*  *

> *Divide both sides by 4  *

> $x^{2}-5x+4=0$*  *

> *Factorise the quadratic expression (for example, by finding two numbers that multiply to give 4 and add to give -5)  *

> $\left(x - 4\right) \left(x - 1\right) = 0$*  *

> *Solve the first bracket equal to zero (by adding 4 to both sides)  *

> $\begin{aligned}x - 4 & = & 0 \\ x & = & 4\end{aligned}$*  *

> *Solve the second bracket equal to zero (by adding 1 to both sides)  *

$\begin{aligned}x - 1 & = & 0 \\ x & = & 1\end{aligned}$

**x**** = 1 or ****x**** = 4*** ***[1]**

parts.problemMd:
The function f is such that $f(x)=x^{2}--8x+5$ where `x space less-than or slanted equal to space 4` Express the inverse function $f^{-1}$ in the form $f^{--1}(x)=...$

$f^{--1}(x)=................$
parts.solutionMd:
> *Finding the inverse of a quadratic function requires completing the square.*

> *Write the function in the form *$y=x^{2}-8x+5$* and then swap the *$x$* and *$y.$*  *

$y=x^{2}-8x+5\,x=y^{2}-8y+5$

> *Rearrange **the expression to make *$y$* the subject again by first completing the square.  *

> *The formula for completing the square for a quadratic in the form*$x^{2}+bx+c$*is*$\left(x + \frac{b}{2}\right)^{2} - \left(\frac{b}{2}\right)^{2} + c$*.*

> *Complete the square by dividing the middle term (-8) by 2.*

$\begin{aligned}y^{2} - 8 y + 5 & = & \left(y - \frac{8}{2}\right)^{2 } - \left(\frac{8}{2}\right)^{2} + 5 \\ & = & \left(y - 4\right)^{2} - 4^{2} + 5\end{aligned}$

**Correct first step to complete square**** [1]**

> *Simplify.*

$\begin{aligned}\left(y - 4\right)^{2} - 4^{2} + 5 & = & \left(y - 4\right)^{2} - 16 + 5 \\ & = & \left(y - 4\right)^{2} - 11\end{aligned}$

> *Set equal to *$x$* and rearrange to make *$y$* the subject.*

$x = \left(y - 4\right)^{2} - 11$

> *Rearrange **the expression to make *$y$* the subject again.*

$\begin{aligned}x + 11 & = & \left(y - 4\right)^{2} \\ y - 4 & = & \pm \sqrt{x + 11} \\ y & = & \pm \sqrt{x + 11} + 4 \\ y & = & 4 \pm \sqrt{x + 11}\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *The domain of f(x) is *$x\leq4$* so this must be the range of the inverse, taking the negative square root will give *$y\leq4$*. *
*Rewrite using the correct notation for an inverse function.*

$f^{-1}(x)=4-\sqrt{x+11}$ **[1]**

> *Finding the inverse of a quadratic function requires completing the square.*

> *Write the function in the form *$y=5+6x-x^{2}$*, rearrange to normal quadratic form and then swap the *$x$* and *$y.$*  *

$y=-x^{2}+6x+5\,x=-y^{2}+6y+5$

> *Rearrange **the expression to make *$y$* the subject again by first completing the square.*

> *Completing the square is easiest when dealing with a single, positive **y*<sup>*2*</sup>* term, so take a factor of -1.*

*This is only necessary for the **y*<sup>*2*</sup>* and **y** terms so leave 5 as it is.*

$- y^{2 } + 6 y + 5 = - \left(y^{2} - 6 y\right) + 5$

> *Complete the square for the part in brackets.*

$- \left(y^{2} - 6 y\right) + 5 = - \left[\left(y - 3\right)^{2} - 9\right] + 5$

**[1]**

> *Expand and rearrange into the required completed square form.*

$\begin{aligned}- \left[\left(y + 3\right)^{2} - 9\right] + 5 & = & - \left(y + 3\right)^{2} + 9 + 5 \\ & = & 14 - \left(y + 3\right)^{2}\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

parts.problemMd:
The functions $f$ and $g$ are such that

$f(x)=x+25g(x)=x^{2}--12x$

The function $h$ is such that $h(x)=\mathrm{fg}(x)$

The domain of $h$ is $\left\{x  :  x \leq 6\right\}$

Express the inverse function $h^{--1}$ in the form $h^{--1}(x)=...$

$h^{--1}(x)=.....................$
parts.solutionMd:
*Find the function h(**x**) by finding the composite function fg(**x**), where fg(**x**) means f(g(**x**)).*

> *Write the algebraic expression for g(**x**) inside f(...).*

$h \left(x\right) = f \left(g \left(x\right)\right) = f \left(x^{2} - 12 x\right)$ * *

> *Find *$f \left(x^{2} - 12 x\right)$* by replacing the **x**'s in f(**x**) with the brackets *$\left(x^{2} - 12 x\right)$*.*

$h \left(x\right) = f \left(x^{2} - 12 x\right) = \left(x^{2} - 12 x\right) + 25 = x^{2} - 12 x + 25$

**[1]**

> *Find the inverse of h(**x**) by completing the square.*

> *Write the function in the form *$y = h \left(x\right)$* and then swap the *$x$* and *$y.$

$y=x^{2}-12x+25\,x=y^{2}-12y+25$

> *Rearrange **the expression to make *$y$* the subject again by first completing the square. *

> *The formula for completing the square for a quadratic in the form*$x^{2}+bx+c$*is*$\left(x + \frac{b}{2}\right)^{2} - \left(\frac{b}{2}\right)^{2} + c$*.*

> *Complete the square by dividing the middle term (-12) by 2.*

$\begin{aligned}y^{2} - 12 y + 25 & = & \left(y - \frac{12}{2}\right)^{2 } - \left(\frac{12}{2}\right)^{2} + 25 \\ & = & \left(y - 6\right)^{2} - 6^{2} + 25\end{aligned}$

**Correct first step to complete square**** [1]**

> *Simplify.*

$\begin{aligned}\left(y - 6\right)^{2} - 6^{2} + 25 & = & \left(y - 6\right)^{2} - 36 + 25 \\ & = & \left(y - 6\right)^{2} - 11\end{aligned}$

> *Set equal to *$x$* and rearrange to make *$y$* the subject.*

$x = \left(y - 6\right)^{2} - 11$

> *Rearrange **the expression to make *$y$* the subject again.*

$\begin{aligned}x + 11 & = & \left(y - 6\right)^{2} \\ y - 6 & = & \pm \sqrt{x + 11} \\ y & = & \pm \sqrt{x + 11} + 6 \\ y & = & 6 \pm \sqrt{x + 11}\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *The domain of h(**x**) is *$x\leq6$* so this must be the range of the inverse, taking the negative square root will give *$y\leq6$*. *

> *Rewrite using the correct notation for an inverse function.*

$h^{-1}(x)=6-\sqrt{x+11}$ **[1]**

parts.solutionMd:

> *Write the algebraic expression for g(**x**) inside f(...).*

$h \left(x\right) = f \left(g \left(x\right)\right) = f \left(x + 3\right)$ * *

$\begin{aligned}h \left(x\right) & = & f \left(x + 3\right) \\ & = & \left(x + 3\right)^{2} - 2 \left(x + 3\right) \\ & = & x^{2} + 6 x + 9 - 2 x - 6 \\ & = & x^{2} + 4 x + 3\end{aligned}$

**substituting x + 3 into f(x) ****[1]**

> *Finding the inverse of h(**x**) will require completing the square*

> *First, write the function in the form *$y = h \left(x\right)$* and then swap the** x** and **y*

$y=x^{2}+4x+3\,x=y^{2}+4y+3$

> *Rearrange** **the expression to make *$y$* the subject again by completing the square *

> *The formula for completing the square for a quadratic in the form*$x^{2}+bx+c$*is*$\left(x + \frac{b}{2}\right)^{2} - \left(\frac{b}{2}\right)^{2} + c$*.*

> *Completing the square requires dividing the middle term, 4, by 2*

$\begin{aligned}y^{2} + 4 y + 3 & = & \left(y + \frac{ 4}{2}\right)^{2 } - \left(\frac{4}{2}\right)^{2} + 3 \\ & = & \left(y + 2\right)^{2} - 2^{2} + 3\end{aligned}$

> *Rearrange** **the expression to make *$y$* the subject again by completing the square *

parts.problemMd:
The function f is defined as $f(x)=\frac{\sqrt{x^{2}+k^{2}}}{x}$ for $x>0$ and where $k$ is a positive number.

Find the value of $p$ for which $f^{-1}(p)=k$

$p=$
parts.solutionMd:
*Method 1*

*Find the inverse function, f*<sup>*-1*</sup>*(**x) **by first replacing f(**x**) with **y* * *

$y=\frac{\sqrt{x^{2}+k^{2}}}{x}$ * *

*Without rearranging the equation, swap the **x**'s and **y**'s* * *

$x=\frac{\sqrt{y^{2}+k^{2}}}{y}$

*Now make **y** the subject of this new equation (for example, by squaring both sides then multiplying both sides by y*<sup>*2*</sup>*)* * *

$\begin{aligned}x^{2} & = & \frac{y^{2} + k^{2}}{y^{2}} \\ x^{2} y^{2} & = & y^{2} + k^{2} \\ x^{2} y^{2} - y^{2} & = & k^{2} \\ y^{2} \left(x^{2} - 1\right) & = & k^{2} \\ y^{2} & = & \frac{k^{2}}{x^{2} - 1}\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Square-root both sides  *

> $y=\pm\sqrt{\frac{k^{2}}{x^{2}-1}}$*   *

*The sign on the right-hand side must be chosen to give us f*<sup>*-1*</sup>*(**x**) The domain of f(**x**) is all positive values (**x** > 0) so the range of f*<sup>*-1*</sup>*(**x**) must be all positive values (take the positive square root)*

$f^{- 1} \left(x\right) = \sqrt{\frac{k^{2}}{x^{2} - 1}}$

*Create the equation* *f*<sup>*-1*</sup>*(**x**) = **k **by substituting **x** = **p** into f*<sup>*-1*</sup>*(**x**) and setting it equal to **k**  *

$\sqrt{\frac{k^{2}}{p^{2}-1}}=k$

**[1]**

> *Solve this equation for **p** (make **p** the subject)  *

$\begin{aligned}\frac{k^{2}}{p^{2} - 1} & = & k^{2} \\ \cancel{k^{2}} & = & \cancel{k^{2}} \left(p^{2} - 1\right) \\ 1 & = & p^{2} - 1 \\ 2 & = & p^{2} \\ \pm \sqrt{2} & = & p\end{aligned}$

> * *

> *p** is an input of the inverse function, which makes it an output of the original function, and all outputs are positive in this question (the domain of f is **x** > 0 which makes *$\frac{\sqrt{x^{2}+k^{2}}}{x}$* positive) **p** must therefore be positive, so choose the positive square root*

$p=\sqrt{2}$* ***[1]**

*Method 2*** **

*Apply the function f to both sides of the equation f*<sup>*-1*</sup>*(**p**) = **k* * *

$ff^{- 1} \left(p\right) = f \left(k\right)$ * *

> *The input **p **on the left first goes through the function f*<sup>*-1*</sup>*, but then has this immediately "undone" by going through the function f *

*The f and the f*<sup>*-1*</sup>* cancel each other out (they are inverses of each other)* * *

$p = f \left(k\right)$

**[1]*** *

*Find f(**k**) by substituting **x** = **k** into f(**x**)*

$p=\frac{\sqrt{k^{2}+k^{2}}}{k}$

**[1]**

*Simplify the right-hand side*

$p = \frac{\sqrt{2 k ^{2} }}{k}$
$p = \frac{ \sqrt{2} \cancel{k} }{ \cancel{k} }$

$p=\sqrt{2}$ **[1]**

parts.problemMd:
The function $g$ is defined as $g(x)=x^{2}\mathrm{for}x>0$

Given that $\mathrm{gf}(a)=k\mathrm{for}k>1$ find an expression for $a$ in terms of $k$.

$a=$
parts.solutionMd:
*gf(**a**) means g(f(**a**))*

*Find f(**a**) by substituting **x** = **a** into f(**x**)* * *

> $f \left(a\right) = \frac{\sqrt{a^{2} + k^{2}}}{a}$*  *

*Now substitute *$x=\frac{\sqrt{a^{2}+k^{2}}}{a}$* into g(**x**) and simplify* * *

$\begin{aligned}gf \left(a\right) & = & \left(\frac{\sqrt{a^{2} + k^{2}}}{a}\right)^{2} \\ & = & \frac{a^{2} + k^{2}}{a^{2}}\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

*Set this equal to **k** and solve to find **a** (make **a** the subject)* * *

$\begin{aligned}\frac{a^{2} + k^{2}}{a^{2}} & = & k \\ a^{2} + k^{2} & = & k a^{2} \\ k^{2} & = & k a^{2} - a^{2}\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

*Factorise out **a*<sup>*2*</sup>* on the right-hand side to continue* * *

$\begin{aligned}k^{2} & = & a^{2} \left(k - 1\right) \\ \frac{k^{2}}{k - 1} & = & a^{2} \\ \pm \sqrt{\frac{k^{2}}{k - 1}} & = & a\end{aligned}$ * *

*k** > 1 so the denominator *$\sqrt{k-1}$* never square roots a negative number, and the numerator can be simplified using *$\sqrt{k^{2}}=k$ * *

$\pm\frac{k}{\sqrt{k-1}}=a$

> * *

> *The first line required substituting **a** into f(**x**), but only positive values can be substituted into f(**x**) as the domain is **x** > 0, so **a** must be a positive value (choose the positive square root)*

$a=\frac{k}{\sqrt{k-1}}$* ***[1]**

$\sqrt{\frac{k^{2}}{k-1}}$** is also accepted**

![q13-4ma1-2h-qp-jan22-paper2-igcse-maths](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-18-higher/3-sequences-functions-and-graphs/graphing-inequalities/assets/026-q13-4ma1-2h-qp-jan22-paper2-igcse-maths.png)

Write down three inequalities that define the shaded region.
parts.solutionMd:
> *Method 1*

> *All three lines are solid lines so take ≤ or ≥ (rather than < or >).*

> *For each line, first find its equation. One of them has already been given in the diagram: *$x+2y=8$*.*

> *The shaded region is below this line so the inequality is;*

$x+2y\leq8$* ***[1]**

> *We then have a vertical line and another diagonal line. Vertical lines are of the form "*$x=k$*" and in this case it passes through -1 on the **x**-axis so the equation is;*

$x=-1$

> *And the shaded area is to the right of the line so the inequality is;*

$x\geq-1$* ***[1]**

> *Diagonal lines are of the form "*$y=mx+c$*" where **m** is the gradient of the line and **c** is the **y**-intercept. We can find the gradient of the unlabelled diagonal line using *$\frac{\mathrm{rise}}{\mathrm{run}}=\frac{y_{1}-y_{2}}{x_{1}-x_{2}}$*, for example between (2, 2) and (0, 0).*

*gradient = *$\frac{\mathrm{rise}}{\mathrm{run}}=\frac{2-0}{2-0}=1$

> *Therefore the line takes the form *$y=x+c$*. And the y-intercept is 0 so the equation of the unlabelled diagonal line is;*

$y=x$

> *The shaded region is above this line so the inequality is;*

$y\geqx$** ****[1]**

> *Method 2*

> *For each first find its equation, one of them has already been given in the diagram - *$x+2y=8$*. *

> *We then have a vertical line and another diagonal line.*

> * Vertical lines are of the form "*$x=k$*". *

> *Diagonal lines are of the form "*$y - y_{1} = m \left(x + x_{1}\right)$*" where **m** is the gradient of the line and (**x*<sub>*1*</sub>*, **y*<sub>*1*</sub>*) is a point the line passes through.  To find the gradient we will need a second point the line passes through.*

*The vertical lines passes through -1 on the ***x***-axis so has equation *$x=-1$* *

*The (unlablelled) diagonal line passes through (0, 0) and (2, 2) and has gradient *$\frac{\mathrm{rise}}{\mathrm{run}}=\frac{2-0}{2-0}=1$*, so has equation *$y - 0 = 1 \left(x - 0\right) , y = x$

> *Now consider the inequalities for all three lines, including the given one.*

*For *$x=-1$* the region shaded is on the right of (above) its line, so the inequality is *$x\geq-1$* *

*For *$y=x$* the region shaded is above the line, so the inequlaity is *$y\geqx$* *

*For *$x+2y=8$* the region shaded is below the line, so the inequality is *$x+2y\leq8$

> *Bring everything together for the final answer.*

**Final answer:** **The shaded region is defined by the inequalities **$x\geq-1,y\geqx\mathrm{and}x+2y\leq8$** **

**One mark for each correct inequality**** [3]**

parts.problemMd: Write $3x^{2}-12x+7$ in the form $a(x+b)^{2}+c$
parts.solutionMd:
> *The formula for completing the square for a quadratic in the form*$ax^{2}+bx+c$* is *$a \left(x + \frac{b}{2 a}\right)^{2} - \frac{b^{2}}{4 a} + c$*. *

> *Applying this formula gives*

$3 x^{2} - 12 x + 7 = 3 \left(x + \frac{- 12}{2 \times 3}\right)^{2} - \frac{\left(- 12\right)^{2}}{4 \times 3} + 7$

**[1]**

> *Simplify.*

$\begin{aligned}3 x^{2} - 12 x + 7 & = & 3 \left(x - 2\right)^{2} - 12 + 7 \\ & = & 3 \left(x - 2\right)^{2} - 5\end{aligned}$

**[1]**
** **$\therefore 3 \mathbf{\mathit{x}}^{2} - 12 \mathbf{\mathit{x}} + 7 = 3 \left(\mathbf{\mathit{x}} - 2\right)^{2} - 5$* ***[1]**

**i.e.  **$a=3,b=-2,c=-5$**.**

parts.problemMd:

parts.solutionMd:
> *Quadratic graphs are parabolas that have a line of symmetry that passes through the turning point.*

> *The quadratic graph *$y=3x^{2}-12x+7$* is a positive quadratic (positive x*<sup>*2*</sup>* term) so its turning point will be a minimum point.*

> *The minimum point is found by completing the square (part (a)).*

$3 x^{2} - 12 x + 7 = 3 \left(x - 2\right)^{2} - 5$

> *The minimum point of *$a \left(x + b\right)^{2} + c$* is *$\left(- b , c\right)$*.*

$\therefore Min . point is \left(2 , - 5\right)$

*The line of symmetry will be a vertical line passing through this point, but we need its equation for the answer.*

> *Vertical lines have equations of the form *$x=k$*.*

**The line of symmetry L has equation** $x=2$** ****[1] **
**You could sketch the graph if it helps you to see the symmetry.**

> *The *$x-$*coordinate of each option is the same, so they can all be tested together. Make sure you type it carefully into your calculator, using brackets around the negative.*

> $\left(- 1\right)^{2} - 4 \left(- 1\right) + 1 = 6$* *

**The correct answer is option 4, (-1, 6)** **[1]**

> *We have the graph of *$y=x^{3}-2x^{2}-3x+4$* (from part (b)). We need to rearrange *$x^{3}-2x^{2}-x+1=0$* so that "*$x^{3}-2x^{2}-3x+4$*" appears on its own on one side of the equation.*

> *For the constants, we have + 1 but we want + 4, so add 3 to both sides.*

parts.problemMd: Express $7+12x--3x^{2}$ in the form $a+b(x+c)^{2}$ where $a,b$ and$c$are integers.
parts.solutionMd:
> *Method 1*

> *The formula for completing the square for a quadratic in the form*$ax^{2}+bx+c$* is *$a \left(x + \frac{b}{2 a}\right)^{2} - \frac{b^{2}}{4 a} + c$*.*

> *Rearrange *$7+12x-3x^{2}$* into the form *$ax^{2}+bx+c.$

$7+12x-3x^{2}=-3x^{2}+12x+7$

> *Therefore *$a=-3,b=12\mathrm{and}c=7$*.*

> *Applying the formula gives*

$- 3 x^{2} + 12 x + 7 = - 3 \left(x + \frac{12}{2 \times - 3}\right)^{2} - \frac{\left(12\right)^{2}}{4 \times - 3} + 7$

**[1]**

> *Simplify.*

$\begin{aligned}- 3 x^{2} + 12 x + 7 & = & - 3 \left(x - 2\right)^{2} + 12 + 7 \\ & = & - 3 \left(x - 2\right)^{2} + 19\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Rearrange into the format required.*

$19 - 3 \left(\mathbf{\mathit{x}} - 2\right)^{2}$* ***[1]**

** i.e.  **$a=19,b=-3,c=-2$**.**

> *Method 2*

> *Expand the given expression in terms of *$a,b\mathrm{and}c.$

$a + b \left(x + c\right)^{2} = a + b \left(x^{2} + 2 c x + c^{2}\right)$

> *Simplify.*

$a + b \left(x + c\right)^{2} = a + b x^{2} + 2 b c x + b c^{2}$

> *Therefore *$7+12x-3x^{2}=a+bx^{2}+2bcx+bc^{2}$*.*

> *Equating the *$x^{2}$* term gives*

$-3x^{2}=bx^{2}\thereforeb=-3$

**[1]**

> *Equating the *$x$* term gives*

$12x=2bcx$

> *Substitute *$b=-3$*.*

$\begin{aligned}12 x & = & 2 \left(- 3\right) c x \\ 12 & = & - 6 c \\ c & = & - 2\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Equating the constant terms gives*

$7=a+bc^{2}$

> *Substitute *$b=-3$* and *$c=-2$*.*

$\begin{aligned}7 & = & a + \left(- 3\right) \left(- 2\right)^{2} \\ 7 & = & a + \left(- 12\right) \\ a & = & 7 + 12 \\ a & = & 19\end{aligned}$

> *Rearrange into the format required.*

$19 - 3 \left(\mathbf{\mathit{x}} - 2\right)^{2}$* ***[1]**

** i.e.  **$a=19,b=-3,c=2$**.**

> *Method 1: Using "transformations of functions"*

> *A translation by *$\begin{pmatrix} 4 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}$* (or a translation +4 in the **x-**axis), means that *$y = f \left(x\right)$* becomes *$y = f \left(x - 4\right)$*; 4 is subtracted inside the bracket.*

$\begin{aligned}f \left(x - 4\right) & = & 9 - 3 \left(x + 2 - 4\right)^{2} \\ & = & 9 - 3 \left(x - 2\right)^{2}\end{aligned}$

**An equation for the curve S is **$y=9-3(x-2)^{2}$*  ***[1] **

**Equivalent equations such as '**$y=-3x^{2}+12x-3$**' are accepted '**$y = f \left(x - 4\right)$**' was also accepted as an answer; but the answer above is what was intended by the question**

> *Method 2: Using "turning point by completing the square"*

> *After translation by *$\begin{pmatrix} 4 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}$* (or a translation +4 in the **x-**axis), the turning point (−2, 9) becomes;*

*(2, 9)*

> *So the equation takes the form;*

$\begin{aligned}y & = & a \left(x - 2\right)^{2} + 9\end{aligned}$

> *And as the curve has not been stretched or reflected, the value of *$\begin{aligned} & & a\end{aligned}$* remains the same as in curve *$\begin{aligned} & & C\end{aligned}$*. i.e. *$\begin{aligned}a & = & 3\end{aligned}$*.*

**An equation for the curve S is **$y=-3(x-2)^{2}+9$*  ***[1] **

**Note this is the same equation as in Method 1, just written in a different order**

parts.problemMd:
The curve $C$ has equation   $y=x^{2}--6x+4$

Using the axes below, sketch the curve $C$.
On your sketch show clearly

(i) the exact coordinates of any points of intersection of $C$ with the coordinate axes, 

(ii) the coordinates of the turning point.

![Cartesian coordinate plane with horizontal x-axis and vertical y-axis intersecting at origin O. Axes are labelled with arrows pointing right and up.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-18-higher/3-sequences-functions-and-graphs/graphs-of-functions/assets/004-cartesian-coordinate-plane-with-horizontal-x-axi.png)
parts.solutionMd:
> **[exam-tip]**
> The question refers to 'exact' coordinates of any points of intersection with the coordinate axes.
> 
> This is a hint that $x^{2}--6x+4=0$  is unlikely to be solvable by factorising. Therefore, either completing the square or the quadratic formula should be used.
> 
> As the completed square form is also a way to find the coordinates of the turning point, it is more efficient here to use this method for both the turning point and the roots.

> *The coordinates of the turning point are found by writing the function in completed square form (*$\left(x - a\right)^{2} + b$*, where *$\left(a ,  b\right)$* are the coordinates of the turning point)*

$\begin{aligned}x^{2} - 6 x + 4 & = & \left(x - 3\right)^{2} - 9 + 4 \\ & = & \left(x - 3\right)^{2} - 5\end{aligned}$

**[M1 A1]**

*The coordinates of the turning point are (3, -5)*

> *The roots of the function (the intersection with **x**-axis) occur when *$y=0$

> *Therefore you can solve the equation for **x** using the completed square form*

$\begin{aligned}\left(x - 3\right)^{2} - 5 & = & 0 \\ \left(x - 3\right)^{2} & = & 5 \\ x - 3 & = & \pm \sqrt{5}\end{aligned}$

$x=3+\sqrt{5}$* or *$x=3-\sqrt{5}$

**[M1 A1]**

*The coordinates of the intersections with the ***x***-axis are *$\left(3 - \sqrt{5} , 0\right)$* and *$\left(3 + \sqrt{5} , 0\right)$

> *The y-intercept can be found by substituting *$x=0$* into the function*

$\left(0\right)^{2} - 6 \left(0\right) + 4 = 4$

*The y-intercept is (0, 4)*

> *Make a sketch of the curve, C, labelling the coordinates of the intersections with the axes and the coordinates of the turning point as below*

![Graph of a quadratic function with a vertex at (3, -5) and intercepts at (3-√5, 0), (3+√5, 0), and (0, 4), showing axes and curve.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-18-higher/3-sequences-functions-and-graphs/graphs-of-functions/assets/005-graph-of-a-quadratic-function-with-a-vertex-at-3.png)

**[B1 B1]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **M1**: Showing a correct first step for a correct method for finding the coordinates of the turning points (e.g. initial completed the square form $\left(x - 3\right)^{2} - 3^{2} + 4$ or differentiating to give $\frac{dy}{dx}=2x-6$ for example)
> 
> **A1**: For calculating the* x*-coordinate of the turning point correctly. This mark will still be awarded for an incorrectly evaluated *x*-coordinate of the turning point as long as the first M1 mark has been awarded.
> 
> **M1**: Showing a  correct method for calculating the roots of the equation will gain this mark (e.g. substituting correctly into the quadratic formula or completing the square).
> 
> **A1**: This mark is awarded for the two exact solutions of the roots of the equations calculated in any equivalent form (e.g. $x=3\pm\sqrt{5}$)
> 
> **B1**: A positive parabola drawn on the axes intercepting the* y*-axis at (0,4) will gain this mark.
> 
> **B1**: For a fully correct graph sketched on the axes with correct labelling of *x*-intercepts, *y*-intercept and coordinate of the turning point.

**any sensible sketch ****[1]**

> *The gradient of **AB** using the gradient formula, *$m=\frac{y_{1}-y_{2}}{x_{1}-x_{2}}$*, is*

$m_{AB}=\frac{1-5}{-2-6}=\frac{1}{2}$

> *AB **and **BC** are perpendicular therefore their gradients are negative reciprocals therefore*

$m_{BC}=-2$

**[1]**

> *Now we can substitute *$m=-2$*, *$\left(6 , 5\right)$* and *$\left(4 , k\right)$* into the gradient formula for **BC **and solve to find *$k$

$\begin{aligned}- 2 & = & \frac{5 - k}{6 - 4} \\ - 2 & = & \frac{5 - k}{2} \\ - 4 & = & 5 - k \\ k & = & 9\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

*Now we know that *$C$* is *$\left(4 , 9\right)$* and we can find the equation of a line through *$A \left(- 2 , 1\right)$* and *$C \left(4 , 9\right)$ *First find the gradient*

$\begin{aligned}9 & = & \frac{4}{3} \left(4\right) + c \\ 9 & = & \frac{16}{3} + c \\ c & = & \frac{11}{3}\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

$\begin{aligned}3 y & = & 4 x + 11 \\ 3 y - 4 x & = & 11\end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned}3 \mathbf{\mathit{y}} - 4 \mathbf{\mathit{x}} & = & 11\end{aligned}$ **[1]**

$\begin{aligned}5 y & = & - 3 x + 39\end{aligned}$

parts.problemMd:
The straight line $L$ passes through point $A$ (– 6, 2) and point $B$ (5, 3) 
The straight line $M$ is perpendicular to $L$ and passes through the midpoint of $A$ and $B$. 
The line $M$ intersects the line $x=--1$ at point $C$.

Calculate the area of triangle $ABC$.
parts.solutionMd:
> *Although you do not know all of the information, sketching a graph with a rough idea of where the lines go will help you to visualise this question. It does not matter if your lines are not in the exact places but make sure that they intersect each other according to the question.*

![PDEXwgHB_edexcel-igcse-tq-mis-linear-graphs-vh-q10](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-18-higher/3-sequences-functions-and-graphs/linear-graphs-y-equals-mx-plus-c/assets/013-pdexwghb-edexcel-igcse-tq-mis-linear-graphs-vh-q.png)

> *We can see from the graph that to find the area of the triangle we will need to find the length of **AB** (the base of the triangle) and the length of **CM** (the height of the triangle).*

> *First let's consider **CM. **We can find the coordinates of **M** using the midpoint formula, *$M = \left(\frac{x_{1} + x_{2}}{2} , \frac{y_{1} + y_{2}}{2}\right)$*.*

$\begin{aligned}M & = & \left(\frac{5 + \left(- 6\right)}{2} , \frac{3 + 2}{2}\right) \\ & = & \left(- \frac{1}{2} , \frac{5}{2}\right)\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *To find **C**, we can find the equation of **CM** and examine where it intersects the line *$x=-1$*.*

> *To find the equation of **CM**, start by finding the gradient of **AB, **which is perpendicular to **CM**, using gradient *$m=\frac{y_{1}-y_{2}}{x_{1}-x_{2}}$*.*

$\begin{aligned}m_{A B} & = & \frac{3 - 2}{5 - \left(- 6\right)} \\ & = & \frac{1}{11}\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Perpendicular gradients are negative reciprocals so from this we can deduce the gradient of **CM** .*

$\begin{aligned}m_{C M} & = & - 1 \div \frac{1}{11} \\ & = & - 11\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Now find the equation of **CM** by substituting the point *$M \begin{aligned} & & \left(- \frac{1}{2} , \frac{5}{2}\right)\end{aligned}$* and the gradient *$-11$* into *$y=mx+c$*, and solving for **c**.*

> * *$\begin{aligned}y & = & m x + c \\ \frac{5}{2} & = & - 11 \left(- \frac{1}{2}\right) + c \\ \frac{5}{2} & = & \frac{11}{2} + c \\ \frac{5 - 11}{2} & = & c \\ c & = & \frac{- 6}{2} = - 3\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Now we know that the equation of **CM** is:*

$\begin{aligned}y & = & - 11 x - 3\end{aligned}$

> *Substitute *$x=-1$* into the equation of **CM** to find the **y**-coordinate of **C.*

$\begin{aligned}y & = & - 11 \left(- 1\right) + 3 \\ & = & 11 - 3 \\ & = & 8\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Now we can find the length of **CM** using the length of a line segment formula, *$length = \sqrt{\left(x_{1} - x_{2}\right)^{2} + \left(y_{1} - y_{2}\right)^{2}}$*.*

$\begin{aligned}C M & = & \sqrt{\left(- \frac{1}{2} - \left(- 1\right)\right)^{2} + \left(\frac{5}{2} - 8\right)^{2}} \\ & = & \sqrt{\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{2} + \left(\frac{11}{2}\right)^{2}} \\ & = & \frac{\sqrt{122}}{2}\end{aligned}$

> *And finding the length of **AB** is straightforward as we already have the coordinates of **A **and** B.*

$\begin{aligned}A B & = & \sqrt{\left(3 - 2\right)^{2} + \left(5 - \left(- 6\right)\right)^{2}} \\ & = & \sqrt{122}\end{aligned}$

**length of CM and AB**** ****found**** [1]**

> *Finally, we are ready to find the area of triangle **ABC** using area of a triangle = *$\frac{1}{2}$*× base × height.*

$\mathrm{Area}=\frac{1}{2}\times\sqrt{122}\times\frac{\sqrt{122}}{2}$

**[1]**

$\begin{aligned} & = & \frac{122}{4} \\ & = & \frac{61}{2}\end{aligned}$

$\mathrm{Area}=30.5\mathrm{units}^{2}$ **[1]**

parts.problemMd:
$ABCD$ is a kite with $AB=AD$ and $CB=CD$

$A$ is the point with coordinates $(--2,10)$

$B$ is the point with coordinates  $\left(- \frac{27}{5} ,  4\right)$

$C$ is the point with coordinates  $(4,-5)$

Work out the coordinates of $D$
parts.solutionMd:
> *Draw a sketch of the kite*

![Quadrilateral with vertices A (-2, 10), B (-27/5, 4), C (4, -5), and D (x, y). Note: Diagram not accurately drawn.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-18-higher/3-sequences-functions-and-graphs/linear-graphs-y-equals-mx-plus-c/assets/001-quadrilateral-with-vertices-a-2-10-b-27-5-4-c-4-.jpg)

> *Calculate the gradient of AC*

$\frac{-5-10}{4--2}=-\frac{15}{6}=-\frac{5}{2}$

**[M1]**

> *Calculate the equation of AC*

$\begin{aligned}y & = & - \frac{5}{2} x + c \\ 10 & = & - \frac{5}{2} \times \left(- 2\right) + c \\ 10 & = & 5 + c\end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned}c & = & 5\end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned}\therefore y & = & - \frac{5}{2} x + 5\end{aligned}$

**[M1]**

> *The diagonals of a kite are perpendicular bisectors of each other*

> *As they are perpendicular, the gradient of BD is the negative reciprocal of AC*

*Gradient of BD *$=\frac{2}{5}$

> *Use this and the coordinate of B to find the equation of BD*

$\begin{aligned}y & = & \frac{2}{5} x + c \\ 4 & = & \frac{2}{5} \times \left(- \frac{27}{5}\right) + c \\ 4 & = & - \frac{54}{25} + c\end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned}c & = & \frac{154}{25}\end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned}\therefore y & = & \frac{2}{5} x + \frac{154}{25}\end{aligned}$

**[M1]**

> *Calculate the point of intersection of the diagonals by equating the two lines*

$\begin{aligned}- \frac{5}{2} x + 5 & = & \frac{2}{5} x + \frac{154}{25} \\ - 125 x + 250 & = & 20 x + 308 \\ - 58 & = & 145 x \\ - \frac{2}{5} & = & x\end{aligned}$

**[M1]**

> *Then substitute *$x$* into one of the equations to get *$y$

$y = - \frac{5}{2} ( - \frac{2}{5} ) + 5$
y equals 6

**[M1]**

> *The point of intersection is the midpoint of BD*

> *Use the midpoint and the coordinates of B to calculate D*

$\left(- \frac{2}{5} , 6\right) = \left(\frac{- \frac{27}{5} + x_{D}}{2} , \frac{4 + y_{D}}{2}\right)$

> *Make an equation for the *$x$*-coordinate*

$\begin{aligned}- \frac{2}{5} & = & \frac{- \frac{27}{5} + x_{D}}{2} \\ - \frac{4}{5} & = & - \frac{27}{5} + x_{D} \\ \frac{23}{5} & = & x_{D}\end{aligned}$

> *Make an equation for the *$y$*-coordinate*

$\begin{aligned}6 & = & \frac{4 + y_{D}}{2} \\ 12 & = & 4 + y_{D} \\ 8 & = & y_{D}\end{aligned}$

$\left(\frac{23}{5} , 8\right) or \left(4 . 6 , 8\right)$

**[A1]**

parts.solutionMd:
> *Method 1*

> *We can't find the cost of 450 kwH of electricity directly from the graph, but we read other values from the graph and scale up to find the cost of 45 kwH (as the graph shows direct proportion).*

> *For example, find the cost of 225 kwH and multiply it by 2 (because 225 × 2 = 450).*

*£28 × 2 *

**[1]**

**Answer = £56** **[1] **

**Any answer between 55.5 and 57 is accepted so long as it is consistent with the reading off the diagram**

> *Method 2*

parts.problemMd:
Debbie drove from Junction 12 to Junction 13 on a motorway.

The travel graph shows Debbie's journey.

Ian also drove from Junction 12 to Junction 13 on the same motorway. 
He drove at an average speed of 66 km/hour.

Who had the faster average speed, Debbie or Ian? 
You must explain your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
> *We need use the travel graph to calculate Debbie's average speed. The gradient on a distance-time graph represents the speed*

> *Method 1*

$\mathrm{average} \mathrm{speed}=\frac{\mathrm{total} \mathrm{distance}}{\mathrm{total} \mathrm{time}}$

> *Read the total distance and the total time off the distance-time graph as below*

![WiYwPfV3_edexcel-tq-mis-2-17-m-2-2](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-18-higher/3-sequences-functions-and-graphs/real-life-graphs/assets/051-wiywpfv3-edexcel-tq-mis-2-17-m-2-2.png)

*average speed *$=\frac{30}{24}$

**dividing total distance by total time ****[1]**

$=\frac{5}{4}\mathrm{km}/\mathrm{minute}$

> *Note that Ian's speed is given in km/hour whereas the time on the graph is given in minutes. *

> *Therefore convert the speed to km/hour by multiplying by 60*

$=\frac{5}{4}\times60$

** converting the units**** [1]**

$=75\mathrm{km}/\mathrm{hour}$

**[1]**

> *75 > 66 so we conclude Debbie's average speed was faster than Ian's*

**Debbie had the faster average speed**** [1]**

> *Method 2*

> *Debbie's journey is a represented by a straight line, so is at constant speed; so the average speed is the same as the gradient at any point on the line*

*Pick any two points on the line and use *$\frac{\mathrm{rise}}{\mathrm{run}}$* or the gradient formula *$\frac{y_{1}-y_{2}}{x_{1}-x_{2}}$ *E.g. picking the points (20, 25) and (0, 0) as shown below*

![edexcel-tq-mis-2-17-m-2](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-18-higher/3-sequences-functions-and-graphs/real-life-graphs/assets/052-edexcel-tq-mis-2-17-m-2.png)

> *Note that Ian's speed is given in km/hour whereas the Time on the graph is given in minutes.*

> * Therefore before calculating the gradient, convert the times to minutes*

*(20, 25) → *$\left(\frac{1}{3} , 25\right)$

** converting the units**** [1]**

*gradient *$=\frac{25-0}{\frac{1}{3}-0}$

**attempt to find gradient using **$\frac{rise}{run}$** or gradient formula ****[1]**

$=75\mathrm{km}/\mathrm{hour}$

**[1]**

> *75 > 66 so we conclude Debbie's average speed was faster than Ian's*

**Debbie had the faster average speed**** [1]**

Note that although it's marked on the diagram between 10 and 11, we don't actually know yet where it will be- it's marked on the diagram for demonstration purposes only. The trick to this question is to find the value of *$t$* that gives an area of 75.*

parts.problemMd:

parts.solutionMd:
> *The formula for the sum to **n **terms of an arithmetic series is given on the formula sheet (first page of exam).*

> $S_{n} = \frac{n}{2} \left[2 a + \left(n - 1\right) d\right]$*, where **a **is the first term, **d** is the common difference and **n** is the number of terms.*

> *Method 1*

> *Consider the sum of the first 100 terms, then subtract the sum of the first 40 terms  *

> *This leaves behind the sum of the 41st to 100th term*

$\begin{aligned} & & S_{100} - S_{40}\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Substitute n = 100, a = 1 and d = 4 into the first sum *

> *Substitute n = 40, a = 1 and d = 4 into the second sum*

$= \frac{100}{2} \left[2 \times 1 + \left(100 - 1\right) \times 4\right] - \frac{40}{2} \left[2 \times 1 + \left(40 - 1\right) \times 4\right]$

**[2]**

> *Simplify*

$=19900-3160$

$16740$* ***[1]**

> *Method 2*

> *Imagine a new sequence starting on the 41st term (n = 1) and going to the 100th term (n = 60) *

> *This new sequence would have a first term of *$a=u_{41}$* where *$u_{41}$* is the 41st term in the old sequence*

*Use *$u_{n} = a + \left(n - 1\right) d$* on the old sequence (not given on formula page) to find *$u_{41}$ * *

* *$\begin{aligned}u_{41} & = & 1 + \left(41 - 1\right) \left(4\right) \\ & = & 161\end{aligned}$

* ***[1]**

> *This means a = 161 on the new sequence *

> *There are 60 terms in the new sequence (the 41st to 100th values from the old sequence) so n = 60*

**n = 60*** ***[1]**

> *Find the sum of all 60 terms by substituting a = 161, n = 60, d = 4 into *$S_{n} = \frac{n}{2} \left[2 a + \left(n - 1\right) d\right]$*  *

> $S_{n} = \frac{n}{2} \left[2 a + \left(n - 1\right) d\right] = \frac{60}{2} \left[2 \left(161\right) + \left(60 - 1\right) \left(4\right)\right]$* *

**[1]**

$16740$ **[1]**

**[1]**

circle enclose 1 space space 41 k plus r equals 206

$k=5$

parts.problemMd:
An arithmetic series has first term $a$ and common difference $d$. 

The sum of the first $2n$ terms of the series is four times the sum of the first $n$ terms of the series.

Find an expression for a in terms of $d$. 
Show your working clearly.
parts.solutionMd:
> *The formula for the sum to **n **terms of an arithmetic series is given on the formula sheet (first page of exam).*

> $S_{n} = \frac{n}{2} \left[2 a + \left(n - 1\right) d\right]$*, where **a **is the first term, **d** is the common difference and **n** is the number of terms.*

> *Use the formula to find an expression in terms of **a **and **d **for 2**n.*

> $S_{2 n} = \frac{2 n}{2} \left[2 a + \left(2 n - 1\right) d\right] = n \left[2 a + \left(2 n - 1\right) d\right]$* *

**[1]**

> *Use the formula to find an expression in terms of **a **and **d **for **n.*

> $S_{n} = \frac{n}{2} \left[2 a + \left(n - 1\right) d\right]$* *

> *S*<sub>*2n *</sub>*= 4 × **S*<sub>*n*</sub>* , use this to form an equation in terms of **a, d **and **n**.*

> $n \left[2 a + \left(2 n - 1\right) d\right] = 4 \left(\frac{n}{2} \left[2 a + \left(n - 1\right) d\right]\right)$* *

**[1]**

> *Simplify and cancel **n **from both sides.*

$\begin{aligned}\cancel{n} \left[2 a + \left(2 n - 1\right) d\right] & = & \frac{4 \cancel{n}}{2} \left[2 a + \left(n - 1\right) d\right] \\ 2 a + \left(2 n - 1\right) d & = & 2 \left[2 a + \left(n - 1\right) d\right]\end{aligned}$

> *Expand the brackets on both sides.*

$\begin{aligned}2 a + 2 n d - d & = & 4 a + 2 \left(n - 1\right) d \\ 2 a + 2 n d - d & = & 4 a + 2 n d - 2 d\end{aligned}$

> * *

> *Cancel 2**nd** from both sides.*

$\begin{aligned}2 a - d & = & 4 a - 2 d\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Rearrange to make **a** the subject*

$\begin{aligned}- 2 a & = & - d \\ a & = & \frac{- d}{- 2}\end{aligned}$

$a=\frac{d}{2}$ **[1]**

* *$\begin{aligned}S_{11} & = & \frac{11}{2} \left[2 a + \left(11 - 1\right) \left(d\right)\right] \\ \left(U_{6}\right)^{2} + 18 & = & \frac{11}{2} \left[2 a + 10 d\right] \\ \left(U_{6}\right)^{2} + 18 & = & 11 \left(a + 5 d\right)\end{aligned}$

> *Substitute the expression for **U*<sub>*6 *</sub>*into the equation for **S*<sub>*4*</sub>*.*

$\begin{aligned}\left(a + 5 d\right)^{2} + 18 & = & 11 \left(a + 5 d\right)\end{aligned}$

* ***[1]**

> *From the first equation we know that *$a+3d=6$*, rearrange this to *$a=6-3d$*. *

> *Simplify the second equation by substituting *$a=6-3d$* in. *

$\begin{aligned}\left(\left(6 - 3 d\right) + 5 d\right)^{2} + 18 & = & 11 \left(\left(6 - 3 d\right) + 5 d\right) \\ \left(6 + 2 d\right)^{2} + 18 & = & 11 \left(6 + 2 d\right)\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Expand the brackets and rearrange to form a quadratic equation in terms of **d.*

$\begin{aligned}\left(6 + 2 d\right) \left(6 + 2 d\right) + 18 & = & 66 + 22 d \\ 36 + 12 d + 12 d + 4 d^{2} + 18 & = & 66 + 22 d \\ 4 d^{2 } + 24 d + 54 & = & 66 + 22 d \\ 4 d^{2 } + 2 d - 12 & = & 0\end{aligned}$

**[1]*** *

parts.problemMd:
$(2x+23),(8x+2)$ and $(20x--52)$ are three consecutive terms of an arithmetic sequence.

Prove that the common difference of the sequence is $12$
parts.solutionMd:
> *The common difference of an arithmetic sequence is the difference between any two consecutive terms.*

> *Find the common difference, *$d$* in terms of *$x$* **using the difference between the first two terms.*

$d = \left(8 x + 2\right) - \left(2 x + 23\right) = 6 x - 21$

> *Find the common difference, *$d$* in terms of *$x$* **using the difference between the second and the third terms.*

$d = \left(20 x - 52 \right) - \left(8 x + 2\right) = \left(12 x - 54\right)$

** ****Either expression for a common difference correct ****[1]**

> *Form an equation in terms of *$x$* by setting the two expressions for *$d$* equal to each other.*

$6x-21=12x-54$

** **** ****[1]**

> *Solve the equation.*

$\begin{aligned}6 x - 21 & = & 12 x - 54 \\ - 6 x & = & - 33 \\ x & = & 5 . 5\end{aligned}$

** **** ****[1]**

> *Substitute this value of *$x$*into either expression for *$d$*.*

$\begin{aligned}d & = & 6 \left(5 . 5\right) - 21 = 33 - 21\end{aligned}$

$d=33-21=12$** **** ****[1]**

parts.problemMd:
An arithmetic series has first term$a$ and common difference $d$, where $d$is a prime number.

The sum of the first n terms of the series is $S_{n}$and

$S_{m}=39$
 $S_{2m}=320$

Find the value of $d$and the value of $m$ Show clear algebraic working.

$\begin{aligned}d & = & . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . \\ m & = & . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . .\end{aligned}$
parts.solutionMd:
> *The formula for the sum to **n **terms of an arithmetic series is given on the formula sheet (first page of exam).*

> $S_{n} = \frac{n}{2} \left[2 a + \left(n - 1\right) d\right]$*, where **a **is the first term, **d** is the common difference and **n** is the number of terms.*

> *Use the formula to find an expression in terms of **a **and **d **for **S*<sub>*m*</sub>*.*

> $S_{m} = \frac{m}{2} \left[2 a + \left(m - 1\right) d\right]$* *

> *Form an equation by setting the expression for **S*<sub>*m  *</sub>*equal to 39.*

> $\frac{m}{2} \left[2 a + \left(m - 1\right) d\right] = 39$* *

**[1]**

> *Use the formula to find an expression in terms of **a **and **d **for **S*<sub>*2m .*</sub>

> $S_{2 m} = \frac{2 m}{2} \left[2 a + \left(2 m - 1\right) d\right]$* *

> *Form an equation by setting the expression for **S*<sub>*2m  *</sub>*equal to 320.*

> $\frac{2 m}{2} \left[2 a + \left(2 m - 1\right) d\right] = 320$* *

**[1]**

> *Simplify the equations.*

$\begin{aligned}m \left[2 a + \left(m - 1\right) d\right] & = & 78 \\ m \left(2 a + m d - d\right) & = & 78 \\ 2 m a + m^{2} d - m d & = & 78 \boxed{1}\end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned}m \left[2 a + \left(2 m - 1\right) d\right] & = & 320 \\ m \left(2 a + 2 m d - d\right) & = & 320 \\ 2 m a + 2 m^{2} d - m d & = & 320 \boxed{2}\end{aligned}$

> *Subtract equation *$\boxed{1}$* from equation *$\boxed{2}$*.*

> $m^{2}d=242$* *

**[1]**

$\begin{aligned}242 & = & 2 \times 121\end{aligned}$

> *The only possibility is that **d **= 2 and **m*<sup>*2 *</sup>*= 121.*

**[1]**

$d=2,m=11$ **[1]**

parts.problemMd:
The sum of the first 48 terms of an arithmetic series is 4 times the sum of the first 36 terms of the same series.

Find the sum of the first 30 terms of this series.
parts.solutionMd:
> *The formula for the sum to **n **terms of an arithmetic series is given on the formula sheet (first page of exam).*

> $S_{n} = \frac{n}{2} \left[2 a + \left(n - 1\right) d\right]$*, where **a **is the first term, **d** is the common difference and **n** is the number of terms.*

> *Use the formula to find an expression in terms of **a **and **d **for the first 48 terms of an arithmetic series (**n** = 48).*

> $S_{48} = \frac{48}{2} \left[2 a + \left(48 - 1\right) d\right] = 24 \left(2 a + 47 d\right)$* *

**[1]**

> *Use the formula to find an expression in terms of **a **and **d **for the first 36 terms of the same arithmetic series (**n** = 36).*

> $S_{36} = \frac{36}{2} \left[2 a + \left(36 - 1\right) d\right] = 18 \left(2 a + 35 d\right)$* *

> *S*<sub>*48 *</sub>*= 4 × **S*<sub>*36*</sub>* , use this to form an equation in terms of **a **and **d**.*

> $24 \left(2 a + 47 d\right) = 4 \left( 18 \left(2 a + 35 d\right)\right)$* *

**[1]**

> *Simplify by canceling 4 from both sides.*

$\begin{aligned} \frac{24 \left(2 a + 47 d\right)}{4} & = & \frac{4 \left( 18 \left(2 a + 35 d\right)\right)}{4} \\ 6 \left(2 a + 47 d\right) & = & 18 \left(2 a + 35 d\right)\end{aligned}$

> *Simplify by canceling 6 from both sides.*

$\begin{aligned}\frac{ 6 \left(2 a + 47 d\right)}{6} & = & \frac{18 \left(2 a + 35 d\right)}{6} \\ 2 a + 47 d & = & 3 \left(2 a + 35 d\right)\end{aligned}$

> *Expand the brackets on the right-hand side.*

> $\begin{aligned}2 a + 47 d & = & 6 a + 105 d\end{aligned}$* *

> *Rearrange to make **a** (or **d**) the subject.*

$\begin{aligned}2 a - 6 a & = & 105 d - 47 d \\ - 4 a & = & 58 d \\ a & = & \frac{58 d}{- 4} = - 14 . 5 d\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Use the formula to find an expression in terms of **a **and **d **for the first 30 terms of an arithmetic series (**n** = 30).*

> $S_{30} = \frac{30}{2} \left[2 a + \left(30 - 1\right) d\right] = 15 \left(2 a + 29 d\right)$* *

**[1]**

> *Substitute **a **= -14.5**d **into the expression found for **S*<sub>*30.*</sub>* *

> $S_{30} = 15 \left(2 \left(- 14 . 5 d\right) + 29 d\right) = 15 \left(- 29 d + 29 d\right) = 15 \times 0$* *

$S_{30}=0$ **[1]**

parts.solutionMd:

> *The formula for the sum to **n **terms of an arithmetic series is given on the formula sheet (first page of exam).*

> $S_{n} = \frac{n}{2} \left[2 a + \left(n - 1\right) d\right]$*, where **a **is the first term, **d** is the common difference and **n** is the number of terms.*

> *Find an equation in terms of **a **and **d ** for the sum of the first 30 terms of the series.*

> $\begin{aligned}S_{n} & = & \frac{n}{2} \left[2 a + \left(n - 1\right) d\right] \\ S_{30} & = & \frac{30}{2} \left[2 a + \left(30 - 1\right) d\right] \\ 765 & = & 15 \left(2 a + 29 d\right)\end{aligned}$* *

**[1]**

> *Simplify by dividing both sides by 15.*

> $\begin{aligned}15 \left(2 a + 29 d\right) & = & 765 \\ \left(2 a + 29 d\right) & = & \frac{765}{15} \\ 2 a + 29 d & = & 51\end{aligned}$* *

> *Solve the two equations simultaneously to find the values of **a **and **d**.   Label the equations.*

$\begin{aligned} a + 24 d & = & 44 . 5 \left(1\right) \\ 2 a + 29 d & = & 51 \left(2\right)\end{aligned}$

> *Multiply equation (1) by 2 to make the **a** terms the same.*

$\begin{aligned}2 a + 48 d & = & 89 \left(3\right) \\ 2 a + 29 d & = & 51 \left(2\right)\end{aligned}$

> *Subtract equation (2) from equation (3).*

$\begin{array}{r} \underline{ 2 a + 48 d = 89 \\ \left(-\right) 2 a + 29 d = 51} \\ 19 d = 38 \\ d = 2 \end{array}$
space space 19 d space equals space 38
d space equals space 2 space space

**[1]**

> *Substitute **d **= 2 into one of the equations to find **a.*

$\begin{aligned}\left(1\right) a + 24 \left(2\right) & = & 44 . 5 \\ a & = & 44 . 5 - 48 \\ a & = & - 3 . 5\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

* *$\begin{aligned}u_{16} & = & - 3 . 5 + \left(16 - 1\right) \left(2\right) = - 3 . 5 + 15 \times 2\end{aligned}$

$u_{16}=26.5$ **[1]**

parts.problemMd:

parts.solutionMd:

> The formula for an arithmetic sequence is $u_{n} = a + \left(n - 1\right) d$ where $a$ is the first term and $d$ is the common difference.

$a+2d=19$

> The formula for the sum of the first  $n$ terms of an arithmetic sequence is $S_{n} = \frac{n}{2} \left[2 a + \left(n - 1\right) d\right]$ where $a$ is the first term and $d$ is the common difference.

> *Form an equation using the fact that the sum of the first 10 terms is 290*

$\begin{aligned}\frac{10}{2} \left(2 a + \left(10 - 1\right) d\right) & = & 290 \\ 5 \left(2 a + 9 d\right) & = & 290 \\ 10 a + 45 d & = & 290\end{aligned}$

**[M1]**

> *Now that two equations have been formed in terms of *$a$* and *$d$*, they can be solved simultaneously using the elimination method for example*

> **[exam-tip]**
> The elimination method or substitution method for solving simultaneous equations will give the same solutions.
> 
> Once you have solved for both variables always substitute both values into one equation to check they work together, although this working is not required to gain full marks.

> *The simultaneous equations to solve are:*

$\begin{aligned}10 a + 45 d & = & 290 \\ a + 2 d & = & 19\end{aligned}$

> *First equate coefficients of one variable by multiplying one or both of the equations*

> *In this case multiply the second equation by 10 to equate the coefficients of *$a$

$\begin{aligned}10 a + 45 d & = & 290 \\ 10 a + 20 d & = & 190\end{aligned}$

> *Subtract the second equation from the first equation to eliminate *$a$* and then solve for *$d$

$\begin{aligned}10 a + 45 d & = & 290 - \\ 10 a + 20 d & = & 190\end{aligned}$

*----------------*

$\begin{aligned}25 d & = & 100 \\ d & = & \frac{100}{25} \\ d & = & 4\end{aligned}$

**[M1]**

> *Substitute the value of *$d$* into one of the original equations (either will work) and solve for *$a$

> *Substituting into *$a+2d=19$* gives:*

$\begin{aligned}a + 2 \left(4\right) & = & 19 \\ a + 8 & = & 19 \\ a & = & 19 - 8 \\ a & = & 11\end{aligned}$

> *Substitute both values into the other equation to check both solutions work together*

> *Substituting into *$10a+45d=290$* gives:*

$\begin{aligned}10 \left(11\right) + 45 \left(4\right) & = & 290 \\ 110 + 180 & = & 290\end{aligned}$

*The solutions satisfy the equation*

> *Substitute these values into the formula for  *$u_{n}$*to find the 10th term*

$11 + \left(10 - 1\right) \times 4$

**[M1]**

**Final answer:** **47**

**[A1]**

> *Method 1: Using "transformations of functions"*

> *A translation by *$\begin{pmatrix} 4 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}$* (or a translation +4 in the **x-**axis), means that *$y = f \left(x\right)$* becomes *$y = f \left(x - 4\right)$*; 4 is subtracted inside the bracket.*

> *As *$f \left(x\right) = 9 - 3 \left(x + 2\right)^{2}$*, then;*

$\begin{aligned}f \left(x - 4\right) & = & 9 - 3 \left(x + 2 - 4\right)^{2} \\ & = & 9 - 3 \left(x - 2\right)^{2}\end{aligned}$

**An equation for the curve S is **$y=9-3(x-2)^{2}$*  ***[1] **

**Equivalent equations such as '**$y=-3x^{2}+12x-3$**' are accepted '**$y = f \left(x - 4\right)$**' was also accepted as an answer; but the answer above is what was intended by the question**

> *Method 2: Using "turning point by completing the square"*

> *After translation by *$\begin{pmatrix} 4 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}$* (or a translation +4 in the **x-**axis), the turning point (−2, 9) becomes;*

*(2, 9)*

> *So the equation takes the form;*

$\begin{aligned}y & = & a \left(x - 2\right)^{2} + 9\end{aligned}$

> *And as the curve has not been stretched or reflected, the value of *$\begin{aligned} & & a\end{aligned}$* remains the same as in curve *$\begin{aligned} & & C\end{aligned}$*. i.e. *$\begin{aligned}a & = & 3\end{aligned}$*.*

**An equation for the curve S is **$y=-3(x-2)^{2}+9$*  ***[1]**

** Note this is the same equation as in Method 1, just written in a different order**

The function f($x$) is defined as ƒ ($x$) = 3 − 8$x$ − 2$x^{2}$

Find the coordinates of the turning point on the graph of $y$ = $f \left(x\right)$
parts.solutionMd:
> *Method 1*

> *Complete the square to rearrange *$f \left(x\right)$* into the form *$y = a \left(x + p\right)^{2} + q$*, as the turning point is *$\left(- p , q\right)$

$\begin{aligned}y & = & - 2 \left(x^{2} + 4 x\right) + 3 \\ & = & - 2 \left[\left(x + 2\right)^{2} - 4\right] + 3 \\ & = & - 2 \left(x + 2\right)^{2} + 8 + 3 \\ & = & - 2 \left(x + 2\right)^{2} + 11\end{aligned}$

**at least one correct step in completing the square ****[1] ****completing the square correctly ****[1]**

> *From this we can state the turning point*

$(-2,11)$** [1]**

> *Method 2*

$f ' \left(x\right)$* is the functions notation for *$\frac{dy}{dx}$ *Differentiate*

$f ' \left(x\right) = - 8 - 4 x$

**[1]**

> *To find the turning point, equate the derivative to zero*

$-8-4x=0$

**[1]**

> *Solve*

$\begin{aligned}- 8 & = & 4 x \\ x & = & - 2\end{aligned}$

> *Note that the question asks for the coordinates, so we need the **y** coordinate too*

$\begin{aligned}y & = & 3 - 8 \left(- 2\right) - 2 \left(- 2\right)^{2} \\ & = & 11\end{aligned}$

$(-2,11)$** [1]**

parts.problemMd:
The graph of $y=x^{3}+6$ is translated 4 units to the right.

The translated graph has equation $y=f(x)$

Work out $f(x)$.

Give your answer in the form $x^{3}+ax^{2}+bx+c$ where $a,b$ and $c$ are integers.
parts.solutionMd:
> *A translation 4 units to the right changes *$y = f \left(x\right)$* to *$y = f \left(x - 4\right)$*. Therefore *$y=x^{3}+6$* becomes;*

$y = \left(x - 4\right)^{3} + 6$

**[1]**

> *Expand the brackets remembering that *$\left(x - 4\right)^{3} = \left(x - 4\right) \left(x - 4\right) \left(x - 4\right)$*. Expand the first two brackets first.*

$=\left(x - 4\right)\left(x - 4\right)\left(x - 4\right)+ 6$
$= ( x ^{2} - 8 x + 16 ) ( x - 4 ) + 6$

**[1]**

> *Expand the brackets again, taking care to multiply each term in the first bracket by each term in the second bracket. Take particular care with the negatives.*

$=x^{3}-4x^{2}-8x^{2}+32x+16x-64+6$

**[1]**

> *Collect like terms.*

$x^{3}-12x^{2}+48x-58$ **[1]**

parts.problemMd:
Curve $P$ has equation $y=2(x--1)^{2}--5$

Curve $Q$ is a reflection in the $y$-axis of curve $P$.

Work out the equation of curve $Q$.

Give your answer in the form    $y=ax^{2}+bx+c$     where $a,b$ and $c$ are integers.
parts.solutionMd:
> *Method 1*

> *A reflection in the *$y$*-axis changes *$y = f \left(x\right)$* to *$y = f \left(- x\right)$*. This changes *$y = 2 \left(x - 1\right)^{2} - 5$* to;*

$y = 2 \left(- x - 1\right)^{2} - 5$

**[1]**

> *Expand the squared brackets.*

$\begin{aligned}y & = & 2 \left(- x - 1\right) \left(- x - 1\right) - 5 \\ & = & 2 \left(x^{2} + x + x + 1\right) - 5 \\ & = & 2 \left(x^{2} + 2 x + 1\right) - 5\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Expand the remaining bracket and collect like terms.*

$\begin{aligned} & = & 2 x^{2} + 4 x + 2 - 5 \\ & = & 2 x^{2} + 4 x - 3\end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned}\mathbf{\mathit{y}} & = & 2 \mathbf{\mathit{x}}^{2} + 4 \mathbf{\mathit{x}} - 3\end{aligned}$ **[1]**

> *Method 2*

> *A quadratic equation in completed square form *$y = a \left(x - p\right)^{2} + q$* has turning point at *$\left(p ,  q\right)$*.*

$y = 2 \left(x - 1\right)^{2} - 5$* **has a turning point at *$\left(1 , - 5\right)$

> *Reflect the turning point in the *$y$*-axis, keeping the value of '*$a$*' the same.*

*turning point at *$\left(- 1 , - 5\right) \rightarrow y = 2 \left(x + 1\right)^{2} - 5$

**[1]**

> *Expand the squared brackets.*

$\begin{aligned}y & = & 2 \left(x + 1\right) \left(x + 1\right) - 5 \\ & = & 2 \left(x^{2} + x + x + 1\right) - 5 \\ & = & 2 \left(x^{2} + 2 x + 1\right) - 5\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Expand the remaining bracket and collect like terms.*

$\begin{aligned} & = & 2 x^{2} + 4 x + 2 - 5 \\ & = & 2 x^{2} + 4 x - 3\end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned}\mathbf{\mathit{y}} & = & 2 \mathbf{\mathit{x}}^{2} + 4 \mathbf{\mathit{x}} - 3\end{aligned}$ **[1]**

![q18-paper2h-nov2020-edexcel-igcse-maths-1](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-18-higher/4-geometry-and-trigonometry/3d-pythagoras-and-trigonometry/assets/071-q18-paper2h-nov2020-edexcel-igcse-maths-1.png)

$\begin{aligned}A B & = & 5 cm \\ A H & = & 4 cm\end{aligned}$

The size of the angle between $CH$ and the plane $ABCD$ is $35^{\circ}$

Calculate the volume of the cuboid. 
Give your answer correct to $3$ significant figures.

..............................................$\mathrm{cm}^{3}$
parts.solutionMd:
> *To find the volume we are missing the "depth" of the cuboid; **BC **or equivalent.*

> *Identify and label the 35° angle between **CH** and the plane **ABCD** by drawing a right angled triangle using **CH **and the line that is perpendicular to the plane:*

![3d-trig-pythag-h4-1](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-18-higher/4-geometry-and-trigonometry/3d-pythagoras-and-trigonometry/assets/072-3d-trig-pythag-h4-1.png)

> *We can see that we have a right-angle triangle with a known side and angle. So we can find **AC**, which will then allow us to find **BC **in triangle **ABC**.*

> *Find **AC** using the tangent ratio.*

$tan \left(35\right) = \frac{4}{A C}$

**[1]**

> *Rearrange to find **AC.*

$\begin{aligned}A C & = & \frac{4}{tan \left(35\right)} \\ & = & 5 . 712592027 . . .\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *It's best to store this result as an exact value on your calculator. If you do round in your working though, round to at least 4 significant figures to preserve accuracy. We can mark this result on the diagram:*

![uz7Ie1aW_3d-trig-pythag-h4-2](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-18-higher/4-geometry-and-trigonometry/3d-pythagoras-and-trigonometry/assets/073-uz7ie1aw-3d-trig-pythag-h4-2.png)

> *Now we can use Pythagoras' Theorem to find **BC.*

$\begin{aligned}5 . 713^{2} & = & 5^{2} + B C^{2}\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Solve for **BC.*

$\begin{aligned}5 . 713^{2} - 5^{2} & = & B C^{2} \\ B C & = & \sqrt{5 . 713^{2} - 5^{2}} \\ & = & 2 . 762916515 . . .\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Now we can find the volume using volume of a cuboid = length × height × depth*

*volume = 4 × 5 × 2.762916515...*

*         = 55.25833029... cm**<sup>3</sup>*

> *Round your answer to 3 significant figures as requested.*

**Answer = 55.3 cm**<sup>**3**</sup>  **[1]**

parts.problemMd:
The diagram shows a triangular prism $ABCDEF$ with a horizontal base $ABEF$.

![q22-4ma1-1h-qp-june21-paper1-igcse-maths](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-18-higher/4-geometry-and-trigonometry/3d-pythagoras-and-trigonometry/assets/049-q22-4ma1-1h-qp-june21-paper1-igcse-maths.png)

$AC=BC=FD=ED=12\mathrm{cm}$       $AB=10\mathrm{cm}$           $BE=15\mathrm{cm}$

Calculate the size of the angle between $AD$ and the base $ABEF$. 
Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures.
parts.solutionMd:
> *To identify the angle between a line and a plane it is helpful to draw a right angled triangle using **AD **and the line that is perpendicular to the plane:*

![3d-trig-pythag-vh3-1](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-18-higher/4-geometry-and-trigonometry/3d-pythagoras-and-trigonometry/assets/050-3d-trig-pythag-vh3-1.png)

> *Triangle** EDF** is isosceles so **M** is the midpoint of **FE. **In order to find the required angle we need to find two lengths on triangle **AMD**. We will find **DM** and **AM** as follows.*

> *We can draw two new right-angle triangles to help us find sides **DM** and **AM **as below. Because **M **is the midpoint of **FE**, we know that **FM **= **ME **= 5cm.*

![3d-trig-pythag-vh3-2](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-18-higher/4-geometry-and-trigonometry/3d-pythagoras-and-trigonometry/assets/051-3d-trig-pythag-vh3-2.png)

> *We can see from the diagrams that to find **DM** and **AM**, we can use Pythagoras' Theorem with two different triangles.*

$DM=\sqrt{12^{2}-5^{2}}=\sqrt{119}$

**[1]**

$AM=\sqrt{15^{2}+5^{2}}=5\sqrt{10}$

**[1]**

> *We can mark these results on our diagram:*

![3d-trig-pythag-vh3-3](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-18-higher/4-geometry-and-trigonometry/3d-pythagoras-and-trigonometry/assets/052-3d-trig-pythag-vh3-3.png)

> *Now we have the opposite and adjacent side so can use the tangent ratio to find the required angle*

$\begin{aligned}tan \left(x\right) & = & \frac{\sqrt{119}}{5 \sqrt{10}}\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Use the inverse tangent function ("SHIFT tan" on your calculator) to find the required angle*

$\begin{aligned}x & = & tan^{- 1} \left(\frac{\sqrt{119}}{5 \sqrt{10}}\right) \\ & = & 34 . 60286258 . . .\end{aligned}$

> *Round your answer to 3 significant figures as requested. Remember to include the units.*

**Answer = **$34.6^{\circ}$ **[1]**

parts.problemMd:
Right-angled triangle$ABC$is the cross section of a prism.

$AB=5\mathrm{cm}BC=12\mathrm{cm}$ 
$M$ is the midpoint of $CF$. 
$AM=16\mathrm{cm}$

![q23-paper-2h-nov-2020-aqa-gcse-maths](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-18-higher/4-geometry-and-trigonometry/3d-pythagoras-and-trigonometry/assets/079-q23-paper-2h-nov-2020-aqa-gcse-maths.png)

Work out the volume of the prism.

......................................cm<sup>3</sup>
parts.solutionMd:
> *To find the volume of the prism, the length **CF **needs to be known.  *
*If **M **is the midpoint of **CF, **then **CF** = 2**CM.** *

> *ACM** is a right-angled triangle. *
*ABC** is a right-angled triangle, where **AB **= 5 cm, **BC** = 12 cm.*

> *Use Pythagoras' theorem with triangle**ABC **to find the length of **AC**.*

*  *$AC^{2}=AB^{2}+BC^{2}\,AC^{2}=5^{2}+12^{2}$

**[1]**

> *Solve**.*

$\begin{aligned}A C^{} & = & \sqrt{5^{2} + 12^{2}} \\ & = & \sqrt{169} \\ & = & 13\end{aligned}$

> *Use Pythagoras' theorem with triangle**ACM **to find the length of **CM**.*

**  **$\begin{aligned}A M^{ 2 } & = & A C^{ 2 } + C M^{ 2} \\ 16^{ 2 } & = & 13^{2} + C M^{2}\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Rearrange and solve to find **CM.*

$\begin{aligned}C \left(M^{2}\right)^{} & = & 16^{2} - 13^{2} \\ C M & = & \sqrt{16^{2} - 13^{2}} \\ & = & \sqrt{87}\end{aligned}$

> *It is better to use the exact value of **CM** in the next part.*

> *Find the length of the prism by multiplying **CM **by 2.*

**  **$\begin{aligned}C F & = & 2 C M = 2 \sqrt{87}\end{aligned}$

> *Find the volume of the prism by multiplying the area of the cross-section (triangle **ABC**) by the length of the prism (**CF**). *
*The area of a right-angled triangle can be found multiplying the base by the height and dividing by 2. *

$\begin{aligned}Volume^{} & = & \frac{1}{2} \left(5\right) \left(12\right) \times 2 \sqrt{87} = 559 . 6427 . . . cm^{3}\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Round the answer to a sensible degree of accuracy, for example 3 significant figures.*

**Volume = 560 cm**<sup>**3**</sup>** **** ****[1]**

parts.problemMd:
The length of the longest diagonal of a cube is 25cm.

Calculate the total surface area of the cube.

................................................... cm<sup>2</sup>
parts.solutionMd:
> *Method 1*

> *Draw a diagram showing a cube with dimensions of *$x$* **cm. Add the longest diagonal to the diagram and give this a length of 25 cm. *

> *It also may help to add the right-angled triangles that the diagonal makes with the edges onto the diagram.*

![ocr-gcse-tq-ma-3dpythagtrig-h-q4-diagram-1](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-18-higher/4-geometry-and-trigonometry/3d-pythagoras-and-trigonometry/assets/047-ocr-gcse-tq-ma-3dpythagtrig-h-q4-diagram-1.png)

> *Use Pythagoras' theorem for 3D shapes, *$x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2}=d^{2}$*, to find an expression for the square of the length of the longest diagonal in terms of *$x.$

$\begin{aligned}x^{2} + x^{2} + x^{2} & = & 3 x^{2}\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Form an equation by setting *$3x^{2}$* equal to the square of the longest diagonal, 25 cm.*

$\begin{aligned}3 x^{2} & = & 25^{2} \\ 3 x^{2} & = & 625\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *At this point you can solve the equation to find *$\begin{aligned} & & x\end{aligned}$*, however it is not necessary as the surface area of a cube is 6 multiplied by the area of one of the squares, so the surface area of the cube = *$\begin{aligned} & & 6 x^{2}\end{aligned}$*.*

$\begin{aligned}SA & = & 6 x^{2} = 2 \left(3 x^{2}\right) = 2 \left(625\right) \end{aligned}$

**Correct formula for surface area**** [1] ****equating to 2 × 25**<sup>**2**</sup>** [1]**

**Surface Area =**$1250\mathrm{cm}^{2}$* ***[1]**

> *Method 2*

> *Draw a diagram showing a cube with dimensions of *$x$* **cm.  Add the longest diagonal to the diagram and give this a length of 25 cm. *

> *It also may help to add the right-angled triangles that the diagonal makes with the edges onto the diagram.*

![ocr-gcse-tq-ma-3dpythagtrig-h-q4-diagram-1](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-18-higher/4-geometry-and-trigonometry/3d-pythagoras-and-trigonometry/assets/047-ocr-gcse-tq-ma-3dpythagtrig-h-q4-diagram-1.png)

> *Use Pythagoras' theorem, *$a^{2}+b^{2}=c^{2}$*, on the right-angled triangle on the base of the crate to find length of the diagonal on the base in terms of *$x.$

$\begin{aligned}x^{2} + x^{2} & = & 2 x^{2}\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

$\begin{aligned}c^{2} & = & 2 x^{2} \\ c & = & \sqrt{2 x^{2}} \\ & = & x \sqrt{2} cm\end{aligned}$

> *Add this to the diagram.*

![q21-4ma1-1hr-qp-jan20-paper1-igcse-maths](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-18-higher/4-geometry-and-trigonometry/3d-pythagoras-and-trigonometry/assets/002-q21-4ma1-1hr-qp-jan20-paper1-igcse-maths.png)

Angle $BEC$= 40° and angle $ACB$is obtuse. $AC$ = 6 cm and $CE$= 13cm

The area of triangle $ABC$is 22 $\mathrm{cm}^{2}$

Calculate the length of $AB$. 
Give your answer correct to one decimal place.

..................$\mathrm{cm}$
parts.solutionMd:
> *Start by marking the given information on the diagram.*

![3d-trig-pythag-vh5-1](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-18-higher/4-geometry-and-trigonometry/3d-pythagoras-and-trigonometry/assets/003-3d-trig-pythag-vh5-1.png)

> *We cannot assume that **BC** is 6 cm as we are not told that triangle **ABC **is isosceles. Therefore we need to use trigonometry with triangle **BCE **to find** BC**.*

$sin \left(40 \circ\right) = \frac{B C}{13}$

**[1]**

> *Multiply both sides by 13 to find **BC.*

$B C = 13 sin \left(40 \circ\right) = 8 . 356 238 . . .$

*Store this result in your calculator to preserve accuracy in future calculations.* *Use this result and "*$\frac{1}{2}absinC$*" with the area of triangle **ABC** to find angle **C.*

$\frac{1}{2} \left(6\right) \left(8 . 356 238 . . .\right) sin C = 22$

**[1]**

> *Rearrange to find angle **C.*

$\begin{aligned}sin C & = & \frac{22}{\frac{1}{2} \left(6\right) \left(8 . 356 238 . . .\right)} \\ C & = & sin^{- 1} \left(\frac{22}{\frac{1}{2} \left(6\right) \left(8 . 356 238 . . .\right)}\right) \\ C & = & 61 . 352 736 . . . \circ\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *We are told that angle **C **is obtuse, so subtract this acute answer from 180° to find the obtuse angle.*

$180^{\circ}-61.352736...^{\circ}=118.647263...^{\circ}$

**[1]**

> *Finally, use the cosine rule "*$a^{2}=b^{2}+c^{2}-2bccosA$*" with triangle **ACB** (we have two sides and the included angle) to find **AB*

$A B^{2} = 6^{2} + \left(8 . 356 . . .\right)^{2} - 2 \left(6\right) \left(8 . 356 . . .\right) c o s \left(118 . 647 . . . \circ\right)$

**[1]**

> *Evaluate and square root both sides to find **AB**.*

$\begin{aligned}A B & = & \sqrt{6^{2} + \left(8 . 356 . . .\right)^{2} - 2 \left(6\right) \left(8 . 356 . . .\right) c o s \left(118 . 647 . . . \circ\right)} \\ A B & = & 12 . 405 647 . . .\end{aligned}$

> *Round your answer to 1 decimal place as requested.*

**AB**** = 12.4 cm** **[1]**

![q1-veryhard-4-12-3d-pythogoras-and-trigonometry-edexcel-gcse-maths](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-18-higher/4-geometry-and-trigonometry/3d-pythagoras-and-trigonometry/assets/033-q1-veryhard-4-12-3d-pythogoras-and-trigonometry-.png)

The base, $ABCD$, of the prism is a square of side length 15 cm. 
Angle $ABE$and angle $CBE$are right angles. 
Angle $EAB$= 35°

$M$is the point on $DA$such that

$DM:MA=2:3$

Calculate the size of the angle between $EM$and the base of the prism. 
Give your answer correct to 1 decimal place.
parts.solutionMd:
> *To identify the angle between a line and a plane it is helpful to draw a right angled triangle using the line that is perpendicular to the plane:*

![4-12-edexcel-gcse-vhq1-1](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-18-higher/4-geometry-and-trigonometry/3d-pythagoras-and-trigonometry/assets/034-4-12-edexcel-gcse-vhq1-1.png)

> *In order to find the required angle you will first need to find the lengths of the side **MB **and **BE**. To find **BE** draw a right angled triangle **ABE **using the other information you are given.*

![4-12-edexcel-gcse-vhq1-2](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-18-higher/4-geometry-and-trigonometry/3d-pythagoras-and-trigonometry/assets/035-4-12-edexcel-gcse-vhq1-2.png)

> *In the triangle **ABE** you know an angle and the length of the adjacent side. You want to find the length of the opposite side so use the tan ratio.*

$tan \left(35\right) = \frac{z}{15}$

**[1]**

> *Multiply both sides by 15. Leave as an exact value.*

$\begin{aligned}z & = & 15 \times tan \left(35\right) \\ & = & 15 tan \left(35\right)\end{aligned}$

> *To find **MB** draw a right angled triangle **ABM **using the other information you are given.*

![4-12-edexcel-gcse-vhq1-3](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-18-higher/4-geometry-and-trigonometry/3d-pythagoras-and-trigonometry/assets/036-4-12-edexcel-gcse-vhq1-3.png)

> *As **DM** : **MA** = 2 : 3, you know that **MA** is *$\frac{3}{2+3}$* of the length of **DA**.*

$MB=\frac{3}{5}\times15=9\mathrm{cm}$

> *In the triangle **ABM** you know two lengths and want to find the hypotenuse so you can use Pythagoras' theorem.*

$\begin{aligned}M A^{2} + A B^{2} & = & M B^{2} \\ 9^{2} + 15^{2} & = & y^{2} \\ 306 & = & y^{2}\end{aligned}$

> *Take the positive square root of both sides. Leave as an exact answer.*

$y=\sqrt{306}$

**[1]**

> *Now you can use the triangle **MBE**. In this triangle you want to find an angle and you know the lengths of the sides that are opposite and adjacent to the angle so use the tan ratio. Use the exact values for the lengths or use your calculator's memory function.*

$\begin{aligned}tan \left(x\right) & = & \frac{15 tan \left(35\right)}{\sqrt{306}} \\ & = & 0 . 600423 . . .\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Find the angle by using the inverse tan function.*

$\begin{aligned}x & = & tan^{- 1} \left(\frac{15 tan \left(35\right)}{\sqrt{306}}\right) \\ & = & tan^{- 1} \left(0 . 600423 . . .\right) \\ & = & 30 . 981574 . . .\end{aligned}$

> *Round your answer to 1 decimal place. Remember to include the units.*

$\mathrm{Angle} \mathrm{between}EM\mathrm{and} \mathrm{the} \mathrm{base}=31.0^{\circ}(1\mathrm{dp})$ **[1]**

Calculate the size of the angle between $AF$ and the plane $ADEH$.

parts.solutionMd:
> *To identify the angle between a line and a plane it is helpful to draw a right angled triangle using **AD** and the line that is perpendicular to the plane:*

![4sE77S~X_3d-trig-pythag-vh4-1](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-18-higher/4-geometry-and-trigonometry/3d-pythagoras-and-trigonometry/assets/018-4se77s-x-3d-trig-pythag-vh4-1.png)
