The diagram shows the prism $ABCDEFGHJK$ with horizontal base $AEFG$

![q21-january-2022-1h-edexcel-igcse-maths](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-18-higher/4-geometry-and-trigonometry/3d-pythagoras-and-trigonometry/assets/023-q21-january-2022-1h-edexcel-igcse-maths.png)

$ABCDE$ is a cross section of the prism where

$ABDE$ is a square 
$BCD$ is an equilateral triangle

$EF=2\timesAE$  
$M$is the midpoint of $GF$ so that $JM$ is vertical.

Angle $MAJ=y^{\circ}$ 
Given that            $\mathrm{tan}y^{\circ}=T$ 
find the value of$T$, giving your answer in the form $\frac{\sqrt{p}+\sqrt{q}}{17}$ where $p$ and $q$ are integers.

$T$ = ...........................
parts.solutionMd:
> *Start by marking the information given on the diagram. We don't know any lengths but we can assign arbitray values so long as they are kept in the given ratios. *
*We can start by labeling the smallest known segments, **GM **and **MF**, as** **"1". *
*We can also mark angle **MAJ** as **y**.*

![3d-trig-pythag-vh6-1](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-18-higher/4-geometry-and-trigonometry/3d-pythagoras-and-trigonometry/assets/024-3d-trig-pythag-vh6-1.png)

> *To find **y**, we need to find two lengths on triangle **AJM**. *

> *First, we will find **AM**.*

> *If **GM **= **MF **= 1 then **GF **= 2 so **AE **= 2.  *
*From the question**, EF** = 2 × **AE** so **EF** = **AG **= 4.*

![3d-trig-pythag-vh6-2](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-18-higher/4-geometry-and-trigonometry/3d-pythagoras-and-trigonometry/assets/025-3d-trig-pythag-vh6-2.png)

> *Using Pythagoras' Theorem with triangle **AGM**, we can find **AM**. *

$\begin{aligned}A M & = & \sqrt{1^{2} + 4^{2}} \\ & = & \sqrt{1 + 16} \\ & = & \sqrt{17}\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Now we turn our attention to finding **MJ**.*

> *Add a point **N** to the line **HK** directly above **M**. Triangle **HJK** is equilateral so **NK** = 1 and **JK **= 2:*

![v-JQcpZB_3d-trig-pythag-vh6-3](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-18-higher/4-geometry-and-trigonometry/3d-pythagoras-and-trigonometry/assets/026-v-jqcpzb-3d-trig-pythag-vh6-3.png)

> *Using Pythagoras' Theorem with triangle **JKN, **we can find **JN*

$\begin{aligned}J N & = & \sqrt{2^{2} - 1^{2}} \\ & = & \sqrt{4 - 1} \\ & = & \sqrt{3}\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *We add **MN** and **JN** to get **MJ.*

$\begin{aligned}M J & = & \sqrt{3} + 2\end{aligned}$

> *Mark **MJ **and **AM** on triangle **AMJ.*

![3d-trig-pythag-vh6-4](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-18-higher/4-geometry-and-trigonometry/3d-pythagoras-and-trigonometry/assets/027-3d-trig-pythag-vh6-4.png)

> *Now we can use trigonometry with triangle** AMJ** to find the value of tan(y), or **T**.*

$\begin{aligned}T & = & tan \left(y\right) = \frac{\sqrt{3} + 2}{\sqrt{17}}\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Finally we need to rationalise the denominator*

$\begin{aligned}T & = & \frac{\sqrt{17} \left(\sqrt{3} + 2\right)}{\sqrt{17} \sqrt{17}} \\ & = & \frac{\sqrt{51} + 2 \sqrt{17}}{17}\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *We are almost there! We need to write the answer in the form requested. 2 is the same as √4 so...*

$\begin{aligned} & = & \frac{\sqrt{51} + \sqrt{4} \sqrt{17}}{17} \\ & = & \frac{\sqrt{51} + \sqrt{68}}{17}\end{aligned}$

$\mathbf{\mathit{T}} \begin{aligned} & = & \end{aligned} \begin{aligned} & & \frac{\sqrt{51} + \sqrt{68}}{17}\end{aligned}$ **[1]**

parts.solutionMd:
> *Method 1*

> *In a parallelogram each pair of adjacent angles are co-interior angles (allied angles) so they add up to 180°.*

*Angles ***BCD*** and*** CDA*** are co-interior angles so add up to 180°* $\begin{aligned}Angle C D A & = & 180 \circ - 58 \circ \\ & = & 122 \circ\end{aligned}$

*Angles ***CDA*** and ***EDF*** are vertically opposite so are equal* $\begin{aligned}Angle E D F & = & 122 \circ\end{aligned}$

*Angles ***DEF ***and ***DFE*** are the base angles in an isosceles triangle so are equal* $\begin{aligned}Angle D E F & = & Angle D F E = x \circ\end{aligned}$

*Angles ***EDF, DEF ***and ***DFE*** are the interior angles in a triangle so add up to 180°* $\begin{aligned}x \circ + x \circ + 122 \circ & = & 180 \circ \\ 2 x + 122 & = & 180 \\ 2 x & = & 58 \\ x & = & 29\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

$\mathrm{Angle}DEF=29^{\circ}$ **[1] **
**One correct reason stated**** [1]**

**[1]**

*Angles ***DEF ***and ***DFE*** are the base angles in an isosceles triangle so are equal* $\begin{aligned}Angle D E F & = & Angle D F E = x \circ\end{aligned}$

> *The sum of two angles in a triangle is equal to the opposite exterior angle.*

*Angles ***DEF ***and ***DFE*** are two interior angles in a triangle opposite the exterior angle ***ADF*** so the sum of the two interior angles is equal to the exterior angle* $\begin{aligned}x \circ + x \circ & = & 58 \circ \\ 2 x & = & 58 \\ x & = & 29\end{aligned}$

![Octagon JABCDEFGHI with interior lines OE and OD, adjoining triangle EDK, angle x° at K; diagram note states "NOT accurately drawn".](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-18-higher/4-geometry-and-trigonometry/angles-in-polygons-and-parallel-lines/assets/003-octagon-jabcdefghi-with-interior-lines-oe-and-od.png)

$ODK$and $FEK$ are straight lines.
Work out the value of $x$
parts.solutionMd:
> *Calculate angle FOE; it is an angle at the centre of a 9-sided regular polygon, so*

$\mathrm{angle}FOE=360\div9=40$

**[M1]**

> *You can use this to calculate angle OFE, as triangle FOE is an isosceles triangle*

$\mathrm{angle}OFE=\frac{180-40}{2}=70$

> *Angle FOD must be double angle FOE*

$\mathrm{angle}FOD=40\times2=80$

**[M1]**

![An octagon labelled A to J with triangles OEF and DEK; angles are 40°, 70°, and x°. Note: Diagram not accurately drawn.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-18-higher/4-geometry-and-trigonometry/angles-in-polygons-and-parallel-lines/assets/004-an-octagon-labelled-a-to-j-with-triangles-oef-an.jpg)

> *Then calculate *$x$* using the sum of angles in triangle FOK*

$180-70-80=30$

**Final answer:** **30**

**[A1]**

$\frac{180 \left(8 - 2\right)}{8} = 135 \circ$

*Let Angle ***GFK *** =** *$x$

> *Find the sum of the interior angles of the hexagon using: *$s u m o f i n t e r i o r a n g l e s = 180 \left(n - 2\right)$* where *$n$* is the number of sides of the polygon.*

$180 \left(6 - 2\right) = 720 \circ$

*Form an equation for the sum of the interior angles of the hexagon and solve for *$x$.

parts.solutionMd:
> *First find the size of angle **b**. Start by dividing 90 (the size of angle **a**) by 5 (the 'angle **a**' number in the ratio).*

$90\div5=18^{\circ}$

> *That gives the size of one of the 'parts' that the ratio divides the angles into. Now multiply that by 3 (the 'angle **b**' number in the ratio) to find the size of angle **b**.*

$b=18\times3=54^{\circ}$

**[1]**

> *Next find the size of angle **x**. The angles in a quadrilateral always add up to 360 degrees. So angles **x **and **y **together must be equal to 360 degrees minus angles **a** and **b.*

$x + y = 360 - \left(90 + 54\right) = 216 \circ$

> *Divide that by 4 (the sum of the **x** : **y** ratio numbers) to find the size of one of the 'parts' that that ratio divides the 216 degrees into. And then because the '**x** number' in the ratio is 1, that part is the same as the size of angle **x.*

$216\div4=54\,\,x=1\times54=54^{\circ}$

**[1]**

> *Finally, state your conclusion.*

**b**** = 54° and ****x ****= 54****°.  ****Therefore ****b**** = ****x.****  [1]**

parts.solutionMd:
> *Remember that in any polygon, an interior angle and its corresponding exterior angle add up to 180° *
*Therefore  **p** + **q** = 180.*

> *Now add up the ratio numbers from the ratio in part (a) to find how many 'parts' the ratio divides the 180° into. *

$1+5=6\,\,180\div6=30$

**[1]**

*And the **p  **number in the ratio is 1. *
*That means that **p** gets 1 part, i.e. that  **p** = 30.*

$p=30\times1=30$

**[1]**

> *Now there are two possibilities:*

> *1)  **p**  is one of the equal angles in the isosceles triangle.      Then there is another angle equal to 30°.      And the third angle is equal to (180 - (30 + 30))°.*

$180 - \left(30 + 30\right) = 180 - 60 = 120$

> *2)  **p**  is not one of the equal angles in the isosceles triangle.      Then the other two angles are the equal angles.      And each is equal to ((180 - 30) ÷ 2)°.*

$\begin{aligned}\left(180 - 30\right) \div 2 & = & 150 \div 2 = 75\end{aligned}$

$PQRST$ is a regular pentagon.
 $R,U$ and $T$ are points on a circle, centre $O$.
 $QR$ and $PT$ are tangents to the circle.
 $RSU$ is a straight line.

Prove that $ST=UT$.
parts.solutionMd:
> *To prove that **ST  **is equal to** UT ** you will need to **prove **that the triangle **STU **is **isosceles**. This can be done by finding the angles. *

> *PQRST **is a regular pentagon, so the angle **TSU** is the exterior angle of a regular pentagon. *
*Exterior angles in any polygon add up to 360°. *
*A regular pentagon has 5 equal exterior angles.*

> * *`T S with hat on top U space equals 360 over 5 equals space 72 degree`

**[1]**

> *To find the size of angle **SUT**, you will need to consider circle theorems.*

> *Begin by joining the point **O** to the points **T** and **R,** marking all the radiuses of the circle as equal lengths on the diagram.*

> *TP** and **TR **are also tangents to the circle, so by the circle theorem 'A tangent always meets a radius at 90°', angles **ORQ **and **OTP **are both 90°. *

`O R with hat on top Q space equals space O T with hat on top P space equals 90 degree`* **(angle between tangent and radius)*

**[1]**

> *Mark these onto the diagram.*

![QLY1pOQ2_4-8-edexcel-gcse-vh-q3-diagram-2](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-18-higher/4-geometry-and-trigonometry/angles-in-polygons-and-parallel-lines/assets/015-qly1poq2-4-8-edexcel-gcse-vh-q3-diagram-2.png)

> *The sum of the interior angles in any polygon can be found using the formula 180°(n - 2). A regular pentagon has 5 equal interior angles, therefore these can be found using the formula *$\frac{180 \left(5 - 2\right)}{5}$*.*

> * *$T \hat{P} Q = P \hat{Q} R = \frac{3 \left(180\right)}{5} = 108 \circ$

> *Add these angles to the diagram.*

![4-8-edexcel-gcse-vh-q3-diagram-3](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-18-higher/4-geometry-and-trigonometry/angles-in-polygons-and-parallel-lines/assets/016-4-8-edexcel-gcse-vh-q3-diagram-3.png)

> *PQROT  **is a pentagon, so the angle **ROT**  can be found by subtracting the other four angles from the sun of the angles in a pentagon.*

> *The sum of the interior angles in any polygon can be found using the formula 180°(n - 2).*

$R \hat{O} T + O \hat{T} P + T \hat{P} Q + P \hat{Q} R + Q \hat{R} O = 180 \left(5 - 2\right) \circ = 540 \circ$

> *Substitute in the angles you know to find angle **ROT**.*

$\begin{aligned}R \hat{O} T + 90 \circ + 90 \circ + 108 \circ + 108 \circ & = & 540 \circ \\ R \hat{O} T + 396 \circ & = & 540 \circ \\ R \hat{O} T & = & 144 \circ\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *By the circle theorem, the angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference, angle **ROT **is twice angle **RUT.*

$R \hat{O} T = 2 \left(R \hat{U} T\right) = 2 \left(S \hat{U} T\right)$

$S \hat{U} T = \frac{R \hat{O} T}{2} = \frac{144}{2} = 72 \circ$

**[1]**

> *This proves that angle **TSU **is equal to angle **SUT **and so triangle **STU **is isosceles.*

**Therefore ****ST ****= ****UT **
**All reasons given clearly [1]**

![q3-4-5-easy-edexcel-gcse-maths](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-18-higher/4-geometry-and-trigonometry/area-and-perimeter/assets/082-q3-4-5-easy-edexcel-gcse-maths.png)

The centre of each semicircle is on $DC$.

Work out the area of the shaded region. 
Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures.
parts.solutionMd:
> *Calculate the area of the trapezium using: *$A = \frac{1}{2} \left(a + b\right) h$*, where *$a$* and *$b$* are the lengths of the parallel sides and *$h$* is the perpendicular height of the trapezium.*

$\begin{aligned}A & = & \frac{1}{2} \times \left(28 + 12\right) \times 14 \\ & = & 280 cm^{2}\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Divide the length of the base of the trapezium by 4 to find the radius of the semi-circles.*

![4-5-5](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-18-higher/4-geometry-and-trigonometry/area-and-perimeter/assets/083-4-5-5.png)

$\begin{aligned}r & = & 12 \div 4 \\ r & = & 3 cm\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Calculate the area of a circle (two semi-circles) using: *$A=πr^{2}$*.*

$A = \mathrm{\pi } ( 3 )^{2}$
A equals 9 straight pi

> *Calculate the area that is shaded by subtracting the area of the circle from the area of the trapezium.*

$\begin{aligned}A & = & 280 - 9 \pi\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

$\begin{aligned}A & = & 251 . 725666 . . .\end{aligned}$

> *Round the answer to 3 significant figures.*

$252\mathrm{cm}^{2}$**[1]**

parts.problemMd:
The diagram shows a wall in the shape of a trapezium.

![q4-4-5-easy-edexcel-gcse-maths](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-18-higher/4-geometry-and-trigonometry/area-and-perimeter/assets/087-q4-4-5-easy-edexcel-gcse-maths.png)

Karen is going to cover this part of the wall with tiles. 
Each tile is rectangular, 15 cm by 7.5 cm.

Tiles are sold in packs. 
There are 9 tiles in each pack.

Karen divides the area of this wall by the area of a tile to work out an estimate for the number of tiles she needs to buy.

Use Karen's method to work out the estimate for the number of packs of tiles she needs to buy.
parts.solutionMd:
> *Calculate the area of the trapezium using: *$A = \frac{1}{2} \left(a + b\right) h$*, where *$a$* and *$b$* are the lengths of the parallel edges and *$h$* is the perpendicular height.*

$\begin{aligned}A & = & \frac{1}{2} \times \left(1 . 8 + 2 . 7\right) \times 0 . 8 \\ & = & 1 . 8 m^{2}\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Convert the lengths of the tile from cm to m by dividing by 100.*

$\begin{array}{rcl} \frac{15}{100} \end{array} = 0.15$
$\begin{array}{rcl} \frac{7.5}{100} \end{array} = 0.075$

**[1]**

> *Calculate the area of a single tile in m*<sup>*2*</sup>*.*

$\begin{aligned}A & = & 0 . 15 \times 0 . 075 \\ & = & 0 . 01125 m^{2} \end{aligned}$

> *Calculate the number of tiles required by dividing the total area of the wall by the area of an individual tile.*

$\frac{1.8}{0.01125}=160$

**[1]**

> *Calculate the number of packs of tiles required by dividing the number of individual tiles required by the number in each pack.*

$\frac{160}{9}=17.777777...$

**[1]**

> *Round to the next pack up to make sure Karen has enough tiles.*

**18 packs**** ****[1]**

parts.problemMd:
Karen is advised to buy 10% more tiles than she estimated. Buying 10% more tiles will affect the number of the tiles Karen needs to buy.

She assumes she will need to buy 10% more packs of tiles.

Is Karen's assumption correct? 
You must show your working.
parts.solutionMd:
> *Look at the percentages in terms of packs.*

> *Calculate the new number of packs required by dividing the number of packs calculated in part (a) by 100 and multiplying by 10, then adding them to the original number of packs required.*

$\frac{18}{100}\times10+180=19.8$

**[1]**

*Karen must buy 20 packs*

> *Look at the number of individual tiles required.*

> *Calculate the new number individual tiles required by dividing the number of tiles calculated in part (a) by 100 and multiplying by 10, then adding them to the original number of individual tiles required.*

$\frac{160}{100}\times10+160=176$

> *Divide the new number of individual tiles by the number in a pack to find the new number of packs required.*

$\frac{176}{9}=19.555555...$* Karen must buy 20 packs*

**Yes Karen's assumption is correct as she must buy two more packs ****[1]**

parts.problemMd:
Here is a diagram showing a rectangle, $ABCD$, and a circle.

![q5-4-5-easy-edexcel-gcse-maths](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-18-higher/4-geometry-and-trigonometry/area-and-perimeter/assets/072-q5-4-5-easy-edexcel-gcse-maths.png)

$BC$ is a diameter of the circle.

Calculate the percentage of the area of the rectangle that is shaded. 
Give your answer correct to 1 decimal place.
parts.solutionMd:
> *The shaded area is formed by a rectangle with a semi-circle removed.*

> *Calculate the area of the rectangle **ABCD.*

$19\times16=304\mathrm{cm}^{2}$

> *Calculate the radius of the circle by dividing the height of the rectangle by 2.*

$\frac{16}{2}=8\mathrm{cm}$

> *Calculate the area of the circle, using: *$A=πr^{2}$*.*

$\begin{aligned}A & = & \pi \times \left(8\right)^{2} \\ & = & 64 \pi cm^{2}\end{aligned}$

**Correct process to find EITHER the area of the rectangle OR the area of the circle**** [1]**

> *Find the area of the shaded section by subtracting the area of half of the circle from the area of the rectangle.*

$\begin{aligned}A & = & 304 - \frac{1}{2} \times 64 \pi \\ & = & 203 . 469035 . . .\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Calculate the percentage of the rectangle that is shaded by dividing the shaded area by the area of the rectangle and multiplying the result by 100%.*

$\frac{203 . 469035 . . .}{304} \times 100 \% = 66 . 930603 . . .$*%*

**[1]**

> *Round the result to 1 decimal place.*

**66.9 % ****[1]**

**Answers in the range of 66 - 68% will be accepted.**

parts.problemMd:
The diagram shows a path around a pond.

![q6-4-5-easy-edexcel-gcse-maths](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-18-higher/4-geometry-and-trigonometry/area-and-perimeter/assets/084-q6-4-5-easy-edexcel-gcse-maths.png)

The pond is in the shape of a rectangle with length 7m and width 4m. 
The path is 3m wide.

Ali is going to cover the path with gravel. 
One bag of gravel will cover 10 m<sup>2</sup> of the path.

How many bags of gravel does Ali need to buy? 
You must show your working.
parts.solutionMd:
> *Find the dimensions of outer edges of the path.*

*Length = 7 + 3 + 3 = 13 m Width = 4 + 3 + 3 = 10 m*

> *Calculate the entire area of the path and the pond.*

*13 x 10 = 130 m**<sup>2</sup>*

> *Calculate the area of the pond.*

*7 x 4 = 28 m**<sup>2</sup>*

**One correct area of EITHER the pond OR the pond and the path**** [1]**

> *Calculate the total area of the path by subtracting the area of the pond from the entire area of the pond and the path.*

*130 - 28 = 102 m**<sup>2</sup>*

**[1]**

> *Calculate the number of bags of gravel that Ali needs to buy by dividing the total area of the path by the area that one bag of gravel will cover.*

*102*$\div$*10 = 10.2*

**[1]**

> *Round up to the next whole number of bags.*

**11 bags**** [1]**

parts.problemMd:
Mr Weaver's garden is in the shape of a rectangle.

In the garden

|   | there is a patio in the shape of a rectangle |
|---|---|
| and | two ponds in the shape of circles with diameter 3.8 m. |

Mr Weaver is going to spread fertiliser over all the grass. 
One box of fertiliser will cover 25 m<sup>2</sup> of grass.

How many boxes of fertiliser does Mr Weaver need?

parts.solutionMd:
> *Calculate the area of the entire garden.*

*17 x 9.5 = 161.5 m**<sup>2</sup>*

> *Calculate the area of the patio.*

*2.8 x 9.5 = 26.6 m**<sup>2</sup>*

**[1]**

> *Find the radius of a pond by dividing its diameter by 2.*

$r=\frac{3.8}{2}=1.9m$

> *Calculate the area of one pond, using *$A=πr^{2}$*.*

$\begin{aligned}A & = & \pi \left(1 . 9\right)^{2} \\ & = & 11 . 341149 . . . m^{2}\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Calculate the area of the grass by subtracting the areas of the patio and two ponds from the area of the entire garden.*

$\begin{aligned}A & = & 161 . 5 - 26 . 6 - 2 \times 11 . 341149 . . .\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

$A \begin{aligned} & = & \end{aligned} \begin{aligned} & & 112\end{aligned} \begin{aligned} & & .\end{aligned} \begin{aligned} & & 2177\end{aligned} \begin{aligned} & & .\end{aligned} \begin{aligned} & & .\end{aligned} \begin{aligned} & & .\end{aligned} \begin{aligned} & & \end{aligned} \begin{aligned} & & m\end{aligned}^{2}$

**Values between 112 - 113 are accepted**** [1]**

> *Calculate the number of boxes that Mr Weaver will need by dividing the area of the grass by the area that one box of fertiliser will cover.*

$\frac{112.2177...}{25}=4.4887...$

> *Round up to the next number of whole boxes.*

**5 boxes**** [1]**

parts.problemMd:

![q8-4-5-easy-edexcel-gcse-maths](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-18-higher/4-geometry-and-trigonometry/area-and-perimeter/assets/074-q8-4-5-easy-edexcel-gcse-maths.png)

 It costs £2.56 to cover each square metre with tarmac.

parts.problemMd:
The diagram shows the plan of a floor.

![q9-4-5-easy-edexcel-gcse-maths](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-18-higher/4-geometry-and-trigonometry/area-and-perimeter/assets/078-q9-4-5-easy-edexcel-gcse-maths.png)

Angie is going to varnish the floor.

She needs 1 litre of varnish for 5m<sup>2</sup> of floor. 
There are 2.5 litres of varnish in each tin of varnish.

Angie has 3 tins of varnish.

Does she have enough varnish for all the floor? 
You must show all your working.
parts.solutionMd:
> *Method 1:*

> *Calculate the area of the rectangle of length 10 m and width 6 m.*

**A*** = 10 x 6 = 60 m**<sup>2</sup>*

> *Calculate the area of the small rectangle at the top centre.*

**A*** = 5 x 2 = 10 m**<sup>2</sup>*

**[1]**

> *Calculate the area of the floor by subtracting the area of the smaller rectangle from the area of the larger rectangle.*

**A*** = 60 - 10 = 50 m**<sup>2</sup>*

**Complete method to find the area of the floor ****[1]**

> *Calculate the area of the floor that Angie can varnish with her three tins. *
*Multiply the number of tins of varnish by the number of litres of varnish in each tin by the area that 1 litre will cover.*

*3 x 2.5 x 5 = 37.5 m**<sup>2</sup>*

**Complete method to find the area the varnish will cover**** [1]**** Correct areas for both the floor and the area the varnish will cover**** [1]**

> *Compare the area that the varnish will cover with the area of the floor.*

*37.5 m**<sup>2</sup>** < 50 m**<sup>2</sup>*

**Angie does not have enough varnish to cover all of the floor**** [1]**

> *Method 2:*

> *Calculate the area of the rectangle of length 10 m and width 6 m.*

**A*** = 10 x 6 = 60 m**<sup>2</sup>*

> *Calculate the area of the small rectangle at the top centre.*

**A*** = 5 x 2 = 10 m**<sup>2</sup>*

**[1]**

> *Calculate the area of the floor by subtracting the area of the smaller rectangle from the area of the larger rectangle.*

**A*** = 60 - 10 = 50 m**<sup>2</sup>*

**Complete method to find the area of the floor ****[1]**

> *Calculate the number of litres required to cover the floor by dividing the area of the floor by the number of m*<sup>*2*</sup>* that each litre will cover.*

*50*$\div$*5 = 10 litres*

**Complete method to find number of litres required to cover the floor**** [1]**

> *Calculate the number of litres of varnish that Angie has by multiply the number of tins by the number of litres in each tin.*

*3 x 2.5 = 7.5 litres*

**Correct values for both the number of litres of varnish required to cover the whole floor and the number of litres of varnish in the three tins**** [1]**

> *Compare the number of litres that Angie has with the number of litres required to cover the whole floor.*

*7.5 litres < 10 litres*

**Angie does not have enough varnish to cover all of the floor**** [1]**

parts.problemMd:
This rectangular frame is made from 5 straight pieces of metal.

![q10-4-5-easy-edexcel-gcse-maths](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-18-higher/4-geometry-and-trigonometry/area-and-perimeter/assets/071-q10-4-5-easy-edexcel-gcse-maths.png)

The weight of the metal is 1.5 kg per metre.

Work out the total weight of the metal in the frame.
parts.solutionMd:
*Calculate the length of the diagonal bar. *
*Substitute the given lengths into Pythagoras' theorem,* $a^{2}+b^{2}=c^{2}$*, where *$a$* and *$b$* are the length of the two shorter sides of a right-angled triangle and *$c$* is the length of the longest side.*

$\begin{aligned}12^{2} + 5^{2} & = & c^{2}\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Simplify.*

$\begin{aligned}169 & = & c^{2}\end{aligned}$

> *Square root both sides.*

$\begin{aligned}13 & = & c\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Find the total length of metal that makes up the frame.*

*12 + 12 + 5 + 5 + 13 = 47 m*

**[1]**

> *Multiply the total length of the frame by the weight of the metal per metre to find the total weight of the metal in the frame.*

*47 x 1.5*

**[1]**

**70.5 kg ****[1]**

**Note that that it is actually the mass of the frame rather than the weight that is discussed in this question.**

parts.solutionMd:
> *The formula for a triangle is *$A=\frac{1}{2}ab\mathrm{sin}C$* where **a **and **b **are the lengths of two sides that form angle **C**.** *
*Let **x** denote the length **PQ**. Triangle **PQR** is an equilateral triangle so all the lengths are equal and all the angles are 60°. Find the area by substituting **a** = **x**, **b** = **x **and **C** = 60. Simplify the expression,*

$\begin{aligned}Area of P Q R & = & \frac{1}{2} \times x \times x \times sin \left(60\right) \\ & = & \frac{1}{2} \times x \times x \times \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \\ & = & \frac{\sqrt{3}}{4} x^{2}\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *The length **PQ** = 1.5**x**. A regular hexagon is made up of 6 equilateral triangles. *
*Find the area of the hexagon by finding substituting **a** = 1.5**x**, **b** = 1.5**x** and **C** = 60 into the formula and multiplying by 6.*

$\begin{aligned}Area of A B C D E F & = & \frac{1}{2} \times 1 . 5 x \times 1 . 5 x \times sin \left(60\right) \times 6 \\ & = & \frac{1}{2} \times 1 . 5 x \times 1 . 5 x \times \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \times 6 \\ & = & \frac{27 \sqrt{3}}{8} x^{2}\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Form an equation using the fact that the difference between the area of the triangle and the hexagon is equal to *$72\sqrt{3}$* cm*<sup>*2*</sup>*.*

$\begin{aligned}\frac{27 \sqrt{3}}{8} x^{2} - \frac{\sqrt{3}}{4} x^{2} & = & 72 \sqrt{3}\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Divide both sides √3 and multiply both sides by 8. Then solve the equation to find **x **(which is a positive value so you can ignore the negative square root).*

$\begin{aligned}27 x^{2} - 2 x^{2} & = & 576 \\ 25 x^{2} & = & 576 \\ x^{2} & = & \frac{576}{25} \\ x & = & \sqrt{\frac{576}{25}} \\ x & = & \frac{24}{5}\end{aligned}$

**The length of ****PQ**** is 4.8 cm ****[1]**

parts.problemMd:
Calvin has $12$ identical rectangular tiles. He arranges the tiles to fit exactly round the edge of a shaded rectangle, as shown in the diagram below.

![q5-paper2h-jan2019-edexcel-igcse-maths](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-18-higher/4-geometry-and-trigonometry/area-and-perimeter/assets/026-q5-paper2h-jan2019-edexcel-igcse-maths.png)

Work out the area of the shaded rectangle.
parts.solutionMd:
*Call the longer length of the tile **x** and the smaller length **y**.* 
*4 long lengths and one short length make up the length of 123 cm.* 
*2 long lengths and one short length make up the length of 67 cm.* 
*Form two equations with this information.*

$\begin{aligned}4 x + y & = & 123 \\ 2 x + y & = & 67\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Subtract the equations to eliminate the **y** variable. Then solve for **x**.*

$4 x + \cancel{y} = 123 - \left(2 x + \cancel{y} = 67\right) 2 x = 56 x = 28$

**[1]**

> *Substitute the value of **x** back into one of the equations to find **y**.*

$\begin{aligned}4 \left(28\right) + y & = & 123 \\ 112 + y & = & 123 \\ y & = & 11\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *The area of the shaded bit can be found by finding the area of the whole rectangle and subtracting the area of 12 tiles.*

$123\times67-12\times28\times11=4545$

**[1]**

> *Include the units for the area.*

**Area is**** 4545 cm**<sup>**2**</sup> **[1]**

parts.problemMd:
The diagram shows a circle and a trapezium.

![q2-paper2h-spec2016-edexcel-igcse-maths](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-18-higher/4-geometry-and-trigonometry/area-and-perimeter/assets/029-q2-paper2h-spec2016-edexcel-igcse-maths.png)

The height of the trapezium is $h\mathrm{cm}$.

The area of the circle is equal to the area of the trapezium.

Work out the value of $h$. 
Give your answer correct to 1 decimal place.
parts.solutionMd:
> *Calculate the area of the circle, using *$A=πr^{2}$*.*

$\begin{aligned}A_{S C} & = & \pi \left(8 . 5\right)^{2} \\ & = & 72 . 25 \pi cm^{2}\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *It is best to leave the area of the circle in terms of π for accuracy.*

> *FInd an expression for the area of the trapezium, using the formula: *$A = \frac{1}{2} \left(a + b\right) h$*, where *$a$* and *$b$* are the lengths of the parallel sides and *$h$*is the perpendicular height.*

$\begin{aligned}A & = & \frac{1}{2} \left(20 + 25\right) \times h \\ & = & 22 . 5 h cm^{2}\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Form an equation by setting the expression for the area of the trapezium equal to the area of the circle.*

$22.5h=72.25π$

> *Rearrange and solve for **h**.*

$\begin{aligned}h & = & 72 . 25 \pi \div 22 . 5 = 10 . 088 . . .\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Round to 1 decimal place.*

**h**** = 10.1 cm**** [1]**

parts.problemMd:
The diagram shows a regular octagon $ABCDEFGH.$

![q22-paper1hr-nov2020-edexcel-igcse-maths](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-18-higher/4-geometry-and-trigonometry/area-and-perimeter/assets/030-q22-paper1hr-nov2020-edexcel-igcse-maths.png)

Each side of the octagon has length $10\mathrm{cm}.$

Find the area of the shaded region $ACDEH.$ 
Give your answer correct to the nearest $\mathrm{cm}^{2}$

............................................. $\mathrm{cm}^{2}$
parts.solutionMd:
> *Find the interior angle of the regular octagon using: *$size of interior angle = \frac{180 \left(n - 2\right)}{n}$*, where *$n$* is the number of sides of the polygon.*

$\frac{180 \left(8 - 2\right)}{8} = 135 \circ$

**[1]**

> *Therefore angle **ABC** = 135°, and triangle **ABC **is an isosceles triangle with sides of 10cm. Mark this on the diagram.*

![ed-igcse-area-and-perimeter-vh-q7](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-18-higher/4-geometry-and-trigonometry/area-and-perimeter/assets/031-ed-igcse-area-and-perimeter-vh-q7.png)

> *Triangle **ABC **is an isosceles triangle, so angle **BAC **= angle **BCA **= 1/2(180 - 135). *

*Angle ***BAC ***= Angle ***BCA ***= ** *$\frac{180-135}{2}=22.5^{\circ}$

> *Find angles **ACD **and **CAD **in triangle **ACD.*

![ed-igcse-area-and-perimeter-vh-q7-diagram-2](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-18-higher/4-geometry-and-trigonometry/area-and-perimeter/assets/032-ed-igcse-area-and-perimeter-vh-q7-diagram-2.png)

*Angle ***ACD*** = Angle ***BCD*** - Angle ***ABC*** = 135 - 22.5 = 112.5°*

*Angle ***CAD*** = Angle ***BAH ***- Angle ***DAH*** - Angle ***BAC ***= 135 - 90 - 22.5 = 22.5°*

> *To find the length of **AD, y**ou know the length of one side (**CD**) and the angle opposite it (**CAD**). You also know angle **ACD** so you can find the length of the side opposite that using the sine rule.*

> *The formula for the sine rule is *$\frac{a}{\mathrm{sin}A}=\frac{b}{\mathrm{sin}B}$*, where **a** and **b** are the lengths of the two sides that are opposite the angles **A **and **B **respectively. Substitute **a** = **AD**, **b** = 10, **A** = 112.5 and **B** = 22.5 into the formula.*

$\frac{A D}{sin \left(112 . 5\right)} = \frac{10}{sin \left(22 . 5\right)}$

**[1]**

> *Multiply both sides by sin(112.5) and type into your calculator.*

$\begin{aligned}A D & = & \frac{10}{sin \left(22 . 5\right)} \times sin \left(112 . 5\right) \\ & = & 24 . 14213 . . .\end{aligned}$

> *Now find the area of rectangle **ADEH.*

**Area ADEH ***= 24.14213... × 10 = 241.4213... cm**<sup>2</sup>*

**[1]**

> *Now look at triangle **ACD**.*

![ed-igcse-area-and-perimeter-vh-q7-diagram-3](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-18-higher/4-geometry-and-trigonometry/area-and-perimeter/assets/033-ed-igcse-area-and-perimeter-vh-q7-diagram-3.png)

> *Find angle **ADC.*

*Angle ***ADC*** = Angle ***CDE*** - Angle ***ADE*** = 135 - 90 = 45°*

> *The formula for the area of a triangle is *$\mathrm{Area}=\frac{1}{2}ab\mathrm{sin}C$*, where **a** and **b** are the lengths of the two sides that form angle **C**. Substitute **a** = 24.14213..., **b** = 10 and **C** = 45 into the formula.*

$\begin{aligned}Area & = & \frac{1}{2} \times 24 . 14213 . . . \times 10 \times sin \left(45\right)\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Type into your calculator.*

$\begin{aligned}Area_{A C D} & = & 85 . 35531 . . . cm^{2}\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Find the shaded area by adding the area of the rectangle to the area of the triangle.*

$\begin{aligned}Area & = & 241 . 4213 . . . + 85 . 35531 . . . = 326 . 776 . . . cm^{2}\end{aligned}$

> *Round to 3 significant figures. Remember to include the units for the area.*

$\mathrm{Area}=327\mathrm{cm}^{2}(3\mathrm{sf})$ **[1]**
** Answers from 326 - 327 accepted.**

parts.problemMd:
$A,B$ and $C$ are points on a circle with centre $O$.

![q8-4ma1-2h-qp-jan21-paper2-igcse-maths](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-18-higher/4-geometry-and-trigonometry/area-and-perimeter/assets/036-q8-4ma1-2h-qp-jan21-paper2-igcse-maths.png)

$AOC$ is a diameter of the circle.

$AB=8\mathrm{cm}BC=15\mathrm{cm}$

Angle $ABC=90^{\circ}$

Work out the total area of the regions shown shaded in the diagram. 
Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures.
parts.solutionMd:
> *The area of the shaded region is equal to the area of the circle minus the area of the triangle.*

> *The radius of the circle is equal to half of the hypotenuse of the right-angled triangle. *
*Use Pythagoras to find the hypotenuse of triangle **ABC.*

$AC^{2}=AB^{2}+BC^{2}\,AC^{2}=8^{2}+15^{2}$

**[1]**

> *Rearrange and solve for **AC.*

$AC=\sqrt{8^{2}+15^{2}}=17\mathrm{cm}$

**[1]**

> *Find the radius by dividing **AC **by 2.*

$r=\frac{AC}{2}=\frac{17}{2}=8.5\mathrm{cm}$

> *Calculate the area of the circle, using *$A=πr^{2}$*.*

$\begin{aligned}A_{C i r c l e} & = & \pi \left(8 . 5\right)^{2} \\ & = & \frac{289}{4} \pi \\ & = & 72 . 25 \pi cm^{2}\end{aligned}$

> *Calculate the area of the triangle.*

*Area triangle = *$\begin{aligned} & & \frac{1}{2}\end{aligned} b h = \frac{1}{2} \times 8 \times 15 = 60 cm^{2}$

**Either area found ****[1]**

> *Calculate the area of the shaded area by subtracting the area of the triangle from the area of the circle.*

$\begin{aligned}A & = & 72 . 25 \pi - 60 = 166 . 9800 . . .\end{aligned}$* **cm**<sup>2</sup>*

**[1]**

> *Round to 3 significant figures.*

**Area = 167 cm**<sup>**2**</sup>** [1]**

parts.problemMd:
The diagram shows a shaded shape $ABCD$made from a semicircle $ABC$and a right-angled triangle $ACD$.

![q11-4ma1-2h-qp-jan20-paper2-igcse-maths](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-18-higher/4-geometry-and-trigonometry/area-and-perimeter/assets/010-q11-4ma1-2h-qp-jan20-paper2-igcse-maths.png)

$AC$is the diameter of the semicircle $ABC$.

Work out the perimeter of the shaded shape. 
Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures.

....................$\mathrm{cm}$
parts.solutionMd:
> *Calculate the length **AC** from the right-angled triangle **ACD** using Pythagoras' theorem, *$a^{2}+b^{2}=c^{2}$*.*

$\begin{aligned}17^{2} & = & 15^{2} + A C^{2}\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

$\begin{aligned}289 & = & 225 + A C^{2} \\ 64 & = & A C^{2}\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

$\begin{aligned}A C & = & 8\end{aligned}$

> *The diameter of the semi-circle is therefore 8 cm.*

> *Calculate the arc length of the semi-circle by using the formula for the circumference of a circle, *$C=πd$*, and multiplying it by *$\frac{1}{2}$*.*

> * *$\begin{aligned}A r c l e n g t h & = & \frac{1}{2} \times \pi \times 8\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

$\begin{aligned}A r c l e n g t h & = & 4 \pi\end{aligned}$

> *Work out the perimeter of the shaded shape by adding together the arc length of the semi-circle and the lengths of the sides **AD** and **CD**.*

$\begin{aligned}P e r i m e t e r & = & 4 \pi + 17 + 15\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

$\begin{aligned}P e r i m e t e r & = & 44 . 5663 . . .\end{aligned}$

> *Round to 3 significant figures.*

**44.6 cm**** [1]**

parts.problemMd:
The diagram shows two circles such that the region $R$, shown shaded in the diagram, is the region common to both circles.

![q25-4ma1-1h-qp-june21-paper1-igcse-maths](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-18-higher/4-geometry-and-trigonometry/area-and-perimeter/assets/007-q25-4ma1-1h-qp-june21-paper1-igcse-maths.png)

One of the circles has centre $O$ and radius 5cm. 
The other circle has centre $P$ and radius 4 cm. 
Angle $AOB=50^{\circ}$

Calculate the area of region $R$. 
Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures.

...................................................... cm<sup>2</sup>
parts.solutionMd:
> *The area of the region **R **is the area of the larger segment from circle centre **O** added to the area of the smaller segment from circle centre **P**. *

![ed-igcse-arcs-and-sectors-vh-q4-diagram-1](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-18-higher/4-geometry-and-trigonometry/area-and-perimeter/assets/008-ed-igcse-arcs-and-sectors-vh-q4-diagram-1.png)

> *To find the area of the segment in circle centre **O, **subtract the area of triangle **AOB **from the area of sector **AOB.*

> *Find the area of triangle **AOB** using the area of a triangle formula, *$A=\frac{1}{2}ab\mathrm{sin}C$*, where *$a$* and *$b$* are the two known sides and *$C$* is the included angle. **OA **and **OB **are both radii so are both equal to 5 cm.*

$A r e a_{t r i a n g l e A O B} = \frac{1}{2} \times \left(5\right) \times \left(5\right) \times sin \left(50\right) = \frac{25}{2} sin 50$

> *It is best to leave working as exact values as you work through the problem, but if you choose to round make sure you use at least 4 significant figures throughout. *

> *Find the area of the sector **AOB **using the formula for area of a sector *$=\frac{θ}{360^{\circ}}\timesπr^{2}$*.*

> *Substitute the given values into the formula, letting *$θ=50$* and *$r=5$*.*

$\frac{50}{360}\timesπ\times5^{2}=\frac{125}{36}π$

**[1]**

> *Find the area of the segment by subtracting the area of triangle **AOB **from the area of sector **AOB.*

*Area segment (circle ***O***) =*$\frac{125}{36}π-\frac{25}{2}\mathrm{sin}50$

> *To find the area of the segment in circle centre **P, **we first need to find angle **APB.*

> *Triangles **AOB **and **APB **are both isosceles triangles so the line **OP **is a line of symmetry. The sine rule can be used with triangle **AOP **to find the value of angle **APO **which can then be doubled to find angle **APB.*

![ed-igcse-arcs-and-sectors-vh-q4-diagram-2](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-18-higher/4-geometry-and-trigonometry/area-and-perimeter/assets/009-ed-igcse-arcs-and-sectors-vh-q4-diagram-2.png)

> *Use the sine rule with the angles on the numerators, *$\frac{\mathrm{sin}A}{a}=\frac{\mathrm{sin}B}{b}=\frac{\mathrm{sin}C}{c}$*.*

$\frac{sin \left(A P O\right)}{5} = \frac{sin \left(25\right)}{4}$

**[1]**

> *Multiply both sides by 5 and use the inverse sin to find the angle **APO**.*

$\text{sin} A P O = 5 \times \frac{ \text{sin} 25}{4} = 0.528272...$
$\text{angle} A P O = \text{sin} ^{ - } 1 ( 0.528272... ) = 31.88883...$

**[1]**

> *Angle **APB **= 2 × angle **APO**.*

$A P B = 2 \left(31 . 88883 . . .\right) = 63 . 77766 . . .$

> *Find the area of triangle **APB** using the area of a triangle formula, *$A=\frac{1}{2}ab\mathrm{sin}C$*.*

$A r e a_{t r i a n g l e A P B} = \frac{1}{2} \times \left(4\right) \times \left(4\right) \times sin \left(63 . 77766 . . .\right) = 7 . 176689 . . .$

> *Find the area of the sector **APB **using the formula for area of a sector *$=\frac{θ}{360^{\circ}}\timesπr^{2}$*.*

$\frac{63.77766...}{360}\timesπ\times4^{2}=8.905041...$

**[1]**

> *Find the area of the segment by subtracting the area of triangle **APB **from the area of sector **APB.*

*Area segment (circle ***P***) = *$8.905041...-7.176689...=1.728352...$

> *Find the area of the shaded section by adding the area of the two segments together.*

*Area shaded = *$\left(\frac{125}{36} \pi - \frac{25}{2} sin 50\right) + 1 . 728352 . . . = 3 . 061104 . . .$

**[1]**

> *Round the final answer to 3 significant figures. *

**Area = 3.06 cm**<sup>**2**</sup>** ****[1]**
**Answers in the range 3 to 3.1 accepted**

$\begin{aligned}9 - \left(3 x + 1\right) & = & 9 - 3 x - 1 \\ & = & 8 - 3 x\end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned}Area_{1} & = & x \left(8 - 3 x\right)\end{aligned}$

**either of the two areas above expressed in terms of x ****[1]**

> *The area of the shape is 65 cm*<sup>*2*</sup>* so add theareas of the two rectangles together and equate to 65.*

> $\begin{aligned}x \left(8 - 3 x\right) + 10 \left(3 x + 1\right) & = & 65\end{aligned}$* *

**[1]**

> *Expand the brackets and collect like terms (on the left hand side).*

$\begin{aligned}8 x - 3 x^{2} + 30 x + 10 & = & 65 \\ - 3 x^{2} + 38 x + 10 & = & 65\end{aligned}$

Although you could try to solve by factorising or completing the square, the numbers look quite daunting and it is a calculator question, so it is probably quicker and less risky to use the quadratic formula. (It does actually factorise if you want to try it)*

> *If **x** = 11 was a solution, then the short side on the diagram marked **x** would be longer than the side marked 10- so 11 would be smaller than 10! This is clearly a contradiction so **x** is not a valid answer. *
*You can acknowledge that **x **= 11** **is a solution to the equation by writing it down, but make sure you cross it out to show that you understand that it cannot be an answer to the question!*

parts.problemMd:
The diagram shows a logo.

$ABE$ and $DCE$ are congruent triangles. 
$BCE$ is a sector of a circle, centre $E$.

![q25-paper2h-june2017-aqa-gcse-maths](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-18-higher/4-geometry-and-trigonometry/area-and-perimeter/assets/011-q25-paper2h-june2017-aqa-gcse-maths.png)

Show that the area of the logo is 510 cm<sup>2</sup> to 2 significant figures.
parts.solutionMd:
> *The area of the logo is the area of the two triangles added to the area of the sector.*

> *Find the area of the triangles using the area of a triangle formula, *$A=\frac{1}{2}ab\mathrm{sin}C$*, where *$a$* and *$b$* are the two known sides and *$C$* is the included angle. The triangles are congruent, which means identical, so the calculation is the same for both of them.*

$Area_{triangle} = \frac{1}{2} \times \left(15\right) \times \left(26\right) \times sin \left(38\right) = 195 sin 38$

**[1]**

> *It is best to leave working as exact values where possible as you work through the problem so leaving it in terms of sin here will make it easier to work with later. *

> *To find the area of the sector, you will first need to find its radius. You know the lengths of two sides and the angle between them of the triangle and the radius of the sector is the side opposite the angle, so you can use the cosine rule, *$a^{2}=b^{2}+c^{2}-2bc\mathrm{cos}A$*, where **b** and **c** are the lengths of the two sides that form angle **A** and **a** is the length of the side opposite **A**.*

$r ^{2} = 26 ^{2} + 15 ^{2} - 2 ( 26 ) ( 15 ) cos ( 38 )$
$r = \sqrt{26 ^{2} + 15 ^{2} - 2 ( 26 ) ( 15 ) \text{cos} ( 38 ) }$

**[1]**

..................................cm<sup>2</sup>
parts.solutionMd:
> *Split 56 cm in the ratio 5 : 12 : 6 : 5 to find the length of each side of the trapezium.*

> *Add the parts of the ratio together.*

$5+12+6+5=28$

> *Divide 56 by the total number of ratio parts.*

$56\div28=2$

**[1]**

> *Multiply each part of the ratio by 2 to find the lengths of each side.*

$\mathrm{AD}=5\times2=10\mathrm{cm}\,\mathrm{AB}=12\times2=24\mathrm{cm}\,\mathrm{DC}=6\times2=12\mathrm{cm}\,\mathrm{BC}=5\times2=10\mathrm{cm}$

**[1]**

> *The area of a trapezium can be found using the formula *$A = \frac{1}{2} \left(a + b\right) h$*, where *$a$* and *$b$* are the parallel sides and *$h$* is the **perpendicular **height.  *
*The perpendicular height is not known, but can be found using Pythagoras' theorem. The trapezium is an isosceles trapezium so the property that there is a line of symmetry down the middle can be used.*

![_Fylc3vx_ocr-gcse-tq-ma-are-and-perimeter-vh-q4-diagram-1](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-18-higher/4-geometry-and-trigonometry/area-and-perimeter/assets/025-fylc3vx-ocr-gcse-tq-ma-are-and-perimeter-vh-q4-d.png)

> *Find the distance from the point **X **(the base of the perpendicular height) to the point B.*

$XB=\frac{24-12}{2}=6\mathrm{cm}$

**[1]**

> *Use Pythagoras' theorem *$a^{2}+b^{2}=c^{2}$* with the sides XB, CX and BC to find the perpendicular height of the trapezium.*

$\begin{aligned}h^{2 } + X B^{2} & = & BC^{2} \\ h^{2 } + 6^{2} & = & 10^{2}\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Rearrange and solve to find **h.*

$\begin{aligned}h^{2 } & = & 10^{2} - 6^{2} \\ & = & 100 - 36 \\ & = & 64 \\ h & = & \sqrt{64} \\ & = & 8 cm\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Substitute into the formula for the area of a trapezium,  *$A = \frac{1}{2} \left(a + b\right) h$*, where *$a=\mathrm{AB}=24\mathrm{cm}$*, *$b=\mathrm{CD}=12\mathrm{cm}$*and *$h=8\mathrm{cm}$*.*

$A = \frac{1}{2} \left(24 + 12\right) \times 8$

**[1]**

**Area = 144 cm**<sup>**2**</sup>** ****[1] **

The diagram shows two similar bottles, $A$ and $B$.

![q21-paper2hr-june2019-edexcel-igcse-maths](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-18-higher/4-geometry-and-trigonometry/area-and-volume-of-similar-shapes/assets/020-q21-paper2hr-june2019-edexcel-igcse-maths.png)

Bottle $A$  has surface area $240\mathrm{cm}^{2}$ 
Bottle $B$ has surface area 540 $\mathrm{cm}^{2}$and volume $2025\mathrm{cm}^{3}$

Work out the volume of bottle $A$.

.......................$\mathrm{cm}^{3}$
parts.solutionMd:
> *Work out the area scale factor by dividing the surface area of **B** by the surface area of **A**.*

$\mathrm{area} \mathrm{scale} \mathrm{factor}=\frac{540}{240}=\frac{9}{4}$

> *Find the length scale factor by taking the square root of the area scale factor.*

$\mathrm{length} \mathrm{scale} \mathrm{factor}=\frac{\sqrt{9}}{\sqrt{4}}=\frac{3}{2}$

**[1]**

> *Find the volume scale factor by cubing the length scale factor.*

$\mathrm{volume} \mathrm{scale} \mathrm{factor}=\frac{3^{3}}{2^{3}}=\frac{27}{8}$

> *Calculate the volume of **A** by dividing the volume of **B** by the volume scale factor.*

$2025\div\frac{27}{8}$

**[1]**

**600 cm**<sup>**3**</sup>** ****[1]**

parts.problemMd:
A and B are similar solid cylinders.

| base area of A : base area of B = 9 : 25 |
|---|

Complete these ratios.

curved surface area of A : curved surface area of B =................... : ................

height of A : height of B =.................... : ................
parts.solutionMd:
> *The ratio for the surface areas of similar shapes, whether they are curved or not, is the same as the ratio for the areas*

**curved surface area of A : curved surface area of B = 9 : 25*** ***[1]**

> *If the ratio for the areas of similar shapes is *$m^{2}:n^{2}$*, then the ratio for corresponding lengths on those shapes is *$m:n$*. The height of A and height of B are corresponding lengths so we can square root the area ratio.*

> * *$\sqrt{9}:\sqrt{25}\,=3:5$

**height of A : height of B = 3 :**** ****5**** ****[1]**

parts.problemMd:
A and B are similar cuboids.

surface area of A : surface area of B = 16 : 25

Work out volume of A : volume of B

Circle your answer.

| 4 : 5 | 16 : 25 | 64 : 125 | 256 : 625 |
|---|---|---|---|
parts.solutionMd:
> *If the ratio for the areas of similar shapes is *$m^{2}:n^{2}$*, then the linear ratio (ratio for corresponding lengths) for those shapes is *$m:n$* and the ratio for the volumes of the similar shapes is *$m^{3}:n^{3}$*.*

> *First find the linear ratio by square rooting the area ratio.*

> * *$\begin{aligned}linear scale factor & = & \sqrt{16} : \sqrt{25} \\ & = & 4 : 5\end{aligned}$

> *Next find the volume ratio by cubing the linear ratio.*

$\begin{aligned}volume scale factor & = & 4^{3} : 5^{3} \\ & = & 64 : 125\end{aligned}$

**The third option is correct, 64 : 125*** ***[1]**

> *The first option, "4 : 5", is the length ratio.*

> *The second option, "16 : 25", is the area (or surface area) ratio.*

> *The fourth option, "256 : 625", is the linear ratio to the power of 4; "4*<sup>*4*</sup>* : 5*<sup>*4*</sup>*". This is not useful for Area & Volume of Similar Shapes questions.*

parts.problemMd:
Solids $X$ and $Y$ are similar.

$X$ has volume 64 cm<sup>3</sup> 
$Y$ has volume 343 cm<sup>3</sup>

The surface area of $X$ is 176 cm<sup>2</sup> 
Work out the surface area of $Y$.

..........................cm<sup>2</sup>
parts.solutionMd:
> *The volume of Solid X and Solid Y are in the ratio 64 : 343. And if the volumes of two solids are in the ratio *$m^{3}:n^{3}$*, then the corresponding lengths are in the ratio *$m:n$* and corresponding areas are in the ratio *$m^{2}:n^{2}$*.*

> *First find the linear ratio (ratio of corresponding lengths) in X and Y by cube rooting the volume ratio.*

$\sqrt[3]{64} : \sqrt[3]{343} = 4 : 7$

**[1]**

> *Now find the area (or surface area) ratio by squaring the linear ratio.*

$4^{2}:7^{2}=16:49$

**[1]**

> *Now use the area ratio with the surface area of X to find the surface area of Y, which we will call *$y$*.*

$16:49=176:y$

> *We can find **y** by scaling up the ratio. 176 ÷ 16 = 11 so both sides of the ratio need to be multiplied by 11.*

$16:49\,\times11\times11\,=176:49\times11\,=176:539$

**The surface area of Y = 539 cm**<sup>**2**</sup>** ****[1]**

> *Alternatively, from *$16:49=176:y$*, we could convert to a fraction and solve:*

$\begin{aligned}\frac{176}{16} & = & \frac{y}{49} \\ y & = & 49 \times \frac{176}{16} \\ & = & 539\end{aligned}$

parts.problemMd:
In the diagram, AED and ABC are straight lines and BE is parallel to CD.

![q13-paper6-nov2020-ocr-gcse-maths](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-18-higher/4-geometry-and-trigonometry/area-and-volume-of-similar-shapes/assets/019-q13-paper6-nov2020-ocr-gcse-maths.png)

The ratio of length AB to length BC is 2 : 3. 
Triangle ABE has an area of 8cm<sup>2</sup> .

Work out the area of triangle ACD.

................................................... cm<sup>2</sup>
parts.solutionMd:
> *Use the given ratio to calculate *$k$*, the scale factor of enlargement for the lengths. *
*If the ratio is 2 : 3 then length AB can be said to be 2**x **cm, BC will be 3**x **cm, and the length AC = 5**x** cm. *

$k=\frac{\mathrm{AC}}{\mathrm{AB}}=\frac{5x}{2x}=\frac{5}{2}=2.5$

**[1]**

> *For similar shapes, if the length scale factor is *$k$*, then the area scale factor is *$k^{2}$* *
$k>1$*and we want to find the **larger** area, so we can **multiply** the smaller area by *$k^{2}$

$8\times2.5^{2}$

**Squaring scale factor ****[1] **
**Multiplying by 8 ****[1]**

$=8\times6.25$

**Area ACD = 50*** ***cm**<sup>**2**</sup>** [1]**

**Always check whether you should be making the shape larger or smaller, and whether your answer matches this**

parts.problemMd:
A transport lorry consists of a cab and a trailer. 
The trailer has a volume of 90m<sup>3</sup>. 
Alfie makes a model of this lorry using a scale of 1 : 72.

Work out the volume of the trailer in Alfie’s model, giving your answer in cm<sup>3</sup>.

................................................... cm<sup>3</sup>
parts.solutionMd:
> *For similar shapes, if the length scale factor is *$k$*, then the volume scale factor is *$k^{3}$*. *
$k>1$*and we want to find the **smaller **volume, so we can **divide **the larger volume by *$k^{3}$

$90\div72^{3}$

**Squaring scale factor ****[1] **
**Dividing ****[1]**

> *The volume of the lorry is given in m*<sup>*3*</sup>* but the answer needs to be in cm*<sup>*3*</sup>*. It is easiest to convert the units first.*

$90m^{3}=90\times100^{3}\mathrm{cm}^{3}=90000000\mathrm{cm}^{3}$

> *Calculate the answer and round to 3 significant figures.*

$90000000\div72^{3}=241.12654...$

**Volume model = 241*** ***cm**<sup>**3**</sup>** [1]**

**Always check whether you should be making the shape larger or smaller, and whether your answer matches this**

parts.problemMd:
Toy building bricks are available in two sizes, small and large.

The small and large bricks are mathematically similar.

A small brick has volume 8cm<sup>3</sup> and width 2.1cm.

A large brick has volume 15.625 cm<sup>3</sup>.

Calculate the width of a large brick.

..................................................... cm
parts.solutionMd:
> *Use the given volumes to calculate *$k$*, the scale factor of enlargement for the volumes. For similar shapes, if the length scale factor is *$k$*, then the volume scale factor is *$k^{3}$*.*

$V_{1}=k^{3}V_{2}\,15.625=k^{3}\times8$

**[1]**

> *Rearrange and solve to find the value of *$k$*.*

$k ^{3} = \frac{15.625}{8} = \frac{125}{64}$
$k = \sqrt[3]{\frac{125}{64}} = \frac{5}{4}$

**[1]**

> *The length scale factor is *$k=\frac{5}{4}$*, multiply this by the smaller width to find the width of the large brick.*

$w=\frac{5}{4}\times2.1$

**[1]**

**Width = 2.625 cm ****[1]**

**Always check whether you should be making the shape larger or smaller, and whether your answer matches this**

parts.problemMd:
Fred is making two rectangular flower beds.

The dimensions of the larger rectangle will be three times the dimensions of the smaller rectangle.

There is going to be the same depth of soil in each flower bed. Fred needs 180 kg of soil for the smaller flower bed.

Work out how much soil Fred needs for the larger flower bed.
parts.solutionMd:
> $k$*, the scale factor of enlargement for the lengths, is 3 (as "the dimensions of the larger rectangle will be three times the dimensions of the smaller rectangle")*

> *The depth of the soil will be the same in both flower beds, so the change in mass of the soil in kg is dependent only on the area. For similar shapes, if the length scale factor is *$k$*, then the area scale factor is *$k^{2}$* *
*To find the larger** **mass, multiply the smaller mass by *$k^{2}$

$180\times3^{2}$

**[1]**

$=180\times9$

**1620 kg**** [1]**

**Always check whether you should be making the shape larger or smaller, and whether your answer matches this**

parts.problemMd:
Mark has made a clay model. 
He will now make a clay statue that is mathematically similar to the clay model.

The model has a base area of 6cm<sup>2</sup> 
The statue will have a base area of 253.5 cm<sup>2</sup>

Clay is sold in 10kg bags. 
Mark has to buy all the clay he needs to make the statue.

$k^{2}=\frac{253.5}{6}$

> *Therefore *$k$*, the scale factor for lengths, is*

$k = \sqrt{\frac{253 . 5}{6}} = \frac{13}{2} \left(or 6 . 5\right)$

**[1]**

> *The mass of the clay is dependent on the volume. For similar shapes, if the length scale factor is *$k$*, then the volume scale factor is *$k^{3}$
* *$k>1$*and we want to find the **larger** mass, so we can **multiply** the larger mass by *$k^{3}$

$\begin{aligned}Volume of statue & = & 2 \times \left(\frac{13}{2}\right)^{3} \\ & = & 549 . 25 kg\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Clay is sold in 10 kg bags so divide this mass by 10*

$549.25\div10=54.925$

> *Round up to the nearest whole number of bags*

**55 bags ****[1]**

parts.problemMd:
The total surface area of a solid hemisphere is equal to the curved surface area of a cylinder.

The radius of the hemisphere is $r$ cm. 
The radius of the cylinder is twice the radius of the hemisphere.

Given that

$\mathrm{volume} \mathrm{of} \mathrm{hemisphere}:\mathrm{volume} \mathrm{of} \mathrm{cylinder}=1:m$

find the value of $m$.
parts.solutionMd:
> *The total surface area of a hemisphere is*

$\begin{aligned}S A_{h e m i s p h e r e} & = & \frac{1}{2} \times 4 \pi r^{2} + \pi r^{2} \\ & = & 3 \pi r^{2}\end{aligned}$

> *Now that we have used *$r$* as the radius of the hemisphere, let *$R$* be the radius of the cylinder (and let its height be *$h$*). The curved surface area of the cylinder is therefore*

$SA_{cylinder}=2πRh$

> *"The radius of the cylinder is twice the radius of the hemisphere" therefore*

$R=2r$

> *Substitute this into the formula for the curved surface area of the cylinder*

$\begin{aligned}S A_{c y l i n d e r} & = & 2 \pi \left(2 r\right) h \\ & = & 4 \pi r h\end{aligned}$

> *Equate the formulae for the surface areas of the hemisphere and the cylinder*

$3πr^{2}=4πrh$

**[1]**

> *Rearrange to get *$h$* in terms of *$r$

$\begin{aligned}3 \cancel{\pi} r^{2} & = & 4 \cancel{\pi} r h \\ 3 r^{\cancel{2}} & = & 4 \cancel{r} h \\ 3 r & = & 4 h \\ h & = & \frac{3}{4} r\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Now find the volume of the hemisphere in terms of *$r$

$\begin{aligned}v o l u m e_{h e m i s p h e r e} & = & \frac{1}{2} \times \frac{4}{3} \pi r^{3} \\ & = & \frac{2}{3} \pi r^{3}\end{aligned}$

> *And find the volume of the cylinder in terms of *$r$

$\begin{aligned}v o l u m e_{c y l i n d e r} & = & \pi R^{2} h \\ & = & \pi \left(2 r\right)^{2} \times \frac{3}{4} r \\ & = & \pi \cancel{4} r^{2} \times \frac{3}{\cancel{4}} r \\ & = & 3 \pi r^{3}\end{aligned}$

** correct expressions for volume of hemisphere and volume of cylinder ****[1]**

> $m$*, the scale factor for the volumes, is the volume of the cylinder divided by the volume of the hemisphere*

$\begin{aligned}m & = & \frac{3 \pi r^{3}}{\frac{2}{3} \pi r^{3}} = \frac{3 \cancel{\pi r^{3}}}{\frac{2}{3} \cancel{\pi r^{3}}} \\ & = & 3 \times \frac{3}{2} \\ & = & \frac{9}{2}\end{aligned}$

$m=\frac{9}{2}\mathrm{or}4.5$ **[1]**

The circle has centre *O* and radius *OA*. *OA* = *OD* = 0.5 cm and *AB* = 1.5 cm. 
*E* is a point on *OC* such that *OE* = 0.25 cm and angle *OED* = 90°.

Calculate the perimeter of the logo.

............................................. cm
parts.solutionMd:
> *The perimeter is the total length around the outside of the shape.*

> *You'll need the length of the arc **AB**. *

> *To help find the angle of the sector, first find the acute angle **DOE**. *

> *Triangle **ODE** is right-angled and we have the hypotenuse (**DO** = 0.5) and the adjacent side (**OE** = 0.25). So we can use *$cos \left(D O E\right) = \frac{Adjacent}{Hypotenuse} .$

$cos \left(D O E\right) = \frac{0 . 25}{0 . 5} = \frac{1}{2}$

**[1]**

> *Use inverse cos on your calculator to find the size of the angle.*

$D O E = cos^{- 1} \left(\frac{1}{2}\right) = 60$

> *Subtract angle **DOE** from 270° to get the size of the angle of the sector.*

$θ=270-60=210$

**[1]**

> *Find the arc length using the formula *$l=\frac{θ}{360}\times2πr$*. Leave your answer in terms of π.*

$l=\frac{210}{360}\times2π\times0.5\,l=\frac{7}{12}π$

**[1]**

*The perimeter is formed by 5 sides: **OC**, **CB**, **BA**, **AD**, **DO**.* 
*OC** = **BA** = 1.5 cm.* 
*CB** = **OA** = 0.5 cm.* 
*DO** is the radius so is also 0.5 cm.*

![cie-igcse-2019-march-p4-q6a](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-18-higher/4-geometry-and-trigonometry/area-and-volume-of-similar-shapes/assets/009-cie-igcse-2019-march-p4-q6a.png)

> *Add together the lengths.*

$\begin{aligned} & & 1 . 5 + 0 . 5 + 1 . 5 + \frac{7}{12} \pi + 0 . 5 \\ & = & 4 + \frac{7}{12} \pi \\ & = & 5 . 8325 . . .\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Round to 3 significant figures.*

**5.83 cm**** ****[1]**

> *The area is made up two shapes: a rectangle and a sector.*

> *Find the area of the rectangular using the formula *$A=bh.$

$0.5\times1.5=0.75$

> *Find the area of the sector using the formula *$A=\frac{θ}{360}\timesπr^{2}.$* Leave your answer in terms of π.*

$\frac{210}{360}\timesπ\times0.5^{2}=\frac{7}{48}π$

**[1]**

> *Add the two areas together.*

$0.75+\frac{7}{48}π=1.2081...$

**[1]**

> *Round to 3 significant figures.*

**1.21 cm**<sup>**2**</sup> **[1]**

parts.problemMd:
Solid **A** is similar to solid **B**

Here is some information about solid **A **and solid **B**

|   | solid A | solid B |
|---|---|---|
| Height (cm) | $3^{x}$ |   |
| Area (cm<sup>2</sup> ) | 7776 | 486 |
| Volume (cm<sup>3</sup> ) | $8^{x}$ | $2^{x+4}$ |

Work out the height of solid **B **
Give your answer as a decimal
parts.solutionMd:
> *Work out the linear scale factor using the area scale factors*

$\sqrt{\frac{7776}{486}}=\sqrt{16}=4$

**[M1]**

> *The volume scale factor is the cube of the linear scale factor*

$4^{3}=64$

> *Form an equation using the information about the volumes*

$8^{x}=2^{x+4}\times64$

**[M1]**

> *Rewrite using powers of 2*

$\left(2^{3}\right)^{x} = 2^{x + 4} \times 2^{6}$

> *Using laws of indices*

- *mutliply the powers on the left-hand side*
- *add the powers on the right-hand side*

$2^{3x}=2^{x+10}$

> *The bases are the same so the powers must be equal*

$3x=x+10$

> *Solve the equation*

$2x=10$

$x=5$

**[M1]**

> *Work out the height of solid B*

$3^{5}\div4=60.75$

**[M1]**

$60.75$

**[A1]**

parts.problemMd:
The diagram shows the positions of three ships, $A,B$ and $C$.

![q16-4ma1-1h-qp-jan21-paper1-igcse-maths](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-18-higher/4-geometry-and-trigonometry/bearings-scale-drawing-and-constructions/assets/012-q16-4ma1-1h-qp-jan21-paper1-igcse-maths.png)

Ship $B$ is due north of ship $A$. 
The bearing of ship $C$from ship $A$ is 120°

Calculate the bearing of ship $C$ from ship $B$. 
Give your answer correct to the nearest degree.
parts.solutionMd:
> *To find the bearing of **C** from **B**, you first need to work out the angle **ABC**. *
*However you currently do not have enough information to work that out.*

![bearings-hq2](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-18-higher/4-geometry-and-trigonometry/bearings-scale-drawing-and-constructions/assets/013-bearings-hq2.png)

> *You know the lengths of two sides and the angle between them. Therefore you can use the cosine rule to find the length of the third side.*

> *The formula for the cosine rule is *$a^{2}=b^{2}+c^{2}-2bc\mathrm{cos}A$*, where **b** and **c** are the lengths of the two sides that form angle **A** and **a** is the length of the side opposite **A**. *
*Substitute **a** = **z**, **b** = 275, **c** = 150 and **A** = 120 into the formula.*

$z^{2} = 275^{2} + 150^{2} - 2 \left(275\right) \left(150\right) cos \left(120\right)$

**[1]**

> *Type the expression into your calculator altogether as one line. If you do it separately you need to remember the order of operations (multiplication before addition). Take the positive square root and leave as an exact answer or store in your calculator.*

$\begin{aligned}z^{2} & = & 139375 \\ z & = & \sqrt{139375} \\ & = & 373 . 329613 . . .\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *You can now find the angle at **B** by using either the sine rule or the cosine rule.*

> *Method 1 - Using the sine rule*

> *The formula for the sine rule is *$\frac{\mathrm{sin}A}{a}=\frac{\mathrm{sin}B}{b}$*, where **a** and **b** are the lengths of the two sides that are opposite the angles **A **and **B **respectively. Substitute **A** = **y**, **B** = 120, **a** = 275 and **b** = √139375 into the formula.*

$\frac{sin y}{275} = \frac{sin \left(120\right)}{\sqrt{139375}}$

**[1]**

> *Multiply both sides by 275 and then use the inverse sin function on your calculator.*

$\begin{aligned}y & = & sin^{- 1} \left(\frac{sin \left(120\right)}{\sqrt{139375}} \times 275\right) \\ & = & 39 . 637403 . . .\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Find the bearing by subtracting from 180.*

$\begin{aligned}x & = & 180 - 39 . 637403 . . . \\ & = & 140 . 362596 . . .\end{aligned}$

> *Round to the nearest degree.140*

$140^{\circ}(\mathrm{nearest} \mathrm{degree})$** [1]**

> *Method 2 - Using the cosine rule*

> *The formula for the cosine rule is *$\mathrm{cos}A=\frac{b^{2}+c^{2}-a^{2}}{2bc}$*, where **a** and **b** are the lengths of the two sides that form the angle **A **and **a** is the length of the side opposite **A**. Substitute **A** = **y**, **a** = 275, **b** = 150 and **c** = √139375 into the formula.*

$cos y = \frac{150^{2} + \left(\sqrt{139375}\right)^{2} - 275^{2}}{2 \times 150 \times \sqrt{139375}}$

**[1]**

> *Use the inverse cos function on your calculator.*

$\begin{aligned}y & = & cos^{- 1} \left(\frac{150^{2} + \left(\sqrt{139375}\right)^{2} - 275^{2}}{2 \times 150 \times \sqrt{139375}}\right) \\ & = & 39 . 637403 . . .\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Find the bearing by subtracting from 180.*

$\begin{aligned}x & = & 180 - 39 . 637403 . . . \\ & = & 140 . 362596 . . .\end{aligned}$

> *Round to the nearest degree.140*

$140^{\circ}(\mathrm{nearest} \mathrm{degree})$** [1]**

> *To find the distance between **A **and **C **you need to know the angle opposite it in the triangle. You know an angle and the length of the side opposite to it, you also know another length so you can therefore find the angle opposite it by using the sine rule.*

> *The formula for the sine rule is *$\frac{\mathrm{sin}A}{a}=\frac{\mathrm{sin}B}{b}$*, where **a** and **b** are the lengths of the two sides that are opposite the angles **A **and **B **respectively. Substitute **a** = 95, **b** = 180, **A** = **y** and **B** = 55 into the formula.*

$\frac{sin \left(y\right)}{95} = \frac{sin \left(55\right)}{180}$

**[1]**

> *Multiply both sides by 95 and then find the angle by using the inverse sin function.*

$\begin{aligned}sin \left(y\right) & = & \frac{sin \left(55\right)}{180} \times 95 \\ y & = & sin^{- 1} \left(\frac{sin \left(55\right)}{180} \times 95\right) \\ y & = & 25 . 615534 . . .\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *The interior angles of the triangle should add up to 180°. Use the answer button on your calculator to find the third angle.*

$\begin{aligned}Angle A C B & = & 180 - 55 - 25 . 615534 . . . \\ & = & 99 . 384465 . . .\end{aligned}$

> *You now have enough information to find the side **LN** using either the sine rule or the cosine rule.*

> *Method 1 - Using the sine rule*

> *The formula for the sine rule is *$\frac{a}{\mathrm{sin}A}=\frac{b}{\mathrm{sin}B}$*, where **a** and **b** are the lengths of the two sides that are opposite the angles **A **and **B **respectively. Substitute **a** = **x**, **b** = 180, **A** = 99.384465... (using the answer button) and **B** = 55 into the formula.*

$\begin{aligned}\frac{x}{sin \left(99 . 384465 . . .\right)} & = & \frac{180}{sin \left(55\right)} \\ x & = & \frac{180}{sin \left(55\right)} \times sin \left(99 . 384465 . . .\right) \\ x & = & 216 . 798523 . . .\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Round to 3 significant figures.*

$217\mathrm{km}(3\mathrm{sf})$** [1]**

> *Method 2 - Using the cosine rule*

> *The formula for the cosine rule is *$a^{2}=b^{2}+c^{2}-2bc\mathrm{cos}A$*, where **b** and **c** are the lengths of the two sides that form angle **A** and **a** is the length of the side opposite **A**. Substitute **a** = **x**, **b** = 95, **c** = 180 and **A** = 99.384465... (using the answer button) into the formula.*

$x ^{2} = 95 ^{2} + 180 ^{2} - 2 ( 95 ) ( 180 ) cos ( 99.384465... )$
$x = \sqrt{95 ^{2} + 180 ^{2} - 2 ( 95 ) ( 180 ) \text{cos} ( 99.384465... ) }$
x equals 216.798523...

**[1]**

> *Round to 3 significant figures. *

$217\mathrm{km}(3\mathrm{sf})$** [1]**

parts.solutionMd:
> *To prove that **ST  **is equal to** UT ** you will need to **prove **that the triangle **STU **is **isosceles**. This can be done by finding the angles. *

> *PQRST **is a regular pentagon, so the angle **TSU** is the exterior angle of a regular pentagon. *
*Exterior angles in any polygon add up to 360°. *
*A regular pentagon has 5 equal exterior angles.*

> * *`T S with hat on top U space equals 360 over 5 equals space 72 degree`

**[1]**

> *To find the size of angle **SUT**, you will need to consider circle theorems.*

> *Begin by joining the point **O** to the points **T** and **R,** marking all the radiuses of the circle as equal lengths on the diagram.*

> *TP** and **TR **are also tangents to the circle, so by the circle theorem 'A tangent always meets a radius at 90°', angles **ORQ **and **OTP **are both 90°. *

`O R with hat on top Q space equals space O T with hat on top P space equals 90 degree`* **(angle between tangent and radius)*

**[1]**

> *Mark these onto the diagram.*

![QLY1pOQ2_4-8-edexcel-gcse-vh-q3-diagram-2](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-18-higher/4-geometry-and-trigonometry/circle-theorems/assets/025-qly1poq2-4-8-edexcel-gcse-vh-q3-diagram-2.png)

> *The sum of the interior angles in any polygon can be found using the formula 180°(n - 2). A regular pentagon has 5 equal interior angles, therefore these can be found using the formula *$\frac{180 \left(5 - 2\right)}{5}$*.*

> * *$T \hat{P} Q = P \hat{Q} R = \frac{3 \left(180\right)}{5} = 108 \circ$

> *Add these angles to the diagram.*

![4-8-edexcel-gcse-vh-q3-diagram-3](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-18-higher/4-geometry-and-trigonometry/circle-theorems/assets/026-4-8-edexcel-gcse-vh-q3-diagram-3.png)

> *PQROT  **is a pentagon, so the angle **ROT**  can be found by subtracting the other four angles from the sun of the angles in a pentagon.*

> *The sum of the interior angles in any polygon can be found using the formula 180°(n - 2).*

$R \hat{O} T + O \hat{T} P + T \hat{P} Q + P \hat{Q} R + Q \hat{R} O = 180 \left(5 - 2\right) \circ = 540 \circ$

> *Substitute in the angles you know to find angle **ROT**.*

$\begin{aligned}R \hat{O} T + 90 \circ + 90 \circ + 108 \circ + 108 \circ & = & 540 \circ \\ R \hat{O} T + 396 \circ & = & 540 \circ \\ R \hat{O} T & = & 144 \circ\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *By the circle theorem, the angle at the centre is twice the angle at the circumference, angle **ROT **is twice angle **RUT.*

$R \hat{O} T = 2 \left(R \hat{U} T\right) = 2 \left(S \hat{U} T\right)$

$S \hat{U} T = \frac{R \hat{O} T}{2} = \frac{144}{2} = 72 \circ$

**[1]**

> *This proves that angle **TSU **is equal to angle **SUT **and so triangle **STU **is isosceles.*

**Therefore ****ST ****= ****UT **
**All reasons given clearly [1]**

parts.solutionMd:
> *Angle **AOC **is made by drawing lines from the points **A** and **C **on the circle which meet at the centre (**O**).*

*The circle theorem states that the angle at the centre is double the angle at the circumference.* 
*Therefore angle **AOC **is double angle **ABC**.*

![ed-igcse-arcs-and-sectors-vh-q5-diagram-1](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-18-higher/4-geometry-and-trigonometry/circle-theorems/assets/021-ed-igcse-arcs-and-sectors-vh-q5-diagram-1.png)

$\mathrm{Angle}AOC=2\times75^{\circ}=150^{\circ}$

**[1]**

> *Form an expression for the area of the sector **AOC **using the formula for area of a sector *$=\frac{θ}{360^{\circ}}\timesπr^{2}$* and substituting the values into the formula, letting *$θ=150$* and *$r=r$*.*

$\mathrm{Area}_{\mathrm{sector}}=\frac{150}{360}\timesπ\timesr^{2}=\frac{5}{12}πr^{2}$

**[1]**

> *Form an expression for the area of the triangle **AOC **using the formula for area of a triangle *$=\frac{1}{2}ab\mathrm{sin}θ$* and substituting the values into the formula, letting *$θ=150$* and *$r=r$*.*

$\mathrm{Area}_{\mathrm{triangle}}=\frac{1}{2}\timesr\timesr\times\mathrm{sin}150=\frac{1}{4}r^{2}$

**[1]**

> *Form an expression for the area of the shaded region by subtracting the area of the triangle from the area of sector **AOC.*

$\mathrm{Area}_{\mathrm{shaded}}=\frac{5}{12}πr^{2}-\frac{1}{4}r^{2}$

> *Form an equation by setting the expression for the area of the shaded region equal to 200 cm*<sup>*2*</sup>*.*

$\frac{5}{12}πr^{2}-\frac{1}{4}r^{2}=200$

**[1]**

> *Factorise out **r*<sup>*2*</sup>*.*

$r^{2} \left(\frac{5}{12} \pi - \frac{1}{4}\right) = 200$

> *Isolate **r*<sup>*2*</sup>*.*

$r^{2} = \frac{200}{\left(\frac{5}{12} \pi - \frac{1}{4}\right) }$

> *Solve to find **r **by taking the square root of both sides.*

$r = \sqrt{\frac{200}{\left(\frac{5}{12} \pi - \frac{1}{4}\right) }} = 13 . 74256 . . .$

> *Round to 3 significant figures.*

**radius = 13.7 cm**<sup>** **</sup>**(3 s.f.)**** [1] **
**Answers in the range 13.7 to 13.8 accepted**

**[1]**

> *Angles in a triangle sum to 180° and triangle **CED  **is isosceles, so angle **ECD  **= angle **EDC.*

*Angle ***DCE  ***=** *$\frac{180-4x}{2}$* *
*(Base angles in an isosceles triangle are equal and angles in a triangle = 180°)*

**[1]**

> *Vertically opposite angles are equal, so angle **ACB  **= angle **DCE.*

*Angle ***ACB*** = angle ***DCE  ***=** *$\frac{180-4x}{2}$* *

> *Angles in a triangle sum to 180°, so angle **ACB  **+ angle **ABC **+ angle** BAC **= 180°.*

* *$\frac{180-4x}{2}+90-x+y=180$* *
*(Angles in a triangle = 180°)*

**[1]**

> *Simplify.*

> *Cancel 180 from both sides and rearrange to make **y **the subject.*

> * *$\begin{aligned}\cancel{180} - 3 x + y & = & \cancel{180} \\ - 3 x + y & = & 0 \\ y & = & 3 x\end{aligned}$

parts.problemMd:
The diagram shows a circle with centre $O$

![q16-january-2022-1h-edexcel-igcse-maths](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-18-higher/4-geometry-and-trigonometry/circles-arcs-and-sectors/assets/046-q16-january-2022-1h-edexcel-igcse-maths.png)

$A,B$ and $C$are points on the circle so that the length of the arc $ABC$ is 5 cm.

Given that angle $AOC$ = 55°

work out the area of the circle. 
Give your answer correct to one decimal place.
parts.solutionMd:
> *Form an equation to find the radius of the circle using the formula for length of an arc *$=\frac{θ^{\circ}}{360^{\circ}}\times2πr$*. *
*Find an expression for the length of the arc in terms of *$r$*, **by substituting *$θ=55$*.*

$\frac{55}{360}\times2\timesπ\timesr$

> *Form an equation by setting it equal to 5 cm.*

$\frac{11}{36}πr=5$

**[1]**

> *Solve the equation to find the radius of the circle.*

$\begin{aligned}\frac{11}{36} \pi r & = & 5 \\ \pi r & = & \frac{5 \times 36}{11} \\ r & = & \frac{180}{11 \pi} \\ r & = & 5 . 208707 . . . .\end{aligned}$

> *Find the area of the circle using the formula for the area of a circle, *$A=πr^{2}$*.*

$\mathrm{Area}=π\times5.208707...^{2}$

**[1]**

> *Use your calculator to find the answer, using the answer button to keep accuracy. *

$\begin{aligned}Area & = & 85 . 233391 . . . cm^{2}\end{aligned}$

> *Round the answer to one decimal place.*

> *The first digit after the decimal point is 2 and the digit following it is 3, which is less than 5 you do not need to round the 2 up. *

$85. \dot{2}\dot{3} 3391... = 85.2 ( 1 \text{ d.p.} )$

**Area = 85.2 cm**<sup>**2 **</sup>**(1 d.p.)**** [1] **
**Answers in the range 84.9 to 85.4 accepted**

parts.problemMd:
The region, shown shaded in the diagram, is a path.

![q8-4ma1-1h-qp-jan21-paper1-igcse-maths](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-18-higher/4-geometry-and-trigonometry/circles-arcs-and-sectors/assets/059-q8-4ma1-1h-qp-jan21-paper1-igcse-maths.png)

The boundary of the path is formed by two semicircles, with the same centre $O$, and two straight lines.

The inner semicircle has a radius of 7 metres. 
The path has a width of 2 metres.

Work out the perimeter of the path. 
Give your answer correct to one decimal place.

...................................................... m
parts.solutionMd:
> *Calculate the arc length of the smaller (inner) semi-circle by using the formula for the perimeter of a semi-circle: *$P = \frac{1}{2} \left(2 \pi r\right)$*where *$r$* is the radius of the circle.*

$\begin{aligned}L e ngth_{s m a l l a r c} & = & \frac{1}{2} \times 2 \times \pi \times 7\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

$\begin{aligned}Length_{s m a l l a r c} & = & 7 \pi cm\end{aligned}$

> *The radius of the larger semi-circle is 2 cm more than the radius of the smaller semi-circle.*

> *Calculate the radius of the larger semi-circle.*

$7+2=9\mathrm{cm}$

> *Calculate the arc length of the larger (outer) semi-circle by using the formula for the perimeter of a semi-circle: *$P = \frac{1}{2} \left(2 \pi r\right)$*where *$r$* is the radius of the circle.*

$\begin{aligned}L e ngth_{l a r g e a r c} & = & \frac{1}{2} \times 2 \times \pi \times 9\end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned}Length_{l a r g e a r c} & = & 9 \pi cm\end{aligned}$

> *Calculate the perimeter of the shaded segment by adding the arc lengths together along with the lengths of the straight edges joining them (2 cm each). *

$\begin{aligned}P & = & 7 \pi + 9 \pi + 2 + 2\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

$\begin{aligned}P & = & 54 . 26548 . . . cm\end{aligned}$

> *Round to one decimal place.*

> *The first digit after the decimal point is 2 and the digit following it is 6, which is 5 or more you will need to round the 2 up. *

$54. \dot{2}\dot{6} 548... = 54.3 ( 1 \text{ d.p.} )$

**54.3 cm ****[1] **
**Answers in the range 54.2 - 54.3 accepted**
