parts.problemMd:
The diagram shows a metal bar in the shape of a prism.

![q5-1-medium-3-4-standard-and-compound-units-edexcel-gcse-maths](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-18-higher/4-geometry-and-trigonometry/standard-and-compound-units/assets/003-q5-1-medium-3-4-standard-and-compound-units-edex.png)

The length of the metal bar is 120 cm. The cross section of the metal bar is shown below.

![q5-2-medium-3-4-standard-and-compound-units-edexcel-gcse-maths](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-18-higher/4-geometry-and-trigonometry/standard-and-compound-units/assets/004-q5-2-medium-3-4-standard-and-compound-units-edex.png)

All corners are right angles. The metal bar is made from steel with density 8 g/cm<sup>3</sup>.

Sean has a trolley. The trolley can carry a maximum mass of 250 kg.

How many metal bars can the trolley carry at the same time? You must show your working.
parts.solutionMd:
> *First we need to find the area of the cross-section. *
*Divide the cross-section into rectangles. *
*Then use the Area = Length × Width formula and add the rectangle areas together.*

$\begin{aligned}12 - 2 - 2 & = & 8 15 - 13 = 2\end{aligned}$

![DHT3VpHv_question](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-18-higher/4-geometry-and-trigonometry/standard-and-compound-units/assets/005-dht3vphv-question.png)

$\begin{aligned}Area & = & \left(15 \times 2\right) + \left(8 \times 2\right) + \left(15 \times 2\right) = 76 cm^{2}\end{aligned}$

**[1] **
**Other ways of dividing the shape into rectangles will also get the mark if done correctly.**

> *Now find the volume of the bar. *
*Use the formula  Volume of Prism = Area of Cross-section × Length.*

$\mathrm{Volume}=76\times120=9120\mathrm{cm}^{3}$

**[1]**

> *Now find the mass of the bar. *
*Use the formula  Mass = Density × Volume.*

$\mathrm{Mass}=9120\times8=72960g$

**[1]**

> *Convert the mass to kg  (1 kg = 1000 g). *
*Then divide 250 by the mass in kilograms to find how many bars the trolley can carry.*

$72960\div1000=72.96\mathrm{kg}\,\,250\div72.96=3.426535...$

**[1]**

> *But we are only dealing with whole numbers of bars. *
*And four bars would go beyond the maximum mass, so be sure to round **down**.*

**3 bars****  [1]**

parts.problemMd:
A gold bar has a mass of 12.5 kg. 
The density of gold is 19.3 g/cm<sup>3</sup>.

Work out the volume of the gold bar. 
Give your answer correct to 3 significant figures.
parts.solutionMd:
> *Density = Mass ÷ Volume  can be rearranged to give  *
*Volume = Mass ÷ Density. *
*But be careful here!  The density is given in g/cm*<sup>*3*</sup>*, so 12.5 kg must first be converted to grams. *
*(Remember there are 1000 g in a kg.)*

$\begin{aligned}12 . 5 \times 1000 & = & 12500 g \\ & & \\ 12500 \div 19 . 3 & = & 647 . 668393 . . .\end{aligned}$

**[2] **
**1 mark for using Volume = Mass ÷ Density.  1 mark for converting kg to g.**

> *Round to 3 s.f. (and remember your units!).*

**648 cm**<sup>**3**</sup>**  [1]**
** ****Answers in range 647 to 648 will get the mark here.**

parts.problemMd:
A force of 70 newtons acts on an area of 20 cm<sup>2</sup>.

| $\mathrm{pressure}=\frac{\mathrm{force}}{\mathrm{area}}$ |
|---|

The force is increased by 10 newtons. 
The area is increased by 10 cm<sup>2</sup>.

Helen says,
       "The pressure decreases by less than 20%"

Is Helen correct? 
You must show how you get your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
> *Use the given formula to find the pressure of 70 newtons on an area of 20 cm*<sup>*2*</sup>*.*

$P_{1}=\frac{70}{20}=3.5$

*The force increases by 10, and the area increases by 10.* *Find the new pressure using the given formula.*

$P_{2}=\frac{70+10}{20+10}=\frac{8}{3}=2.666666...$

** [1] **
**Mark is for finding ****both**** values for pressure**

> *Find the percentage decrease using *$\frac{\mathrm{Difference}}{\mathrm{Original}}\times100$*.*

$\frac{3 . 5 - 2 . 666 . . .}{3 . 5} \times 100 = 23 . 8 \%$

**[1]**

**It decreases by 23.8%, and as 23.8% > 20%, Helen is incorrect **** ****[1]**

parts.problemMd:
$\mathrm{Pressure}=\frac{\mathrm{force}}{\mathrm{area}}$

Find the pressure extered by a force of 900 newtons on an area of 60cm<sup>2</sup>. 
Give your answer in newtons/m<sup>2</sup>.
parts.solutionMd:
> *First convert the area to m*<sup>*2*</sup>*, to match the units asked for in the answer. *
*Remember that 1 m*<sup>*2*</sup>* = (100 cm) × (100 cm) = (100 × 100) cm*<sup>*2*</sup>*.*

$\frac{60}{100\times100}=\frac{60}{10000}=0.006m^{2}$

**[1]**

> *Now put the force and the converted area into the formula given.*

$\mathrm{Pressure}=\frac{900}{0.006}=150000$

**150000 newtons/m**<sup>**2**</sup>**  [1]**

parts.problemMd:
Tame Valley is a company that makes yoghurt.

A machine fills trays of 20 pots with yoghurt. In one hour, the machine fills a total of 15 000 pots.

Work out how many seconds the machine takes to fill each tray of 20 pots.
parts.solutionMd:
> *We want the answer to be in seconds per tray. Start by converting 1 hour into seconds. Remember that there are 60 minutes in an hour, and 60 seconds in a minute.*

$1\mathrm{hour}=60\mathrm{minutes}=60\times60=3600\mathrm{seconds}$

**[1]**

> *Now divide 15000 by 20 to find how many trays are filled in an hour.*

$15000\div20=750\mathrm{trays} \mathrm{per} \mathrm{hour}$

**[1]**

> *Finally divide 3600 by 750 to find the number of seconds per tray.*

$3600\div750=4.8$

**[1]**

**4.8 seconds****  [1]**

parts.problemMd:
There are 18500 gallons of fuel in a fuel tank.

The fuel is pumped from the fuel tank into a plane at a rate of 1700 litres per minute.

1 gallon = 4.5 litres.

How many minutes will it take to empty the fuel tank completely? Give your answer to the nearest minute.
parts.solutionMd:
> *The fuel pumping rate is given in litres per minute. Start by converting 18500 gallons into litres. Each gallon has 4.5 litres, so **multiply** 18500 by 4.5.*

$18500\times4.5=83250\mathrm{litres}$

**[1]**

> *And each minute, 1700 litres of fuel are pumped. So **divide** 83250 by 1700 to find the number of minutes.*

$83250\div1700=48.970588...\mathrm{minutes}$

**[1]**

> *Finally round to the nearest minute as asked for in the question.*

**49 minutes****  [1]**

**Answers in the range 48.9 - 49.1 will get the mark here.**

parts.problemMd:
Axel and Lethna are driving along a motorway.

They see a road sign. The road sign shows the distance to Junction 8 It also shows the average time drivers take to get to Junction 8

| To Junction 8 30 miles 26 minutes |
|---|

The speed limit on the motorway is 70 mph.

Lethna says      
 "We will have to drive faster than the speed limit to drive 30 miles in 26 minutes."

Is Lethna right? 
You must show how you get your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
> *Start by converting '30 miles in 26 minutes' into miles per minute.*

$30\div26=\frac{15}{13}\mathrm{miles} \mathrm{per} \mathrm{minute}$

**[1]**

> *So they would need to travel 15/13 miles every minute. And there are 60 minutes in an hour. So **multiply** that speed by 60 to convert to miles per hour.*

$\frac{15}{13} \times 60 = 69 . 230769 . . . = 69 . 2 mph \left(3 s . f .\right)$

**[1]**

> *Express your results in the context of the question.*

**30 miles in 26 minutes corresponds to an average speed of 69.2 mph.  So Lethna is not correct.****  [1]**

**You can also earn full marks by showing that going 70 mph for 26 minutes means you will go 30.333... miles. Or by showing that at 70 mph, it will only take 25.714... minutes to travel 30 miles.**

parts.problemMd:
Change a speed of 50 metres per second to a speed in kilometres per hour.

.......................... kilometres per hour
parts.solutionMd:
*Convert each unit separately.* 
*There are 60 seconds in a minute. Multiply by 60 to find how many metres are travelled in a minute.*

$\begin{aligned}50 metres per second & = & 50 \times 60 metres per minute \\ & = & 3000 metres per minute\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *There are 60 minutes in an hour. Multiply by 60 to find how many metres are travelled in an hour.*

$\begin{aligned}3000 metres per minute & = & 3000 \times 60 metres per hour \\ & = & 180000 metres per hour\end{aligned}$

> *There are 1000 metres in a kilometre. Divide by 1000 to find how many kilometres are travelled in an hour.*

$\begin{aligned}18000 metres per hour & = & \frac{180000}{1000} kilometres per hour\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

$180\mathrm{kilometres} \mathrm{per} \mathrm{hour}$ **[1]**

parts.problemMd:
A block of wood has a mass of $3.5\mathrm{kg}$. 
The wood has density $0.65\mathrm{kg}/m^{3}$

Work out the volume of the block of wood. 
Give your answer correct to $3$ significant figures.
parts.solutionMd:
$\mathrm{Density}=\frac{\mathrm{Mass}}{\mathrm{Volume}}.$* If you forget this formula then you can derive it using the units for density, kg/m*<sup>*3*</sup>*. Kilograms measure a mass and cubic metres measure a volume.* 
*Substitute 0.65 for the density and 3.5 for the mass.*

$0.65=\frac{3.5}{\mathrm{Volume}}$

**[1]**

> *Multiply both sides by the volume and divide both sides by 0.65.*

$\begin{aligned}Volume & = & \frac{3 . 5}{0 . 65} \\ & = & \frac{70}{13} \\ & = & 5 . 384615 . . .\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Round to 3 significant figures. Your answer will be in cubic metres.*

**Volume is 5.38 m**<sup>**3**</sup>** (3sf)** **[1]**

parts.problemMd: Change a speed of $630$ kilometres per hour to a speed in metres per second.
parts.solutionMd:
*Convert each unit separately.* 
*There are 60 seconds in a minute. Divide by 60 to find how many kilometres are travelled in a minute.*

$\begin{aligned}630 kilometres per hour & = & \frac{ 630 }{60} kilometres per minute \\ & = & 10 . 5 kilometres per minute\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *There are 60 minutes in an hour. Divide by 60 to find how many kilometres are travelled in a second.*

$\begin{aligned}10 . 5 kilometres per minute & = & \frac{ 10 . 5 }{60} kilometres per second \\ & = & 0 . 175 kilometres per second\end{aligned}$

> *There are 1000 metres in a kilometre. Multiply by 1000 to find how many metres are travelled in a second.*

$\begin{aligned}0 . 175 kilometres per second & = & 1000 \times 0 . 175 metres per second\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

$175\mathrm{metres} \mathrm{per} \mathrm{second}$ **[1]**

parts.problemMd:
$\mathrm{Density}=\frac{\mathrm{mass}}{\mathrm{volume}}$

The mass is divided by 2 and the volume is multiplied by 4 What happens to the density? Circle your answer.

| $\times2$ | $\div2$ | $\times8$ | $\div8$ |
|---|---|---|---|
parts.solutionMd:
> *Method 1*

*If the top of a fraction gets smaller then the overall value of the fraction also gets smaller. Therefore dividing the mass by 2 causes the density to be divided by 2.* 
*If the bottom of a fraction gets bigger then the overall value of the fraction gets smaller. Therefore multiplying the volume by 4 causes the density to be divided by 4.* 
*Combine both effects, dividing by 2 then dividing by 4 is equivalent to dividing by 8.*

**÷ 8** **[1]**

> *Method 2*

> *Use actual numbers. Say the mass is 100 and the volume is 1.*

$\mathrm{Density}=\frac{100}{1}=100$

> *Divide the mass by 2 and multiply the volume by 4 and calculate the new density.*

$\mathrm{Density}=\frac{100\div2}{1\times4}=\frac{50}{4}=12.5$

> *Choose the option takes you from 100 to 12.5.*

**÷ 8** **[1]**

parts.problemMd:
Which **one** of these is a unit of density? Circle your answer.

| $\mathrm{kg}/m^{2}$ | $m^{2}/\mathrm{kg}$ | $\mathrm{kg}/m^{3}$ | $m^{3}/\mathrm{kg}$ |
|---|---|---|---|
parts.solutionMd:
> *Density measures how heavy something is per a unit of volume. The formula is *$\mathrm{Desnity}=\frac{\mathrm{Mass}}{\mathrm{Volume}}.$* Kilograms (kg) is a measure of mass and cubic metres (m*<sup>*3*</sup>*) is a measure of volume, therefore kg/m*<sup>*3*</sup>* is a measure of density.*

**kg/m**<sup>**3**</sup>** [1]**

parts.problemMd:
Arron ran a distance of 5 km at an average speed of 2.2 m/s.

How long did Arron run for? 
                   Give your answer in minutes and seconds, to the nearest second.

.............. minutes ................ seconds
parts.solutionMd:
> *The measurements need to use consistent units. 1 km = 1000 m so convert 5 km to m.*

$5\mathrm{km}=5000m$

* ***[1]**

> $\mathrm{Average} \mathrm{Speed}=\frac{\mathrm{Distance}}{\mathrm{Time}}.$* Substitute 5000 for the distance and 2.2 for the speed.*

$2.2=\frac{5000}{\mathrm{Time}}$

> *Rearrange by multiplying both sides by the time and dividing both sides by 2.2. The units for the time will be seconds.*

$\begin{aligned}Time & = & \frac{5000}{2 . 2} \\ & = & 2272 . 727 . . . s\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Round to the nearest second.*

$2273s$

> *1 minute = 60 seconds. Divide by 60 to convert to minutes.*

$\frac{2273}{60}=37.83333...$

* ***[1]**

> *This 37 minutes. Convert the decimal part to seconds by subtracting the integer part and multiplying by 60.*

$0.83333...\times60=53$

**37 minutes 53 seconds**** (nearest second)** **[1]**

parts.problemMd:
$\mathrm{pressure}=\frac{\mathrm{force}}{\mathrm{area}}$

Find the pressure exerted by a force of 810 newtons on an area of 120 cm<sup>2</sup> .
Give your answer in newtons/m<sup>2</sup>.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[exam-tip]**
> Always check the units given in a question against the units required for the answer.
> 
> Here the given area units (cm<sup>2</sup>) do not match the area units needed for the pressure in the answer (m<sup>2</sup>), so those will have to be converted.

> *Convert the area units*

> *There are 100 cm in 1 m, which means 100*<sup>*2*</sup>* cm*<sup>*2*</sup>* in 1 m*<sup>*2*</sup>*; therefore*

$120\div100^{2}=0.012m^{2}$

**[M1]**

> *Substitute into the formula*

$\frac{810}{0.012}=67500$

**Final answer:** **67500 newtons/m**<sup>**2 **</sup>

**[A1]**

parts.problemMd: Change a speed of 27 kilometres per hour to a speed in metres per second.
parts.solutionMd:
> *Change the kilometres to metres; there are 1000 m in 1 km, so*

*27×1000 = 27000*

> *That gives the speed in metres per hour, so you need to change the time to seconds*

> *There are 60 minutes in an hour and 60 seconds in a minute, so divide by 60 twice*

$\frac{27000}{60\times60}$

**[M1]**

**Final answer:** **7.5**

**[A1]**

$\mathrm{pressure}=\frac{\mathrm{force}}{\mathrm{area}}$

Find the pressure exerted by a force of 980 newtons on an area of $400\mathrm{cm}^{2}$.

Give your answer in  $\mathrm{newtons}/m^{2}$

parts.problemMd:
Henry is thinking of having a water meter. These are the two ways he can pay for the water he uses. | **Water Meter** A charge of £28.20 per year

**plus** 91.22p for every cubic metre of water used

1 cubic metre = 1000 litres | |---| | **No Water Meter** A charge of £107 per year | |---| Henry uses an average of 180 litres of water each day. Use this information to determine whether or not Henry should have a water meter.
parts.solutionMd:
> *First divide 180 by 1000 to find out how many cubic metres Henry uses each day.*

$180\div1000=0.18\mathrm{cubic} \mathrm{metres}$

**[1]**

> *Now multiply by 91.22p to find the cost per day with the water meter.*

$0 . 18 \times 91 . 22 = 16 . 4196 p = \pounds 0 . 164196$

**[1]**

> *Then multiply by 365 (the number of days in a normal year) to find the price for water used per year. (You don't need to worry about leap years here!)*

$0 . 164196 \times 365 = \pounds 59 . 93154$

**[1]**

> *Add £28.20 to find the total cost with a water meter per year.*

$59 . 93154 + 28 . 20 = 88 . 13154 = \pounds 88 . 13 \left(nearest penny\right)$

**[1]**

> *And finally interpret your results in the context of the question.*

**It will cost Henry £88.13 per year with the water meter, which is cheaper than the £107 without the meter.  Therefore he should have a water meter.****  [1]**

parts.problemMd:
Sumeet has a pond in the shape of a prism.

![q2-hard-3-4-standard-and-compound-units-edexcel-gcse-maths](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-18-higher/4-geometry-and-trigonometry/standard-and-compound-units/assets/001-q2-hard-3-4-standard-and-compound-units-edexcel-.png)

The pond is completely full of water. 
Sumeet wants to empty the pond so he can clean it. 
Sumeet uses a pump to empty the pond.

The volume of water in the pond decreases at a constant rate. The level of the water in the pond goes down by 20 cm in the first 30 minutes.

Work out how much more time Sumeet has to wait for the pump to empty the pond completely.
parts.solutionMd:
> *Start by finding the volume of the pond.*
* It is in the form of a prism with its cross-section being a trapezium (the front face in the diagram). *
*Use the  Area = *$\frac{1}{2}$*(**a** + **b**)**h  **formula to find the area of the trapezium. *
*Then use the  Volume = Area of Cross-section × Length  formula to find the volume of the prism.*

$\frac{1}{2} \times ( 1.3 + 0.5 ) \times 2 = 1.8 \mathrm{m} ^{2}$

$1.8 \times 1 = 1.8 \mathrm{m} ^{3}$

**[1]**

> *Now find the volume of water that goes out in the first 30 minutes. *
*The volume of the water lost is in the form of a 2 m by 1 m by 20 cm cuboid. *
*Use the formula  Volume of Cuboid = Length × Width × Height. Don't forget to turn 20 cm into metres first, so the units all match!*

$20\div100=0.2m\,\,2\times1\times0.2=0.4m^{3}$

**[1]**

> *Now turn that into a rate of water lost per hour.*

$0.4m^{3}\mathrm{in}30\mathrm{minutes}=0.8m^{3}/\mathrm{hour}$

**[1]**

> *Be careful now. *
*The question asks for how much **more **time it will take to empty the pond.*
*So subtract 0.4 from 1.8 to find the volume of water left in the pond after 30 minutes.*

$1.8-0.4=1.4m^{3}\mathrm{remaining}$

**[1]**

> *Every hour 0.8 m*<sup>*3*</sup>* are removed from the pond. *
*So divide 1.4 by 0.8 to find out how many hours are left until the pond is emptied completely.*

$1.4\div0.8=\frac{7}{4}=1\frac{3}{4}$

**[1]**

$1\frac{3}{4}$** hours****  [1]**

**1.75 hours or 1 hour 45 minutes will also get the mark here.**

parts.problemMd:
The distance from Fulbeck to Ganby is 10 miles. The distance from Ganby to Horton is 18 miles.

![q3-hard-3-4-standard-and-compound-units-edexcel-gcse-maths](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-18-higher/4-geometry-and-trigonometry/standard-and-compound-units/assets/002-q3-hard-3-4-standard-and-compound-units-edexcel-.png)

Raksha is going to drive from Fulbeck to Ganby. 
Then she will drive from Ganby to Horton.

Raksha leaves Fulbeck at 10 00 
She drives from Fulbeck to Ganby at an average speed of 40 mph.

Raksha wants to get to Horton at 10 35 
Work out the average speed Raksha must drive at from Ganby to Horton.
parts.solutionMd:
> *First find out how long it takes her to go from Fulbeck to Ganby. Use the formula  Time = Distance ÷ Speed. *
*It's easiest to convert to minutes at this point.  (Remember there are 60 minutes in an hour!)*

$\frac{10}{40}=\frac{1}{4}\mathrm{hour}=15\mathrm{minutes}$

**[1]**

> *10.00 to 10.35 is 35 minutes, so subtract 15 from 35 to find how many minutes she has to get from Ganby to Horton. *
*Then divide 18 by that to see how many miles per minute she needs to go. *
*And multiply that by 60 to convert miles per minute to miles per hour.*

$35-15=20\mathrm{minutes}\,\,\frac{18}{20}=0.9\mathrm{miles} \mathrm{per} \mathrm{minute}\,\,0.9\times60=54$

**[1]**

**54 mph****  [1]**

parts.problemMd:
Liquid A has a density of 0.7 g/cm<sup>3</sup>. 
Liquid B has a density of 1.6 g/cm<sup>3</sup>.

140 g of liquid A and 128 g of liquid B are mixed to make liquid C.

Work out the density of liquid C.
parts.solutionMd:
> *First find the mass of liquid C.*

$140+128=268g$

**[1]**

> *Now use  Volume = Mass ÷ Density  to find the volumes of Liquids A and B. *
*Then add those together to find the volume of Liquid C.*

$\mathrm{Liquid}A:\frac{140}{0.7}=200\mathrm{cm}^{3}\,\,\mathrm{Liquid}B:\frac{128}{1.6}=80\mathrm{cm}^{3}\,\,200+80=280\mathrm{cm}^{3}$

**[1]**

> *Use  Density = Mass ÷ Volume  to find the density of Liquid C.*

$\frac{268}{280}=0.957142...$

**[1]**

** **

**0.957 g/cm**<sup>**3**</sup>** (3 s.f.)****  [1]**

**Answers between 0.957 and 0.96 will get the mark here**

parts.problemMd:
Ibrar mixes 74 g of lead and 126 g of tin to make 200 g of an alloy.

Lead has a density of 11.34 g/cm<sup>3</sup>.
 Tin has a density of 7.31 g/cm<sup>3</sup>.

Work out the density of the alloy. 
Give your answer correct to 1 decimal place.
parts.solutionMd:
> *Use  Volume = Mass ÷ Density  to find the volumes of lead and tin.*

$\mathrm{lead}:\frac{74}{11.34}=6.5255...\mathrm{cm}^{3}\,\,\mathrm{tin}:\frac{126}{7.31}=17.2366...\mathrm{cm}$

**[1] **
**Mark is for using Volume = Mass ÷ Density to try to find either volume**

> *Now add the volumes together to find the total volume of the alloy. *
*Then use  Density = Mass ÷ Volume  to find the density of the alloy.*

$6.5255...+17.2366...=23.7622...\mathrm{cm}^{3}\,\,\frac{200}{23.7622...}=8.4167...$

**[1]**

*Round to 1 d.p., as asked for in the question.*** **

**8.4 g/cm**<sup>**3**</sup>** (1 d.p.)****  [1]**

**Answers between 8.4 and 8.44 will get the mark here**

parts.problemMd:
Olly drove 56 km from Liverpool to Manchester. 
He then drove 61 km from Manchester to Sheffield.

Olly's average speed from Liverpool to Manchester was 70 km/h. 
Olly took 75 minutes to drive from Manchester to Sheffield.

Work out Olly's average speed for his total drive from Liverpool to Sheffield.
parts.solutionMd:
> *We need to find the total distance travelled, and the total time it took. *
*Start by finding the time from Liverpool to Manchester. *
*Use the formula  Time = Distance ÷ Speed.*

$56\div70=0.8\mathrm{hours}$

**[1]**

> *Now find the total distance and the total time. *
*For time, first convert 75 minutes into decimal hours. (Remember there are 60 minutes in an hour!)*

$\mathrm{total} \mathrm{distance}=56+61=117\mathrm{km}\,\,75\mathrm{minutes}=\frac{75}{60}=1.25\mathrm{hours}\,\,\mathrm{total} \mathrm{time}=0.8+1.25=2.05\mathrm{hours}$

**[1] **
**This mark is for a correct process to find total distance ****or**** total time.**

> *Use  Speed = Distance ÷ Time to find the average speed.*

$117\div2.05=57.07317...$

**[1]**

**57.1 mph (3 s.f.)****  [1]**

**Answers between 57 and 57.1 will get the mark here.**

parts.problemMd:
Janie drove from Barnsley to York.

Janie's average speed from Barnsley to Leeds was 80 km/h. 
Her average speed from Leeds to York was 60 km/h.

Janie says that the average speed from Barnsley to York can be found by working out the mean of 80 km/h and 60 km/h.

If Janie is correct, what does this tell you about the two parts of Janie's journey?
parts.solutionMd:
> *In general, the total average speed can only be equal to the mean of the speeds of the two parts of the journey if the times were the same for each part.*

**The times from Barnsley to Leeds and from Leeds to York must have been the same.****  [1]**

**You can also get the mark here for saying that the distance from Leeds to York must be 3/4 of the distance from Barnsley to Leeds.  (With the given speeds, that relation of distances would mean that the two times were the same.)**

parts.problemMd:
The density of apple juice is 1.05 grams per cm<sup>3</sup>.

The density of fruit syrup is 1.4 grams per cm<sup>3</sup>.

The density of carbonated water is 0.99 grams per cm<sup>3</sup>.

25 cm<sup>3 </sup>of apple juice are mixed with 15 cm<sup>3 </sup>of fruit syrup and

parts.problemMd:
James and Peter cycled along the same $50$km route.

James took  $2\frac{1}{2}$ hours to cycle the $50$km.

Peter started to cycle $5$ minutes after James started to cycle. Peter caught up with James when they had both cycled $15$ km.

James and Peter both cycled at constant speeds. 
Work out Peter's speed.
parts.solutionMd:
> *Start by finding James' speed. *
*Use the formula  Speed = Distance ÷ Time.*

$\mathrm{James}:50\div2.5=20\mathrm{km}/\mathrm{hour}$

**[1]**

> *Now use the formula  Time = Distance ÷ Speed  to find how long it took James to cycle 15 km. *
*It's easiest also to convert to minutes at this point.  *
*(Remember 1 hour = 60 minutes, so 1/4 hour = 15 minutes!)*

$15\div20=\frac{15}{20}=\frac{3}{4}\mathrm{hours}=45\mathrm{minutes}$

**[1]**

> *Peter started 5 minutes after James. *
*So subtract 5 from 45 to find how many minutes it took Peter to cycle the same distance.*

$45-5=40\mathrm{minutes}$

**[1]**

> *Divide 15 by 40 to find Peter's speed in km/minute. *
*Then multiply that by 60 to find his speed in km/hour.*

$15\div40=\frac{15}{40}=\frac{3}{8}\mathrm{km}/\mathrm{minute}\,\,\frac{3}{8}\times60=\frac{45}{2}$

**[1]**

** **

$\frac{45}{2}$** km/h****  [1]**

**22.5 km/h (decimal form) will also get the mark here**

$\mathrm{total} \mathrm{distance}=150+150=300\mathrm{miles}\,\,\mathrm{total} \mathrm{time}=3+5=8\mathrm{hours}\,\,300\div8=37.5$

**[1]**

> *Interpret your result in the context of the question.*

**Final answer:** **Sean is not right, because his average speed was actually 37.5 mph.****  [1]**

> *If the cylinder is melted down and reformed into a sphere, then the cylinder and sphere will have the same volume.*

> *Calculate the volume of the cylinder, using the formula: *$V=πr^{2}h$*, where *$r$* is the radius of the cylinder and *$h$*is its height.  *

> *Leave your answer in terms of *$π$*.*

$V = \pi \times \left(2 x\right)^{2} \times 9 x$

**[1]**

$\begin{aligned}V & = & \pi \times 4 x^{2} \times 9 x \\ & = & 36 \pi x^{3} cm^{3}\end{aligned}$

> *Using the formula for the volume of a sphere: *$V=\frac{4}{3}πr^{3}$*, where *$r$* is the radius of the sphere, substitute the calculated value for the volume and rearrange to find an expression for the radius of the sphere.*

$36πx^{3}=\frac{4}{3}π\timesr^{3}\,$

**[1]**

> *Divide both sides by *$π$*.*

$36x^{3}=\frac{4}{3}r^{3}$

> *Divide both sides by 4.*

$9x^{3}=\frac{1}{3}r^{3}$

> *Multiply both sides by 3.*

$27x^{3}=r^{3}$

> *Take the cube root of both sides.*

$3x=r$

$3x$* ***[1]**

**Final answer:** **Any algebraic expression equivalent to **$3x$** will be accepted**

$\begin{aligned}V_{L} & = & \frac{1}{3} \times \pi \times 15^{2} \times 40\end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned}V_{L} & = & 3000 \pi cm^{3}\end{aligned}$

> *The large and small cones are similar objects.*

$\mathrm{LSF}=\frac{40}{20}=2$

> *Divide the radius of the large cone by the LSF to work out the radius of the small cone.*

$\begin{aligned}r & = & \frac{15}{2} \\ & = & 7 . 5 cm\end{aligned}$

$V_{S}=375π\mathrm{cm}^{3}$

$\begin{aligned}V & = & 3000 \pi - 375 \pi\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

$\begin{aligned}V & = & 2625 \pi \\ & = & 8246 . 68071 . . . cm^{3}\end{aligned}$

$8250\mathrm{cm}^{3}$* ***[1]**

![screenshot-2023-05-26-at-2-22-08-pm](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-18-higher/4-geometry-and-trigonometry/volume-and-surface-area/assets/041-screenshot-2023-05-26-at-2-22-08-pm.png)

The tank is empty.

Oil flows into the tank.

Assume that oil continues to flow into the tank at this rate.

Work out how many **more** minutes it takes for the tank to be 85% full of oil. (1m<sup>3 </sup>= 1000 litres)
parts.solutionMd:
> *Calculate the area of the cross-section of the tank, using the formula for the area of a trapezium: *$A = \frac{1}{2} \left(a + b\right) h$*, where *$a$* and *$b$* are the lengths of the parallel sides and *$h$* is the perpendicular height.*

$\begin{aligned}A & = & \frac{1}{2} \times \left(3 + 1 . 4\right) \times 2 . 4\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

$\begin{aligned}A & = & 5 . 28 m^{2}\end{aligned}$

> *Calculate the volume of the tank by multiplying the cross-sectional area by the length of the tank.*

$\begin{aligned}V & = & 5 . 28 \times 2 . 5 \\ & = & 13 . 2 m^{3}\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Divide the given percentage by 100 and multiply it by the volume to calculate the volume of oil required to fill the tank up to 85% capacity.*

$\begin{aligned}V_{85 \%} & = & \frac{85}{100} \times 13 . 2 \\ & = & 11 . 22 m^{3}\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Convert the volume of oil required in m*<sup>*3*</sup>* to litres by multiplying the volume in m*<sup>*3*</sup>* by 1000.*

*1000 litres = 1 m**<sup>3</sup>*

$\begin{aligned}V_{85 \%} & = & 11 . 22 \times 1000 \\ & = & 11220 litres\end{aligned}$

> *Work out the volume of oil required to fill the tank up to 85% after the initial 300 litres by subtracting 300 from the 85% volume.*

$\begin{aligned}V_{r e m a i n i n g} & = & 11220 - 300 \\ & = & 10920\end{aligned}$

> *Calculate the time taken, in minutes, for the remaining oil to flow into the tank by dividing the volume by 300.*

$\frac{10920}{300}$

**[1]**

$36.4\mathrm{minutes}$ **[1]**

parts.problemMd:
The length of the longest diagonal of a cube is 25cm.

parts.solutionMd:
> *Method 1*

> *Draw a diagram showing a cube with dimensions of *$x$* **cm. Add the longest diagonal to the diagram and give this a length of 25 cm. *

> *It also may help to add the right-angled triangles that the diagonal makes with the edges onto the diagram.*

![ocr-gcse-tq-ma-3dpythagtrig-h-q4-diagram-1](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-18-higher/4-geometry-and-trigonometry/volume-and-surface-area/assets/052-ocr-gcse-tq-ma-3dpythagtrig-h-q4-diagram-1.png)

> *Use Pythagoras' theorem for 3D shapes, *$x^{2}+y^{2}+z^{2}=d^{2}$*, to find an expression for the square of the length of the longest diagonal in terms of *$x.$

$\begin{aligned}x^{2} + x^{2} + x^{2} & = & 3 x^{2}\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Form an equation by setting *$3x^{2}$* equal to the square of the longest diagonal, 25 cm.*

$\begin{aligned}3 x^{2} & = & 25^{2} \\ 3 x^{2} & = & 625\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *At this point you can solve the equation to find *$\begin{aligned} & & x\end{aligned}$*, however it is not necessary as the surface area of a cube is 6 multiplied by the area of one of the squares, so the surface area of the cube = *$\begin{aligned} & & 6 x^{2}\end{aligned}$*.*

$\begin{aligned}SA & = & 6 x^{2} = 2 \left(3 x^{2}\right) = 2 \left(625\right) \end{aligned}$

**Correct formula for surface area**** [1] **

**equating to 2 × 25**<sup>**2**</sup>** ****[1]**

**Surface Area =**$1250\mathrm{cm}^{2}$* ***[1]**

> *Method 2*

> *Draw a diagram showing a cube with dimensions of *$x$* **cm.  Add the longest diagonal to the diagram and give this a length of 25 cm. *

> *It also may help to add the right-angled triangles that the diagonal makes with the edges onto the diagram.*

![ocr-gcse-tq-ma-3dpythagtrig-h-q4-diagram-1](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-18-higher/4-geometry-and-trigonometry/volume-and-surface-area/assets/052-ocr-gcse-tq-ma-3dpythagtrig-h-q4-diagram-1.png)

> *Use Pythagoras' theorem, *$a^{2}+b^{2}=c^{2}$*, on the right-angled triangle on the base of the crate to find length of the diagonal on the base in terms of *$x.$

$\begin{aligned}x^{2} + x^{2} & = & 2 x^{2}\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

$\begin{aligned}c^{2} & = & 2 x^{2} \\ c & = & \sqrt{2 x^{2}} \\ & = & x \sqrt{2} cm\end{aligned}$

> *Add this to the diagram.*

![ocr-gcse-tq-ma-3dpythagtrig-h-q4-diagram-2](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-18-higher/4-geometry-and-trigonometry/volume-and-surface-area/assets/053-ocr-gcse-tq-ma-3dpythagtrig-h-q4-diagram-2.png)

> *Use Pythagoras' theorem on the right-angled triangle made up of the diagonal at the base, the side with length *$x$* cm and the longest diagonal, 25 cm.*

$\begin{aligned}\left(x \sqrt{2}\right)^{2} + x^{2} & = & 25^{2} \\ 2 x^{2} + x^{2} & = & 25^{2} \\ 3 x^{2} & = & 625\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Solve the equation to find *$\begin{aligned} & & x\end{aligned}$*.*

$\begin{aligned}x^{2} & = & \frac{625}{3} \\ x & = & \sqrt{\frac{625}{3}} = \frac{25}{\sqrt{3}}\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Find the area of one face of the cube.*

$\begin{aligned}Area & = & x^{2} = \left(\frac{25}{\sqrt{3}}\right)^{2} = \frac{625}{3}\end{aligned}$

> *The surface area of a cube is 6 multiplied by the area of one of the squares, so the surface area of the cube = *$\begin{aligned} & & 6 x^{2}\end{aligned}$*.*

$\begin{aligned}SA & = & 6 x^{2} = 6 \left(\frac{625}{3}\right)\end{aligned}$

** [1]**

**Surface Area =**$1250\mathrm{cm}^{2}$* ***[1]**

parts.solutionMd:
> *Using the variable, **h**, for height allows the radius to be expressed as 2**h** as shown below:*

![Illustration of a right circular cone with height labelled "h," diameter "2h," and a right angle at the base centre.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-18-higher/4-geometry-and-trigonometry/volume-and-surface-area/assets/002-illustration-of-a-right-circular-cone-with-heigh.png)

$\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3} \times \pi \times 4 h^{2} \times h & = & 562 . 5 \pi \\ \frac{1}{3} \times \pi \times 4 h^{3} & = & 562 . 5 \pi \\ \frac{4}{3} \pi h^{3} & = & 562 . 5 \pi\end{aligned}$

**[M1]**

> *Divide through by *$π$

$\begin{aligned}\frac{4}{3} h^{3} & = & 562 . 5\end{aligned}$

> *Continue to solve the equation for *$h$

$\begin{aligned}4 h^{3} & = & 3 \times 562 . 5 \\ h^{3} & = & \frac{1687 . 5}{4} \\ h & = & \sqrt[3]{421 . 875} \\ h & = & 7 . 5\end{aligned}$

**[M1]**

> *Since *$h=7.5$* then *$2h=15$* which is the length of the radius of the cone*

> *Substitute these values into Pythagoras' theorem (*$a^{2}+b^{2}=c^{2}$*) to calculate the length of the sloping edge of the cone, *$l$

![Diagram of a right circular cone with a height of 7.5 units and a base radius of 15 units, showing a perpendicular from the vertex to the base.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-18-higher/4-geometry-and-trigonometry/volume-and-surface-area/assets/003-diagram-of-a-right-circular-cone-with-a-height-o.png)

**[M1]**

> *Substitute values into the formula for the curved surface area of a cone, *$πrl$

$π\times15\times\sqrt{281.25}=790.291...$

parts.problemMd:

![q1-4-7-very-hard-edexcel-gcse-maths](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-18-higher/4-geometry-and-trigonometry/volume-and-surface-area/assets/033-q1-4-7-very-hard-edexcel-gcse-maths.png)

The container is a cylinder on top of a cone.
The cylinder has a radius of 3 m and a height of $h$m.
The cone has a base radius of 3 m and a vertical height of 4 m.

The container is empty.
The container is then filled with grain at a constant rate.

After 5 hours the depth of the grain is 6 metres above the vertex of the cone.
After 9 hours the container is full of grain.

Work out the value of $h$.
Give your answer as a fraction in its simplest form.
You must show all your working.
parts.solutionMd:
> *Calculate the volume of grain that is poured into the container in the first 5 hours, by adding together the volume of the cone *$\left(V = \frac{1}{3} \pi r^{2} h\right)$* and the volume of a cylinder, *$\left(V = \pi r^{2} h\right)$*, of height 2m.*

![4-7-2](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-18-higher/4-geometry-and-trigonometry/volume-and-surface-area/assets/034-4-7-2.png)

$\begin{aligned}V & = & \frac{1}{3} \pi \left(3\right)^{2} \left(4\right) + \pi \left(3\right)^{2} \left(2\right)\end{aligned}$

**For correct substitution into the volume formula for either the cone or the cylinder ****[1]**

$\begin{aligned}V & = & \frac{1}{3} \pi \times 36 + \pi \times 18 \\ & = & 12 \pi + 18 \pi\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

$\begin{aligned}V & = & 30 \pi m^{3}\end{aligned}$

> *Calculate the rate of flow of the grain by dividing the volume of grain by the time taken to pour it.*

$\begin{aligned} & & \frac{30 \pi}{5} \\ & = & 6 \pi m^{3} h^{- 1}\end{aligned}$

> *Calculate the volume of grain that will be poured in 4 hours by multiplying the rate of flow of the grain by 4.*

$\begin{aligned} & & 6 \pi \times 4 \\ & = & 24 \pi m^{3}\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *The grain poured in the last 4 hours will just fill the remainder of the cylinder, so calculate the height of the remainder of the cylinder that is filled by substituting the volume into the formula for the volume of a cylinder.*

$\begin{aligned}24 \pi & = & \pi \left(3\right)^{2} h\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

$\begin{aligned}24 \pi & = & 9 \pi h \\ \frac{24}{9} & = & h \\ h & = & \frac{8}{3} m\end{aligned}$

> *Work out the value of *$h$* by adding together the height of the cylindrical parts from the two volumes.*

$\begin{aligned}h & = & 2 + \frac{8}{3}\end{aligned}$

$\frac{14}{3}m$* ***[1]**

**Leave your working in terms of **$π$** throughout, in a non-calculator paper question it will frequently cancel out.**

The solid cylinder has a base radius of 3 cm and a height of $h$ cm.

The total surface area of the cylinder is twice the total surface area of the sphere.

Work out the ratio of the volume of the sphere to the volume of the cylinder.
Give your answer in its simplest form.
You must show all your working.
parts.solutionMd:
> *Calculate the surface area of the sphere, using the formula: *$A=4πr^{2}$*.*

$\begin{aligned}A_{s p h} & = & 4 \pi \left(6\right)^{2} \\ & = & 144 \pi cm^{2}\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Double the surface area of the sphere to work out the surface area of the cylinder.*

$A_{cyl}=144π\times2=288π\mathrm{cm}^{2}$

**[1]**

> *Using the formula for the surface area of a cylinder *$\left(A = 2 \pi r^{2} + 2 \pi r h\right)$*, calculate the height of the cylinder.*

$\begin{aligned}288 \pi & = & 2 \pi \left(3\right)^{2} + 2 \pi \left(3\right) h \\ 288 \pi & = & 18 \pi + 6 \pi h \\ 270 \pi & = & 6 \pi h \\ \frac{270}{6} & = & h \\ h & = & 45 cm\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Calculate the volume of the sphere, using the formula: *$V=\frac{4}{3}πr^{3}$*.*

$\begin{aligned}V_{s p h} & = & \frac{4}{3} \pi \left(6\right)^{3} \\ & = & 288 \pi cm^{3}\end{aligned}$

> *Calculate the volume of the cylinder, using the formula: *$V=πr^{2}h$*.*

$\begin{aligned}V_{c y l} & = & \pi \left(3\right)^{2} \left(45\right) \\ & = & 405 \pi cm^{3}\end{aligned}$

**Correct expression for the volume of the sphere and the cylinder**** [1]**

> *Find the ratio of the volume of the sphere to the volume of the cylinder.*

$\begin{aligned} & & 288 \pi : 405 \pi\end{aligned}$

> *Simplify.*

$\begin{aligned} & & 288 : 405\end{aligned}$

$32:45$* ***[1]**

parts.problemMd:

Water from 3 water tankers is going to be put into the pool.

Sam thinks that the surface of the water in the pool will be 10 cm below the top of the pool.

Is Sam correct?

(1 m<sup>3</sup> = 1000 litres)
parts.solutionMd:
> *The volume of the swimming pool can be calculated by finding the cross-sectional area and multiplying it by the width of the pool as it is a prism.*

> *Split the cross-sectional area into a rectangle and a trapezium.*

![4-7-3](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-18-higher/4-geometry-and-trigonometry/volume-and-surface-area/assets/025-4-7-3.png)

> *Calculate the area of the rectangle, *$\left(A = l \times w\right)$*, and the area of the trapezium, *$\left(A = \frac{1}{2} \left(a + b\right) h\right)$*, then add them together to work out the cross-sectional area.*

$\begin{aligned}A & = & 1 \times 10 + \frac{1}{2} \left(6 + 2\right) \times 1\end{aligned}$

**Correct method to split up the cross-section and find the area of one part**** [1] **

**Correct complete method to find the total area of the cross-section**** [1]**

$\begin{aligned}A & = & 14 m^{2}\end{aligned}$

> *Work out the volume of the swimming pool by multiplying the cross-sectional area by the width.*

$\begin{aligned}V_{P o o l} & = & 14 \times 5\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

$\begin{aligned}V_{P o o l} & = & 70 m^{3}\end{aligned}$

> *Convert the volume of water from the three tankers from litres to m*<sup>*3*</sup>* by dividing the total number of litres by 1000.*

$\begin{aligned}V_{W a t e r} & = & \frac{20000 \times 3}{1000} \\ & = & 60 m^{3}\end{aligned}$

> *Subtract the volume of the water from the volume of the swimming pool to find out the the volume that will not be filled with water.*

$\begin{aligned}V_{E m p t y} & = & 70 - 60 \\ & = & 10 m^{3}\end{aligned}$

> *Assuming that the part of the swimming pool that is not filled by water is a cuboid, with length 10 m and width 5 m, calculate the height of the cuboid.*

![4-7-4](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-18-higher/4-geometry-and-trigonometry/volume-and-surface-area/assets/026-4-7-4.png)

$\begin{aligned}10 & = & 10 \times 5 \times h\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

$\begin{aligned}10 & = & 50 h \\ h & = & 0 . 2 m\end{aligned}$

**Sam is incorrect****, the surface of the water will be ****20 cm**** below the top of the pool ****[1]**

parts.problemMd:
A frustum is made by removing a small cone from a large cone as shown in the diagram.

![q4-4-7-very-hard-edexcel-gcse-maths](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-18-higher/4-geometry-and-trigonometry/volume-and-surface-area/assets/022-q4-4-7-very-hard-edexcel-gcse-maths.png)

The frustum is made from glass. 
The glass has a density of 2.5 g / cm<sup>3</sup>

Work out the mass of the frustum. 
Give your answer to an appropriate degree of accuracy.
parts.solutionMd:
> *Find the radius of the large cone, given that the radius is half of the diameter.*

$\begin{aligned}r & = & \frac{12}{2} \\ & = & 6 cm\end{aligned}$

> *Calculate the volume of the large cone, using the formula: *$V=\frac{1}{3}πr^{2}h$*, where *$r$* is the radius of the cone and *$h$* is the perpendicular height.*

$\begin{aligned}V_{L} & = & \frac{1}{3} \times \pi \times 6^{2} \times 15\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

$\begin{aligned}V_{L} & = & 180 \pi cm^{3}\end{aligned}$

> *Work out the height of the small cone by subtracting the height of the frustum from the height of the large cone.*

$h=15-10=5\mathrm{cm}$

> *The large and small cones are similar objects. *
*Work out the length scale factor (LSF) by dividing the height of the large cone by the height of the small cone.*

$\mathrm{LSF}=\frac{15}{5}=3$

> *Divide the radius of the large cone by the LSF to work out the radius of the small cone.*

$\begin{aligned}r & = & \frac{6}{3} \\ & = & 2 cm\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Calculate the volume of the small cone.*

$V_{S}=\frac{1}{3}\timesπ\times2^{2}\times5$

$V_{S}=\frac{20}{3}π\mathrm{cm}^{3}$

> *Work out the volume of the frustum by subtracting the volume of the small cone from the volume of the large cone.*

$\begin{aligned}V & = & 180 \pi - \frac{20}{3} \pi\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

$\begin{aligned}V & = & \frac{520}{3} \pi cm^{3}\end{aligned}$

> *Calculate the mass of the frustum by multiplying the density of the glass by the volume of the frustum, *$\left(M a s s = D e n s i t y \times V o l u m e\right)$*.*

$M=2.5\times\frac{520}{3}π$

**[1]**

$M=1361.35681...g$

> *The dimensions of the object and the density are given to an accuracy of 2 significant figures, so this would be a suitable accuracy to round the final answer to.*

$1400g$* ***[1]**

**Answers rounded to 1400, 1360 or 1361 will be accepted**

parts.solutionMd:
> *Calculate the length of the slant height of the cone by applying Pythagoras' theorem, *$a^{2}+b^{2}=c^{2}$*, to the right-angled triangle involving the slant height, the radius and the perpendicular height of the cone.*

![4-7-18](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-18-higher/4-geometry-and-trigonometry/volume-and-surface-area/assets/029-4-7-18.png)

$\begin{aligned}\left(16 x\right)^{2} + \left(12 x\right)^{2} & = & l^{2} \\ 256 x^{2} + 144 x^{2} & = & l^{2} \\ 400 x^{2} & = & l^{2} \\ l & = & 20 x\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Substitute the value of the surface area of the cone along with the algebraic expressions for the slant height and the radius into the formula for the surface area of the cone.*

$2160π=π\times12x\times20x$

**[1]**

> *Solve to find the value of *$x$*.*

$\begin{aligned}2160 \pi & = & 240 \pi x^{2} \\ 2160 & = & 240 x^{2} \\ 9 & = & x^{2} \\ x & = & 3\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Substitute the relevant values into the formula for the volume of a cone, *$V=\frac{1}{3}πr^{2}h$*.*

$V = \frac{1}{3} \times \left(12 \times 3\right)^{2} \times \left(16 \times 3\right)$

**[1]**

> *Solve to find the volume.*

$V=20736π\mathrm{cm}^{3}$

> *Write down the value of **V.*

$20736$** [1]*** *

parts.problemMd:
A solid is made by putting a hemisphere on top of a cone.

![q6-1-4-7-very-hard-edexcel-gcse-maths](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-18-higher/4-geometry-and-trigonometry/volume-and-surface-area/assets/035-q6-1-4-7-very-hard-edexcel-gcse-maths.png)

The total height of the solid is $5x.$

The radius of the base of the cone is $x.$

The radius of the hemisphere is $x.$

![q6-2-4-7-very-hard-edexcel-gcse-maths](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-18-higher/4-geometry-and-trigonometry/volume-and-surface-area/assets/036-q6-2-4-7-very-hard-edexcel-gcse-maths.png)

A cylinder has the same volume as the solid.
The cylinder has radius $2x$ and height $h.$
All measurements are in centimetres.

Find a formula for $h$ in terms of $x.$
Give your answer in its simplest form.
parts.solutionMd:
> *Find an expression for the volume of the hemisphere in terms of *$x$*, by substituting the expression for the radius, *$r$*, into the formula for the volume of a sphere, *$V=\frac{4}{3}πr^{3}$*, and multiplying the result by *$\frac{1}{2}$*.*

$\begin{aligned}V_{h e m i s p h e r e} & = & \frac{1}{2} \times \frac{4}{3} \times \pi \times x^{3}\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

$\begin{aligned}V_{h e m i s p h e r e} & = & \frac{2}{3} \pi x^{3}\end{aligned}$

> *Write down the perpendicular height, *$h$*, of the cone.*

$\begin{aligned}h & = & 5 x - x \\ & = & 4 x\end{aligned}$

> *Find an expression for the volume of the cone in terms of *$x$*, using the formula for the volume of a cone: *$V=\frac{1}{3}πr^{2}h$*.*

$V_{cone}=\frac{1}{3}\timesπ\timesx^{2}\times4x$

> *Calculate the total volume of the solid by adding together the volume of the hemisphere and the cone.*

$\begin{aligned}V_{t o t a l} & = & \frac{2}{3} \pi x^{3} + \frac{4}{3} \pi x^{3}\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

$\begin{aligned}V_{t o t a l} & = & 2 \pi x^{3} cm^{3}\end{aligned}$

*Find an expression for the volume of the cylinder, using the formula for the volume of a cylinder: *$V=πr^{2}h$.

$V_{c y l i n d e r} = \pi \times \left(2 x\right)^{2} \times h$

**[1]**

$V_{cylinder}=4x^{2}πh$

> *The cylinder has the same volume as the solid, so make the two volumes equal and rearrange to find an expression for the perpendicular height in terms of *$x$*. *

$\begin{aligned}2 \pi x^{3} & = & 4 x^{2} \pi h\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

$\begin{aligned}2 x^{3} & = & 4 x^{2} h \\ \frac{1}{2} x^{3} & = & x^{2} h\end{aligned}$

$h=\frac{1}{2}x$* ***[1]**

parts.problemMd:
A frustum is made by removing a small cone from a large cone. The cones are mathematically similar.

![q16-paper1h-june2018-edexcel-igcse-maths](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-18-higher/4-geometry-and-trigonometry/volume-and-surface-area/assets/015-q16-paper1h-june2018-edexcel-igcse-maths.png)

The large cone has base radius $r$ cm and height $h$ cm. Given that

$\frac{\mathrm{volume} \mathrm{of} \mathrm{frustum}}{\mathrm{volume} \mathrm{of} \mathrm{large} \mathrm{cone}}=\frac{98}{125}$

find an expression, in terms of $h$, for the height of the frustum.

....................................................... cm
parts.solutionMd:
> *First sketch a diagram of a side view of the cones and frustum. We will let the height of the frustum be *$f$*, the height of the small cone be *$H$* and the radius of the small cone be *$R$

![edexcel-tq-mis-area-and-volume-similar-shapes-vh-5](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-18-higher/4-geometry-and-trigonometry/volume-and-surface-area/assets/016-edexcel-tq-mis-area-and-volume-similar-shapes-vh.png)

> *We need *$f$* and we can see that *$f=h-H$*. So we need *$H$* in terms of *$h$

> *If *$\frac{98}{125}$* represents the fraction of the large cone that the frustum occupies, then the fraction of the large cone that the small cone occupies is *

$1-\frac{98}{125}=\frac{27}{125}$

**[1]**

> *This *$\frac{27}{125}$* is effectively the scale factor of the small cone to the large cone*

> *Therefore if we cube root *$\frac{27}{125}$*, we have the length scale factor of the small cone to the large cone*

$\sqrt[3]{\frac{27}{125}} = \frac{3}{5}$

**[1]**

> *Therefore *

$H=\frac{3}{5}h$

> *And*

$\begin{aligned}f & = & h - H \\ & = & h - \frac{3}{5} h\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

**The height of the frustum is **$\begin{aligned} & & \frac{2}{5} \mathbf{\mathit{h}}\end{aligned}$** ****[1]**

parts.problemMd:
Here is a sector, $AOB$ , of a circle with centre $O$and angle $AOB$= $x^{\circ}$

![q26-4ma1-2h-qp-jan20-paper2-igcse-maths](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-18-higher/4-geometry-and-trigonometry/volume-and-surface-area/assets/008-q26-4ma1-2h-qp-jan20-paper2-igcse-maths.png)

The sector can form the curved surface of a cone by joining $OA$to $OB$ .

![q26-14ma1-2h-qp-jan20-paper2-igcse-maths](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-18-higher/4-geometry-and-trigonometry/volume-and-surface-area/assets/009-q26-14ma1-2h-qp-jan20-paper2-igcse-maths.png)

The height of the cone is $25\mathrm{cm}$.
The volume of the cone is $1600\mathrm{cm}^{3}$

Work out the value of $x.$ 
Give your answer correct to the nearest whole number.

$x=$.......................
parts.solutionMd:
> *The formula for the volume of a cone, *$V=\frac{1}{3}πr^{2}h$*, is given at the beginning of the paper. Use the formula with the given volume of the cone to find the value of the radius of the base circle. *

> *Using the known volume of 1600 cm*<sup>*3*</sup>* we can write the following equation.*

$\frac{1}{3}\timesπ\timesr^{2}\times25=1600$

**[1]**

> *Divide both sides by 25 and *$\frac{1}{3}π$*.*

$\frac{1}{3}πr^{2}=\frac{1600}{25}=64$

$r^{2}=\frac{64}{\frac{π}{3}}=\frac{192}{π}=61.11549...$

> *Square root both sides.*

$r=\sqrt{61.11549...}=7.817640...$

**[1]**

> *The formula for the curved surface area of a cone, *$πrl$* , is given at the beginning of the paper.*

> *Use Pythagoras' Theorem to find the value of *$l$*, the slant height of the cone. *

![ed-igcse-arcs-and-sectors-vh-q6-diagram-1](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-18-higher/4-geometry-and-trigonometry/volume-and-surface-area/assets/010-ed-igcse-arcs-and-sectors-vh-q6-diagram-1.png)

> *It is a right angled triangle so you can use Pythagoras' Theorem: *$a^{2}+b^{2}=c^{2}$*, where **c** is the length of the hypotenuse (the slant height) and **a** and **b **are the height and the radius. *

$\begin{aligned}l^{2} & = & 7 . 81764 . . .^{2} + 25^{2} \\ l & = & \sqrt{7 . 81764 . . .^{2} + 25^{2}} \\ & = & 26 . 193806 . . .\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Substitute the values of *$l$* and *$r$* into the formula for the curved surface area of a cone.*

$\begin{aligned}C S A & = & \pi r l = \pi \left(7 . 817640 . . .\right) \left(26 . 193806 . . .\right) = 643 . 313706 . . .\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *The area of the sector is equal to the curved surface area of the cone. Use the formula for area of a sector *$\frac{θ}{360^{\circ}}\timesπr^{2}$*, where the radius of the sector is equal to the slant height of the cone, to find the value of the angle, *$x$*.*

$\frac{x}{360} \times \pi \times \begin{aligned} & & 26\end{aligned} \begin{aligned} & & .\end{aligned} \begin{aligned} & & 193806\end{aligned} . . .^{2} = \begin{aligned} & & 643\end{aligned} \begin{aligned} & & .\end{aligned} \begin{aligned} & & 313706\end{aligned} \begin{aligned} & & .\end{aligned} \begin{aligned} & & .\end{aligned} \begin{aligned} & & .\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Rearrange and solve to find *$x$*.*

$\begin{aligned}\frac{x}{360} & = & \frac{643 . 313706 . . .}{ 26 . 193806 . . .^{2} \times \pi } \\ \frac{x}{360} & = & 0 . 298452 . . . \\ x & = & 0 . 298452 . . . \times 360 = 107 . 4430 . . .\end{aligned}$

$x=107^{\circ}$ **[1]**

**Rounded to 3 significant figures 107 - 108 allowed**

parts.problemMd:
A solid, $S$, is made from a hemisphere and a cylinder.

The centre of the circular face of the hemisphere and the centre of the top face of the cylinder are at the same point.

![q17-4ma1-1h-qp-jan21-paper1-igcse-maths](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-18-higher/4-geometry-and-trigonometry/volume-and-surface-area/assets/032-q17-4ma1-1h-qp-jan21-paper1-igcse-maths.png)

The radius of the cylinder and the radius of the hemisphere are both $x$ cm.

The height of the cylinder is $(20--4x)\mathrm{cm}.$

The volume of $S$ is $V$cm<sup>3</sup> where $V=\frac{1}{3}πy$

Find the maximum value of $y$. 
Show clear algebraic working.
parts.solutionMd:
> *Find the volume of S by adding together the volume of a cylinder ("*$V=πr^{2}h$*") and the volume of the hemisphere (half the volume of a sphere so "*$V=\frac{1}{2}\times\frac{4}{3}πr^{3}$*").*

$V = \pi \left(x\right)^{2} \left(20 - 4 x\right) + \frac{1}{2} \left(\frac{4}{3} \pi \left(x\right)^{3}\right)$

**[1]**

> *Equate this to the given expression for the volume of S, and simplify to make things easier.*

$\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3} \pi y & = & \pi \left(x\right)^{2} \left(20 - 4 x\right) + \frac{1}{2} \left(\frac{4}{3} \pi \left(x\right)^{3}\right)\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

$\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{3} \pi y & = & 20 \pi x^{2} - 4 \pi x^{3} + \frac{2}{3} \pi x^{3} \\ \frac{1}{3} \pi y & = & 20 \pi x^{2} - \frac{10}{3} \pi x^{3} \\ \pi y & = & 60 \pi x^{2} - 10 \pi x^{3} \\ \cancel{\pi} y & = & 10 \cancel{\pi} x^{2} \left(6 - x\right) \\ y & = & 10 x^{2} \left(6 - x\right)\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *To find the maximum value of y we need to use differentiation.*

$\begin{aligned}y & = & 60 x^{2} - 10 x^{3} \\ \frac{d y}{d x} & = & 120 x - 30 x^{2} \\ \frac{d y}{d x} & = & 30 x \left(4 - x\right)\end{aligned}$

> *At a maximum value, *$\frac{dy}{dx}=0$*.*

$30x\left(4 - x\right)= 0$
$\cancel{x = 0} , x = 4$

**[1]**

> *Reject *$x=0$* as a solution since the radius of the hemisphere and cylinder cannot be zero! *

> *So *$x=4$* (we can assume) is the **x** value at the maximum for **y**. Substitute this into our equation for **y** in terms of **x**.*

$\begin{aligned}y & = & 10 \times 4^{2} \times \left(6 - 4\right) \\ y & = & 10 \times 16 \times 2 \\ y & = & 320\end{aligned}$

**Therefore the maximum value of ****y**** is 320*** ***[1]**

parts.problemMd:
The diagram shows a solid prism $ABCDEFGH$.

![q17-4ma1-2h-qp-jan21-paper2-igcse-maths](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-18-higher/4-geometry-and-trigonometry/volume-and-surface-area/assets/019-q17-4ma1-2h-qp-jan21-paper2-igcse-maths.png)

The trapezium $ABCD$, in which $AD$ is parallel to $BC$, is a cross section of the prism.

The base $ADEH$ of the prism is a horizontal plane.
$ADEH$ and $BCFG$ are rectangles.
The midpoint of $BC$ is vertically above the midpoint of $AD$ so that $BA=CD$.

$AD=37\mathrm{cm}$   $GF=28\mathrm{cm}$    $DE=24\mathrm{cm}$

The perpendicular distance between edges $AD$ and $BC$ is 20 $\mathrm{cm}$.

Work out the total surface area of the prism.
parts.solutionMd:
*To find the total surface area we need to find the area of the individual 2D shapes that make up the prism.* 
*There are two congruent (identical) trapeziums.*
*Two congruent rectangles making up the 'sloping' sides (left and right as we look at the diagram).*
*A rectangle for the 'top' and a different rectangle for the base.*

*It may help to draw a net of the prism.  It does not need to be accurate.* 
*We do not know the length of the sloping side so we shall call that **x** for now.*

![C6XhjQIv_edx-igcse-pptq-vol-surf-area-vh-q10](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-18-higher/4-geometry-and-trigonometry/volume-and-surface-area/assets/020-c6xhjqiv-edx-igcse-pptq-vol-surf-area-vh-q10.png)

> *So using the standard formulae for the area of trapeziums and rectangles we can write down a formula for the total surface area, **S** say, of the prism.*

$\begin{aligned}S & = & 2 \times \left(\frac{1}{2} \times 20 \times \left(37 + 28\right)\right) + 2 \times \left(24 \times x\right) + \left(24 \times 28\right) + \left(24 \times 37\right) \\ S & = & 1300 + 48 x + 672 + 888 \\ S & = & 2860 + 48 x\end{aligned}$

**Method for area of a trapezium ****[1]** 
**Method for total surface area ****[1]**

Given that the volume of the frustum is$\frac{4212}{25}π\mathrm{cm}^{3}$, work out the value of $x$ 
Show clear algebraic working.
parts.solutionMd:
> *Work out the volume of the large cone*

$V=\frac{1}{3}\timesπ\times6^{2}\times15\,V=180π$

**[M1]**

> *The ratio of the height of the small cone to the radius of the small cone will be the same as the ratio of the height of the large cone to the radius of the large cone*

$x:h=6:15$

> *Form a formula for *$x$* and *$h$

$\begin{aligned}6 h & = & 15 x \\ h & = & \frac{ 15 x}{6} \\ & = & \frac{ 5 x}{2}\end{aligned}$

**[M1]**

> *Work out an expression for the volume of the small cone*

$V=\frac{1}{3}\timesπ\timesx^{2}\timesh\,V=\frac{1}{3}\timesπ\timesx^{2}\times\frac{5}{2}x\,V=\frac{5}{6}πx^{3}$

**[M1]**

> *The volume of the frustum is the volume of the large cone subtract the volume of the small cone*

$\frac{4212}{25}π=180π-\frac{5}{6}πx^{3}$

> *Divide through by *$π$

$\frac{4212}{25}=180-\frac{5}{6}x^{3}$

**[M1]**

> *Rearrange*

$\begin{aligned}\frac{5}{6} x^{3} & = & 180 - \frac{4212}{25} \\ & = & \frac{ 288}{25}\end{aligned}$

> *Divide both sides by *$\frac{5}{6}$

$x^{3}=\frac{1728}{125}$

> *Take the cube root of both sides*

$x=\frac{12}{5}$

$x=\frac{12}{5}$

parts.solutionMd:
*The vector *$\overset{\rightarrow}{AC}$* means move from **A** to **C* *This is the same as moving from **A** to** B** to** C* * *

parts.problemMd:

parts.solutionMd:
*Use the ratio to write **AP** as a fraction of **AB**.*
 *AP** : **PB**  = 3 : 1 therefore **AP** is *$\frac{3}{3+1}$* of the length **AB**.*

$\overset{\rightarrow}{AP}=\frac{3}{4}\times\overset{\rightarrow}{AB}$

> *Use the vector for *$\overset{\rightarrow}{AB}.$

$\begin{aligned}\overset{\rightarrow}{A P} & = & \frac{3}{4} \times \left(\underline{b} - \underline{a}\right) \\ & = & \frac{3}{4} \underline{b} - \frac{3}{4} \underline{a}\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Find a path starting at **O** and ending at **P**.*

$\overset{\rightarrow}{OP}=\overset{\rightarrow}{OA}+\overset{\rightarrow}{AP}$

**[1]**

> *Substitute the expressions for the vectors.*

$\begin{aligned}\overset{\rightarrow}{O P} & = & \underline{a} + \frac{3}{4} \underline{b} - \frac{3}{4} \underline{a} \\ & = & \underline{a} - \frac{3}{4} \underline{a} + \frac{3}{4} \underline{b}\end{aligned}$

> *Simplify.*

$\begin{aligned}\overset{\rightarrow}{\mathbf{\mathit{O}} \mathbf{\mathit{P}}} & = & \frac{1}{4} \underline{\mathbf{a}} + \frac{3}{4} \underline{\mathbf{b}}\end{aligned}$ **[1]**

**Factorising is acceptable:** $\begin{aligned}\overset{\rightarrow}{O P} & = & \frac{1}{4} \left(\underline{a} + 3 \underline{b}\right)\end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned}\overset{\rightarrow}{M O} & = & - \overset{\rightarrow}{O M} \\ \overset{\rightarrow}{M N} & = & - \overset{\rightarrow}{O M} + \overset{\rightarrow}{O N} \\ \overset{\rightarrow}{M N} & = & \overset{\rightarrow}{O N} - \overset{\rightarrow}{O M}\end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned}\overset{\rightarrow}{A B} & = & 2 \overset{\rightarrow}{O N} - 2 \overset{\rightarrow}{O M} \\ & = & 2 \underline{n} - 2 \underline{m}\end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned}\overset{\rightarrow}{A B} & = & 2 \left(\underline{n} - \underline{m}\right)\end{aligned}$

$\overset{\rightarrow}{AB}=2\overset{\rightarrow}{MN}$* ***therefore ****AB**** is parallel to ****MN ****[1]**

parts.problemMd:
![q1a-hard-4-13-vectors-edexcel-gcse-maths](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-18-higher/5-vectors-and-transformation-geometry/vectors/assets/028-q1a-hard-4-13-vectors-edexcel-gcse-maths.png)

$APB$ is a triangle. 
$N$ is a point on $AP$.

$\overset{\rightarrow}{AB}=a\overset{\rightarrow}{AN}=2b\overset{\rightarrow}{NP}=b$

Find the vector $\overset{\rightarrow}{PB}$, in terms of $a$ and $b$.
parts.solutionMd:
> *Find a path starting at **P** and ending at **B** using known vectors.*

$\overset{\rightarrow}{PB}=\overset{\rightarrow}{PN}+\overset{\rightarrow}{NA}+\overset{\rightarrow}{AB}$

> *Use the property that reversing the direction of the vector is the same as multiplying it by -1.*

$\begin{aligned}\overset{\rightarrow}{P B} & = & - \overset{\rightarrow}{N P} - \overset{\rightarrow}{A N} + \overset{\rightarrow}{A B} \\ & = & - \underline{b} - 2 \underline{b} + \underline{a}\end{aligned}$

> *Simplify.*

$\overset{\rightharpoonup}{\mathbf{\mathit{P}} \mathbf{\mathit{B}}} = \underline{\mathbf{a}} - 3 \underline{\mathbf{b}}$ **[1]**

parts.problemMd:
$B$ is the midpoint of $AC$.
 $M$ is the midpoint of $PB$.

Show that $NMC$ is a straight line.
parts.solutionMd:
> *To show that three points form a straight line you need to choose two pairs of points and show that the two vectors between these points are parallel. As there are three points, the two vectors will share a common point and therefore form a straight line.*

> *Find the vector *$\overset{\rightarrow}{NM}$* by finding a path between **N** and **M**.*

$\overset{\rightarrow}{NM}=\overset{\rightarrow}{NP}+\overset{\rightarrow}{PM}$

> *M** is the midpoint of **PB** therefore *$\overset{\rightarrow}{PM}=\frac{1}{2}\times\overset{\rightarrow}{PB}.$

$\begin{aligned}\overset{\rightarrow}{N M} & = & \overset{\rightarrow}{N P} + \frac{1}{2} \times \overset{\rightarrow}{P B} \\ & = & \underline{b} + \frac{1}{2} \left(\underline{a} - 3 \underline{b}\right) \\ & = & \underline{b} + \frac{1}{2} \underline{a} - \frac{3}{2} \underline{b} \\ & = & \frac{1}{2} \underline{a} - \frac{1}{2} \underline{b} \\ & = & \frac{1}{2} \left(\underline{a} - \underline{b}\right)\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Find the vector *$\overset{\rightarrow}{MC}$* by finding a path between **M** and **C**.*

$\overset{\rightarrow}{MC}=\overset{\rightarrow}{MB}+\overset{\rightarrow}{BC}$

*M** is the midpoint of **PB** therefore *$\overset{\rightarrow}{M B} = \frac{1}{2} \times \overset{\rightarrow}{P B} = \frac{1}{2} \underline{a} - \frac{3}{2} \underline{b}$*.* *B** is the midpoint of AC therefore *$\overset{\rightarrow}{A B} = \overset{\rightarrow}{B C} = \underline{a}$*.*

$\begin{aligned}\overset{\rightarrow}{M C} & = & \frac{1}{2} \underline{a} - \frac{3}{2} \underline{b} + \underline{a} \\ & = & \frac{3}{2} \underline{a} - \frac{3}{2} \underline{b} \\ & = & \frac{3}{2} \left(\underline{a} - \underline{b}\right)\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Two vectors are parallel if one of them is a scalar multiple of the other.*

$\begin{aligned}\overset{\rightarrow}{M C} & = & \frac{3}{2} \left(\underline{a} - \underline{b}\right) = 3 \times \frac{1}{2} \left(\underline{a} - \underline{b}\right) = 3 \overset{\rightarrow}{N M} \\ & & \therefore M C \& N M are parallel\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

**NMC**** is a straight line as ****NM**** and ****MC**** are ****parallel**** lines that join at the ****common point ****M**** ****[1]**

parts.problemMd:
$S$ is the point on $PR$ such that $PS:SR$ = 1 : 3

Find $\overset{\rightarrow}{OS}$ in terms of $a$ and $b$. 
Give your answer in its simplest form.
parts.solutionMd:
*Use the ratio to write **PS** as a fraction of **PR**.* *PS** : **SR**  = 1 : 3 therefore **PS** is *$\frac{1}{1+3}$* of the length **PR**.*

$\overset{\rightarrow}{PS}=\frac{1}{4}\times\overset{\rightarrow}{PR}$

> *Use the vector for *$\overset{\rightarrow}{PR}.$

$\begin{aligned}\overset{\rightarrow}{P S} & = & \frac{1}{4} \times \left(3 \underline{b} - \underline{a}\right) \\ & = & \frac{3}{4} \underline{b} - \frac{1}{4} \underline{a}\end{aligned}$

> *Find a path starting at **O** and ending at **S**.*

$\overset{\rightarrow}{OS}=\overset{\rightarrow}{OP}+\overset{\rightarrow}{PS}$

**[1]**

> *Substitute the expressions for the vectors.*

$\begin{aligned}\overset{\rightarrow}{O S} & = & \underline{a} + \frac{3}{4} \underline{b} - \frac{1}{4} \underline{a} \\ & = & \underline{a} - \frac{1}{4} \underline{a} + \frac{3}{4} \underline{b}\end{aligned}$

> *Simplify.*

$\begin{aligned}\overset{\rightarrow}{\mathbf{\mathit{O}} \mathbf{\mathit{S}}} & = & \frac{3}{4} \underline{\mathbf{a}} + \frac{3}{4} \underline{\mathbf{b}}\end{aligned}$ **[1]**

**Factorising is acceptable:** $\begin{aligned}\overset{\rightarrow}{O P} & = & \frac{3}{4} \left(\underline{a} + \underline{b}\right)\end{aligned}$

parts.problemMd: What does your answer to part (b) tell you about the position of point $S$?

$\overset{\rightarrow}{OS}=\frac{3}{4}\overset{\rightarrow}{OT}$

**OT*** and ***OS*** are parallel with a common point ***O***, therefore ***OST*** is a straight line*

parts.problemMd:
![q3-hard-4-13-vectors-edexcel-gcse-maths](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-18-higher/5-vectors-and-transformation-geometry/vectors/assets/024-q3-hard-4-13-vectors-edexcel-gcse-maths.png)

$OAB$is a triangle.
 $\overset{\rightarrow}{OA}=5a\,\overset{\rightarrow}{OB}=2b$

$T$ is the point on $AB$such that $AT:TB=5:1$

Show that $OT$is parallel to the vector $a+2b$
parts.solutionMd:
> *Two vectors are parallel if one is scalar multiple of the other.*

> *Find the vector *$\overset{\rightarrow}{AB}$* by finding a path from **A** to **B**.*

$\overset{\rightarrow}{AB}=\overset{\rightarrow}{AO}+\overset{\rightarrow}{OB}$

> *Use the property that reversing the direction of the vector is the same as multiplying it by -1.*

$\begin{aligned}\overset{\rightarrow}{A O} & = & - \overset{\rightarrow}{O A} \\ \overset{\rightarrow}{A B} & = & - \overset{\rightarrow}{O A} + \overset{\rightarrow}{O B} \\ \overset{\rightarrow}{A B} & = & \overset{\rightarrow}{O B} - \overset{\rightarrow}{O A}\end{aligned}$

> *Use the given vectors.*

$\begin{aligned}\overset{\rightarrow}{A B} & = & 2 \underline{b} - 5 \underline{a}\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

*Use the ratio to write **AT** as a fraction of **AB**.* *AT** : **TB**  = 5 : 1 therefore **AT** is *$\frac{5}{5+1}$* of the length **AB**.*

$\overset{\rightarrow}{AT}=\frac{5}{6}\times\overset{\rightarrow}{AB}$

> *Use the vector for *$\overset{\rightarrow}{AB}.$

$\begin{aligned}\overset{\rightarrow}{A T} & = & \frac{5}{6} \times \left(2 \underline{b} - 5 \underline{a}\right) \\ & = & \frac{5}{3} \underline{b} - \frac{25}{6} \underline{a}\end{aligned}$

> *Find a path starting at **O** and ending at **T**.*

$\overset{\rightarrow}{OT}=\overset{\rightarrow}{OA}+\overset{\rightarrow}{AT}$

**[1]**

> *Substitute the expressions for the vectors.*

$\begin{aligned}\overset{\rightarrow}{O T} & = & 5 \underline{a} + \frac{5}{3} \underline{b} - \frac{25}{6} \underline{a} \\ & = & 5 \underline{a} - \frac{25}{6} \underline{a} + \frac{5}{3} \underline{b}\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Simplify.*

$\begin{aligned}\overset{\rightarrow}{O T} & = & \frac{5}{6} \underline{a} + \frac{5}{3} \underline{b}\end{aligned}$

> *Factorise out the *$\frac{5}{6}$*. It will help to write *$\frac{5}{3}$* as *$\frac{10}{6}$*.*

$\begin{aligned}\overset{\rightarrow}{O T} & = & \frac{5}{6} \underline{a} + \frac{10}{6} \underline{b} \\ & = & \frac{5}{6} \left(\underline{a} + 2 \underline{b}\right)\end{aligned}$

$\overset{\rightarrow}{\mathbf{\mathit{O}} \mathbf{\mathit{T}}} = \frac{5}{6} \left(\underline{a} + 2 \underline{b}\right)$** ****therefore ****OT**** is parallel to **$\underline{\mathbf{a}} + 2 \underline{\mathbf{b}}$** ****[1]**

parts.problemMd:
![q4a-hard-4-13-vectors-edexcel-gcse-maths](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/main/SME-ExamQuestion/igcse-maths-a-18-higher/5-vectors-and-transformation-geometry/vectors/assets/029-q4a-hard-4-13-vectors-edexcel-gcse-maths.png)

$\overset{\rightarrow}{OA}=6a$ and $\overset{\rightarrow}{OB}=6b$ 
$M$ is the midpoint of $AB$.

Write $\overset{\rightarrow}{OM}$in terms of $a$ and $b$. 
Give your answer in its simplest form.
parts.solutionMd:
> *Method 1*

> *The position vector of the midpoint of the line **AB** is found using the formula *$\frac{1}{2} \left(\overset{\rightarrow}{O A} + \overset{\rightarrow}{O B}\right)$*.*

$\overset{\rightarrow}{O M} = \frac{1}{2} \left(6 \underline{a} + 6 \underline{b}\right)$

**[1]**

> *Simplify.*

$\overset{\rightarrow}{\mathbf{\mathit{O}} \mathbf{\mathit{M}}} = 3 \underline{\mathbf{a}} + 3 \underline{\mathbf{b}}$ **[1]**

> *Method 2*

> *Find a path starting at **A** and ending at **B** using known vectors.*

$\overset{\rightarrow}{AB}=\overset{\rightarrow}{AO}+\overset{\rightarrow}{OB}$

> *Use the property that reversing the direction of the vector is the same as multiplying it by -1.*

$\begin{aligned}\overset{\rightarrow}{A O} & = & - \overset{\rightarrow}{O A} \\ \overset{\rightarrow}{A B} & = & - \overset{\rightarrow}{O A} + \overset{\rightarrow}{O B} \\ \overset{\rightarrow}{A B} & = & \overset{\rightarrow}{O B} - \overset{\rightarrow}{O A}\end{aligned}$

> *Use the given vectors.*

$\begin{aligned}\overset{\rightarrow}{A B} & = & 6 \underline{b} - 6 \underline{a}\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *M** is the midpoint of **AB** therefore *$\overset{\rightarrow}{AM}=\frac{1}{2}\times\overset{\rightarrow}{AB}$*.*

$\begin{aligned}\overset{\rightarrow}{A M} & = & \frac{1}{2} \times \left(6 \underline{b} - 6 \underline{a}\right) \\ & = & 3 \underline{b} - 3 \underline{a}\end{aligned}$

> *Find a path from **O** to **M**.*

$\begin{aligned}\overset{\rightarrow}{O M} & = & \overset{\rightarrow}{O A} + \overset{\rightarrow}{A M} \\ & = & 6 \underline{a} + 3 \underline{b} - 3 \underline{a}\end{aligned}$

> *Simplify.*

** **$\overset{\rightarrow}{\mathbf{\mathit{O}} \mathbf{\mathit{M}}} = 3 \underline{\mathbf{a}} + 3 \underline{\mathbf{b}}$** [1]**

parts.problemMd:
$N$ is the midpoint of $OB$. 
$G$ is the point on $OM$ such that $OG:GM$= 2 : 1

Show that $AGN$ is a straight line.
parts.solutionMd:
> *To show that three points form a straight line you need to choose two pairs of points and show that the two vectors between these points are parallel. As there are three points, the two vectors will share a common point and therefore form a straight line.*

> *Find the vector *$\overset{\rightarrow}{AN}$* by finding a path between **A** and **N**.*

$\overset{\rightarrow}{AN}=\overset{\rightarrow}{AO}+\overset{\rightarrow}{ON}$

> *N** is the midpoint of **OB** therefore *$\overset{\rightarrow}{ON}=\frac{1}{2}\times\overset{\rightarrow}{OB}.$* Reversing the direction of a vector is the same as multiplying the vector by -1, therefore *$\overset{\rightarrow}{AO}=-\overset{\rightarrow}{OA}.$

$\begin{aligned}\overset{\rightarrow}{A N} & = & - \overset{\rightarrow}{O A} + \frac{1}{2} \times \overset{\rightarrow}{O B} \\ & = & - 6 \underline{a} + \frac{1}{2} \times 6 \underline{b} \\ & = & - 6 \underline{a} + 3 \underline{b} \\ & = & 3 \left(- 2 \underline{a} + \underline{b}\right)\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Find the vector *$\overset{\rightarrow}{AG}$* by finding a path between **A** and **G**.*

$\overset{\rightarrow}{AG}=\overset{\rightarrow}{AO}+\overset{\rightarrow}{OG}$

> *G** splits **OM **in the ratio 2:1 therefore **OG** is *$\frac{2}{2+1}$* of the length **OM**.*

$\begin{aligned}\overset{\rightarrow}{O G} & = & \frac{2}{3} \times \overset{\rightarrow}{O M} \\ & = & \frac{2}{3} \left(3 \underline{a} + 3 \underline{b}\right) \\ & = & 2 \underline{a} + 2 \underline{b}\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Substitute in to the find vector *$\overset{\rightarrow}{AG}$*.*

$\begin{aligned}\overset{\rightarrow}{A G} & = & - \overset{\rightarrow}{O A} + \overset{\rightarrow}{O G} \\ & = & - 6 \underline{a} + 2 \underline{a} + 2 \underline{b} \\ & = & - 4 \underline{a} + 2 \underline{b} \\ & = & 2 \left(- 2 \underline{a} + \underline{b}\right)\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Two vectors are parallel if they are both scalar multiples of a common vector.*

$\begin{aligned}\overset{\rightarrow}{A N} & = & 3 \left(- 2 \underline{a} + \underline{b}\right) \& \begin{matrix} & & \overset{\rightarrow}{A G}\end{matrix} \begin{matrix} & = & \end{matrix} \begin{matrix} & & 2\end{matrix} \begin{matrix} & & \left(- 2 \underline{a} + \underline{b}\right)\end{matrix} \begin{matrix} & & \end{matrix} \begin{matrix} & & \end{matrix} \\ & & \therefore A N \& A G are parallel\end{aligned}$

**AGN**** is a straight line as ****AN**** and ****AG**** are ****parallel**** lines that have a ****common point**** ****A**** ****[1]**

$\overset{\rightarrow}{OA}=2a\,\overset{\rightarrow}{OB}=2b$

$\overset{\rightarrow}{OP}=k(3a+5b)$ where $k$ is a scalar quantity.

Find the value of $k$.
parts.solutionMd:
> *Find the vector *$\overset{\rightarrow}{AB}$* by finding a path starting at **A** and ending at **B** using known vectors.*

$\overset{\rightarrow}{AB}=\overset{\rightarrow}{AO}+\overset{\rightarrow}{OB}$

> *Use the property that reversing the direction of the vector is the same as multiplying it by -1.*

$\begin{aligned}\overset{\rightarrow}{A O} & = & - \overset{\rightarrow}{O A} \\ \overset{\rightarrow}{A B} & = & - \overset{\rightarrow}{O A} + \overset{\rightarrow}{O B} \\ \overset{\rightarrow}{A B} & = & \overset{\rightarrow}{O B} - \overset{\rightarrow}{O A}\end{aligned}$

> *Use the given vectors.*

$\begin{aligned}\overset{\rightarrow}{A B} & = & 2 \underline{b} - 2 \underline{a}\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

*Use the ratio to write **AP **as a fraction of **AB**.* *AP** : **PB**  = 5 : 3 therefore **AP** is *$\frac{5}{5+3}$* of the length **AB**.*

$\overset{\rightarrow}{AP}=\frac{5}{8}\times\overset{\rightarrow}{AB}$

> *Use the vector for *$\overset{\rightarrow}{AB}.$

$\begin{aligned}\overset{\rightarrow}{A P} & = & \frac{5}{8} \times \left(2 \underline{b} - 2 \underline{a}\right) \\ & = & \frac{5}{4} \underline{b} - \frac{5}{4} \underline{a}\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Find a path starting at **O** and ending at **P**.*

$\overset{\rightarrow}{OP}=\overset{\rightarrow}{OA}+\overset{\rightarrow}{AP}$

**[1]**

> *Substitute the expressions for the vectors.*

$\begin{aligned}\overset{\rightarrow}{O P} & = & 2 \underline{a} + \frac{5}{4} \underline{b} - \frac{5}{4} \underline{a} \\ & = & 2 \underline{a} - \frac{5}{4} \underline{a} + \frac{5}{4} \underline{b}\end{aligned}$

> *Simplify.*

$\begin{aligned}\overset{\rightarrow}{O P} & = & \frac{3}{4} \underline{a} + \frac{5}{4} \underline{b}\end{aligned}$

> *Factorise out the *$\frac{1}{4}.$

$\begin{aligned}\overset{\rightarrow}{O P} & = & \frac{1}{4} \left(3 \underline{a} + 5 \underline{b}\right)\end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned}\mathbf{\mathit{k}} & = & \frac{1}{4}\end{aligned}$ **[1]**

parts.problemMd:
Given that

$m \begin{pmatrix} 4 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}  +  n \begin{pmatrix} 5 \\ 2 \end{pmatrix}  =  \begin{pmatrix} 12 \\ 6 \end{pmatrix}$

find the value of $m$ and the value of $n$.

$m$ = .......................

$n$ = .......................
parts.solutionMd:
*This is a vector equation.* 
*m** and **n** are scalars.*

*The 'top row' would give as an equation in **m** and **n** by considering the **x**-direction of the vector.* 
*The 'bottom row' would give us an equation in **m** and **n** by considering the **y**-direction of the vector.*

$\begin{aligned}4 m + 5 n & = & 12 \\ m + 2 n & = & 6\end{aligned}$

**One for each equation ****[2]**

> *As **m** is already isolated in the second equation, the easiest method to solve these equations simultaneously would be to rearrange the second to make **m** the subject, and then substitute that into the first equation.*

$m=6-2n$

$\therefore 4 \left(6 - 2 n\right) + 5 n = 12$

**[1]**

> *Expand, simplify and solve this equation to find **n**.*

$\begin{aligned}24 - 8 n + 5 n & = & 12 \\ 24 - 3 n & = & 12 \\ 3 n & = & 12 \\ n & = & 4\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Substitute **n** = 4 into either of the original equations (second one is easiest) to find **m**.*

$\begin{aligned}m + 2 \left(4\right) & = & 6 \\ m & = & 6 - 8 \\ m & = & - 2\end{aligned}$

$\thereforem=-2,n=4$** ****[1]**

> *Find the vector *$\overset{\rightarrow}{AB}$* by finding a path starting at **A** and ending at **B** using known vectors.*

$\overset{\rightarrow}{AB}=\overset{\rightarrow}{AO}+\overset{\rightarrow}{OB}$

> *Use the property that reversing the direction of the vector is the same as multiplying it by -1.*

$\begin{aligned}\overset{\rightarrow}{A O} & = & - \overset{\rightarrow}{O A} \\ \overset{\rightarrow}{A B} & = & - \overset{\rightarrow}{O A} + \overset{\rightarrow}{O B} \\ \overset{\rightarrow}{A B} & = & \overset{\rightarrow}{O B} - \overset{\rightarrow}{O A}\end{aligned}$

> *Use the given vectors.*

$\begin{aligned}\overset{\rightarrow}{A B} & = & \underline{b} - \underline{a}\end{aligned}$

$\overset{\rightarrow}{AN}=\frac{2}{3}\times\overset{\rightarrow}{AB}$

> *Use the vector for *$\overset{\rightarrow}{AB}.$

$\begin{aligned}\overset{\rightarrow}{A N} & = & \frac{2}{3} \times \left(\underline{b} - \underline{a}\right) \\ & = & \frac{2}{3} \underline{b} - \frac{2}{3} \underline{a}\end{aligned}$

**[1]**

> *Find a path starting at **O** and ending at **N**.*

$\overset{\rightarrow}{ON}=\overset{\rightarrow}{OA}+\overset{\rightarrow}{AN}$

$\begin{aligned}\overset{\rightarrow}{\mathbf{\mathit{O}} \mathbf{\mathit{N}}} & = & \frac{1}{3} \underline{\mathbf{a}} + \frac{2}{3} \underline{\mathbf{b}}\end{aligned}$* ***[1]**

**It is acceptable to write in factorised form:*** *$\begin{aligned}\overset{\rightarrow}{O N} & = & \frac{1}{3} \left(\underline{a} + 2 \underline{b}\right)\end{aligned}$

$\begin{aligned}\overset{\rightarrow}{A B} & = & - \overset{\rightarrow}{O A} + \overset{\rightarrow}{O B} \\ & = & - \left(2 \underline{a} + \underline{b}\right) + 3 \underline{a} + 2 \underline{b} \\ & = & - 2 \underline{a} + 3 \underline{a} - \underline{b} + 2 \underline{b} \\ & = & \underline{a} + \underline{b}\end{aligned}$

> *AB** : **BC** = 2 : 5 therefore **AB** is *$\frac{2}{2+5}$* of the length of **AC**.*

$\overset{\rightarrow}{AB}=\frac{2}{7}\times\overset{\rightarrow}{AC}$

> *Rearrange to find *$\overset{\rightarrow}{AC}$*.*

$\begin{aligned}\overset{\rightarrow}{A C} & = & \frac{7}{2} \times \overset{\rightarrow}{A B} \\ & = & \frac{7}{2} \left(\underline{a} + \underline{b}\right) \\ & = & \frac{7}{2} \underline{a} + \frac{7}{2} \underline{b}\end{aligned}$

> *Find the vector *$\overset{\rightarrow}{OC}$* by finding a path from **O** to **C**.*

> *Simplify.*

$\overset{\rightarrow}{\mathbf{\mathit{O}} \mathbf{\mathit{C}}} = \frac{11}{2} \underline{\mathbf{a}} + \frac{9}{2} \underline{\mathbf{b}}$ **[1]**
